तस्मात्सर्वाणि भूतानि न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि ॥ ३० ॥
Translation: O descendant of Bharata, the soul residing within the body is eternal and cannot be destroyed. Therefore, you should not grieve for any living being.
Purport: Chapter 2, Text 30 Lord Krishna concludes this chapter by enlightening Arjuna about the eternal nature of the soul. By emphasizing the immortality of the soul and the impermanence of the body, Lord Krishna advises Arjuna, as a warrior, not to shirk his duty due to the fear of losing his revered elders, Bhishma and Drona, in battle. It is essential to understand, based on Lord Krishna's teachings, that the soul exists distinct from the physical body, and is not a byproduct of chemical reactions or material development. While violence is not promoted, it may be necessary during warfare under the guidance of divine sanction, rather than impulsively.

Chapter 2, Verse 31:
Translation: Even considering your own duty, you should not waver. O Kshatriya, there is no better engagement for you than fighting on religious principles. Therefore, there should be no hesitation on your part.
Purport: Chapter 2, Text 31 Among the four social orders, the second order is known as Kshatriya, responsible for the protection and administration of society. The term "Kshatriya" originates from the root word 'kshat,' meaning to protect. Kshatriyas are trained in combat and are skilled in the art of warfare. In the past, Kshatriyas would bravely face dangers in the forest, even challenging and fighting tigers with swords. The slain tiger would be given a royal cremation, a tradition that continued in the Jaipur state. The role of the Kshatriya involves facing and overcoming violence when necessary for religious or righteous causes.  Therefore, Kshatriyas are not meant to renounce their duties and take up the path of renunciation directly. While nonviolence may be a strategy in politics, in religious contexts, it is not always feasible. The scriptures mention that in battles, kings and warriors fighting for a righteous cause are eligible to attain heavenly realms after death, similar to how Brahmins achieve higher realms through sacrificial rituals involving animal offerings. Such acts are not considered violence, as they are performed for the benefit of all involved.  There exist two types of specific duties (sva-dharma). Until one attains liberation, fulfilling the duties according to one's body and religious principles is essential for spiritual progress. After liberation, sva-dharma transcends the material bodily concept and becomes spiritual. The duties of Brahmins and Kshatriyas are inherent to their respective natures and cannot be avoided. Sva-dharma is ordained by the Supreme Lord and will be further explained in the Fourth Chapter. These duties serve as stepping stones for spiritual realization, guiding individuals towards a higher state of consciousness.

Chapter 2, Verse 32:

Chapter 2, Verse 38:

Translation: Engage in battle without being swayed by thoughts of pleasure or pain, gain or loss, victory or defeat. By doing so, you will not incur sin.

This is highlighted in the following verse from the Srimad Bhagavatam (11.5.41):  devarshi-bhutapta-nrinam pitrinam na kinkaro nayam rini cha rajan sarvatmana yah saranam sharanyam gato mukundam parihritya kartam  "One who has completely surrendered to Krishna, Mukunda, forsaking all other duties, is no longer indebted to anyone—not the demigods, sages, relatives, humanity, or ancestors." Chapter 2, Verse 39:
Translation: "O Arjuna, I have explained this knowledge to you in terms of analytical study (Sankhya) and now listen as I elaborate on it in the context of working without attachment to the fruits of actions. By acting in this knowledge, you can liberate yourself from the bondage of karma."
Purport: Chapter 2, Text 39 The term 'Sankhya' refers to a detailed description, particularly of the true nature of the soul. On the other hand, 'Yoga' involves controlling the senses. Arjuna's reluctance to fight stemmed from a desire for personal pleasure. He considered that refraining from killing his relatives would bring him more happiness than gaining the kingdom through victory over his cousins and brothers. Both perspectives were driven by self-gratification, neglecting his duty and wisdom. Krishna sought to clarify to Arjuna that by killing the physical body, he would not harm the eternal soul within. Every individual, including the Supreme Lord, is an eternal soul. We retain our individuality even after liberation from material bondage, changing our bodily forms while preserving our essence. Lord Krishna vividly explains the relationship between the soul and the body, termed as Sankhya in the Vedic dictionary. This Sankhya is distinct from the atheistic Sankhya philosophy of Kapila. The true Sankhya philosophy was expounded by Lord Kapila in the Shrimad-Bhagavatam, emphasizing the active role of the Supreme Lord in creation. The ultimate truth is realized when a soul, after countless lifetimes of seeking enjoyment, surrenders to Lord Krishna.  Arjuna has surrendered to Krishna as his spiritual guide, and now Krishna will instruct him on buddhi-yoga, the practice of devotional service solely for the pleasure of the Lord. Buddhi-yoga involves direct communion with the Lord, residing as the Paramatma in every heart, through devotional service. Only those engaged in loving service to the Lord attain this stage of buddhi-yoga by His grace. The devotee, endowed with pure love and devotion, easily reaches the blissful abode of God.  The buddhi-yoga mentioned here signifies devotional service to the Lord, distinct from the atheistic Sankhya philosophy. One should not confuse the Sankhya mentioned here with atheistic Sankhya-yoga. Real Sankhya philosophy, as elucidated by Lord Kapila in the Shrimad-Bhagavatam, is focused on analytical understanding of the body and soul. Krishna's Sankhya and Kapila's Sankhya are essentially the same, emphasizing devotion. The distinction between Sankhya-yoga and bhakti-yoga is made by those lacking wisdom, as both paths ultimately lead to devotion. Working in Krishna consciousness, purely for His pleasure, leads to transcendental bliss and knowledge. Such engagement results in complete liberation without the need for additional endeavors for acquiring spiritual wisdom. Working in Krishna consciousness differs greatly from working for material gains or sense gratification, leading to true liberation and eternal happiness.

Chapter 2, Verse 40:

A mere one percent progress in Krishna consciousness yields lasting results, enabling the practitioner to start the next phase from two percent. Chapter 2, Verse 47:
कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन । मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि ॥
Translation: You have the right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of actions. Never consider yourself as the cause of the results of your activities, and never be attached to not doing your duty.
Purport: In this verse, three important considerations are highlighted: prescribed duties, whimsical actions, and inaction. Prescribed duties refer to activities ordained based on one's inherent material qualities. Whimsical actions are those undertaken without proper authorization, and inaction denotes neglecting one's prescribed duties. The Lord advises Arjuna to not remain inactive but to fulfill his duties without attachment to the outcomes. Being attached to the fruits of one's labor makes one the instigator of the action, leading to either enjoyment or suffering of the results.  Prescribed duties can be categorized into three types: regular duties, duties in emergencies, and desired activities. Regular duties performed as obligations according to scriptural injunctions, without craving for results, are considered actions in the mode of goodness. Actions motivated by desire for results lead to bondage and are therefore inauspicious. While everyone has the right to perform their prescribed duties, they should do so without attachment to the outcomes, as such selfless obligatory actions undoubtedly guide one towards liberation.  Arjuna is counseled by the Lord to engage in battle as a duty without being attached to the results. His reluctance to participate in the war stems from attachment, which hinders the path to salvation. Any form of attachment, whether positive or negative, binds an individual. Inaction is deemed sinful, hence fighting dutifully was the sole righteous path to salvation for Arjuna.""" Chapter 2, Text 47 """

Translation: One who remains undisturbed in the midst of sorrows, unattached in happiness, free from cravings, fears, and anger, is known as a sage of steady wisdom.

As stated in the Mahabharata, "A sage is one whose views do not differ from those of other sages." However, a "sthita-dhir muni," as described here by Lord Krishna, transcends the ordinary sage. This sage is perpetually absorbed in Krishna consciousness, having exhausted all speculative endeavors. Such a sage is known as "prashanta-nihshesha-mano-rathantara," indicating one who has transcended mental speculations and firmly believes that Lord Krishna, or Vasudeva, is the supreme reality. This sage is resolute in mind. Fully absorbed in Krishna consciousness, he remains unperturbed by the onslaught of life's tribulations, seeing them as the mercy of the Lord. He humbly accepts any suffering as just recompense for past misdeeds, viewing his troubles as minimized by the Lord's grace. Likewise, in times of joy, he attributes his happiness solely to the Lord's benevolence, feeling unworthy of such bliss. Recognizing that his comfort and ability to serve the Lord are gifts from the Divine, he remains fearless and active in the Lord's service, unaffected by attachment or aversion. Attachment involves seeking gratification for oneself, while detachment is the absence of such self-centered desires. However, a Krishna-conscious individual transcends both attachment and detachment, dedicating their life to the service of the Lord. Thus, such a person remains undisturbed even in the face of failure. Whether successful or not, a Krishna-conscious soul remains steadfast in their resolve.``` Chapter 2, Text 56 ```

Chapter 2, Verse 57:
यः सर्वत्रानभिस्नेहस्तत्तत्प्राप्य शुभाशुभम् । नाभिनन्दति न द्वेष्टि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥
Translation: One who remains unaffected by whatever good or evil comes his way, neither praising nor despising it, is firmly established in true wisdom.
Purport: In this material realm, there are constant fluctuations of good and evil. However, a person who remains undisturbed by these external circumstances, who neither overly celebrates good fortune nor abhors misfortune, is truly anchored in the consciousness of the Supreme. The material world is inherently dualistic, offering both positive and negative experiences. Yet, one who is absorbed in the awareness of the Supreme Lord remains untouched by these dualities, as their focus is solely on the all-good Absolute, Krishna. This unwavering Krishna consciousness places one in a state of perfect transcendence known as samadhi.``` Chapter 2, Text 57 ```

Chapter 2, Verse 58:
यदा संहरते चायं कूर्मोऽङ्गानीव सर्वशः ।
इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥ ५८ ॥
Translation: When one can restrain the senses from their objects, just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs, their wisdom is firmly established.
Purport: Chapter 2, Text 58 The mark of a yogi, devotee, or self-realized soul is their ability to govern the senses as per their will. Most individuals, on the other hand, become slaves to their senses, allowing them to dictate their actions. This explains the state of being of a yogi. The senses are likened to poisonous serpents, inclined to act unrestrainedly. The yogi or devotee must possess great strength to control these serpents, akin to a snake charmer. They never permit the senses to act independently. The scriptures contain numerous guidelines, some instructing what not to do, while others prescribe what to do. Without adhering to these guidelines, refraining from indulging the senses, one cannot firmly establish themselves in Krishna consciousness. The tortoise serves as a perfect example here. It can retract its senses at will and extend them when necessary for specific purposes. Similarly, the senses of those devoted to Krishna are utilized solely in His service and withdrawn otherwise. Arjuna is being instructed to engage his senses in the service of the Lord rather than for personal gratification. The analogy of the tortoise underscores the significance of keeping the senses perpetually dedicated to the Lord.

Chapter 2, Verse 59:
विषया विनिवर्तन्ते निराहारस्य देहिनः । रसवर्जं रसोऽप्यस्य परं दृष्ट्वा निवर्तते ॥
Translation: While the embodied soul may refrain from indulging in sense objects, the taste for such objects persists. However, by experiencing a higher taste, one can transcend such engagements and remain steadfast in consciousness.
Purport: Without attaining a higher spiritual state, it is challenging to give up sense gratification. Trying to curb sense enjoyment through rules and regulations is akin to restricting certain foods for a sick person. The patient may not appreciate these restrictions and may still crave those foods. Similarly, spiritual practices like ashtanga-yoga, involving yama (restraints), niyama (observances), asana (postures), pranayama (breath control), pratyahara (withdrawal of senses), dharana (concentration), and dhyana (meditation), are prescribed for those with limited understanding. However, as one progresses in Krishna consciousness and experiences the divine beauty of Lord Krishna, the allure of material pleasures naturally diminishes. Restrictions are beneficial for spiritual beginners, but they become obsolete once a genuine taste for Krishna consciousness is developed. A truly Krishna-conscious person loses interest in mundane pleasures as they pale in comparison to the spiritual bliss derived from connecting with the Supreme Lord.``` Chapter 2, Text 59 ```

Chapter 2, Verse 60:
यततो ह्यपि कौन्तेय पुरुषस्य विपश्चितः ।
इन्द्रियाणि प्रमाथीनि हरन्ति प्रसभं मनः ॥ ६० ॥
Translation: The senses, O Arjuna, are turbulent and powerful. They can forcibly carry away the mind of even a person of discrimination who is striving to control them.
Purport: Chapter 2, Text 60 Despite the efforts of many learned sages, philosophers, and transcendentalists to conquer the senses, even the most accomplished among them can sometimes succumb to material sense gratification due to the restless nature of the mind. For instance, the great sage and yogi Vishvamitra was enticed by Menaka into indulging in sensual pleasures, despite his rigorous penances and yoga practices aimed at sense control. Such instances are not uncommon in history.  Thus, it is extremely challenging to restrain the mind and senses without being fully absorbed in Krishna consciousness. Without directing the mind towards Krishna, one cannot easily renounce material entanglements. This is illustrated by the words of Sri Yamunacharya, a revered saint and devotee:  "Since my mind has been engrossed in serving the lotus feet of Lord Krishna, relishing ever-fresh transcendental bliss, the mere thought of engaging in sexual activities with a woman repulses me, causing me to turn away and reject such desires."  Krishna consciousness is so sublime that material enjoyment loses its allure. It is akin to a starving person being completely satisfied by a nourishing meal. Maharaja Ambarisha overcame the challenge posed by the great yogi Durvasa Muni simply because his mind was absorbed in Krishna consciousness.

Chapter 2, Verse 61:
तानि सर्वाणि संयम्य युक्त आसीत मत् परः । वशे हि यस्येन्द्रियाणि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥
Translation: One who restrains all the senses and remains connected with Me is considered to have steady wisdom.
Purport: This verse clearly elucidates that the pinnacle of yoga perfection is Krishna consciousness. Controlling the senses is only achievable through Krishna consciousness. For instance, the sage Durvasa Muni, due to pride, failed to control his senses and quarreled with Maharaja Ambarisha. In contrast, the king, though not as adept in yoga as the sage, triumphed by silently enduring the sage’s unjust behavior. The king's sense control stemmed from his devotion to the Lord, as evidenced in Srimad-Bhagavatam (9.4.18–20).  King Ambarisha directed his mind to Lord Krishna's lotus feet, spoke of the Lord's divine qualities, engaged in temple service, listened to the Lord’s pastimes, beheld the Lord’s forms, associated with devotees, relished the fragrance of tulasi leaves offered to the Lord, visited holy places and temples, offered obeisances, and dedicated his desires to the Lord's mission. These qualities made him a mat-para devotee.  The term mat-para holds great significance. Maharaja Ambarisha exemplified how one can become mat-para. Srila Baladeva Vidyabhusana, a revered scholar, emphasized that devotion to Krishna empowers one to master the senses. Just as fire consumes impurities, Lord Vishnu within the yogi's heart purges all impurities. The Yoga-sutra advocates meditating on Vishnu, not emptiness. Yogis fixated on non-Vishnu entities waste their efforts. True yoga entails being Krishna conscious, devoted to the Supreme Personality of Godhead.""" Chapter 2, Text 61 ```

Chapter 2, Verse 62:
ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते । सङ्गात्सञ्जायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते ॥
Translation: While contemplating the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment for them. From such attachment, lust develops, and from lust, anger arises.
Purport: A person who is not Krishna conscious becomes entangled in material desires when contemplating sense objects. The senses naturally seek engagement, and if they are not absorbed in the transcendental loving service of the Lord, they will inevitably pursue materialistic pleasures. In the material realm, even powerful beings like Lord Shiva and Lord Brahma, not to mention other demigods in the heavenly realms, are influenced by sense objects. The only way to break free from this cycle of material existence is to awaken Krishna consciousness. For example, when Parvati tempted Lord Shiva for sensual pleasure, he succumbed, leading to the birth of Kartikeya. Similarly, the young devotee Haridasa Thakura was tested by the illusory energy of Maya, but his unwavering devotion to Lord Krishna helped him pass the test effortlessly. As Yamunacharya's verse illustrates, a sincere devotee of the Lord renounces all material sense pleasures due to their higher taste for spiritual bliss in the divine presence. This is the key to success. A person not established in Krishna consciousness, no matter how adept at controlling the senses through artificial means, is bound to falter eventually. The mere hint of sense gratification will stir up desires that are hard to resist.``` Chapter 2, Text 62 ```

Chapter 2, Verse 63:
क्रोधाद्भवति सम्मोहः सम्मोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः । स्मृतिभ्रंशाद्बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति ॥
Translation: From anger, complete delusion arises, and from delusion comes bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, intelligence is lost, and with the loss of intelligence, one falls back into the material pool.
Purport: Srila Rupa Gosvami provides us with this guidance:  "By considering things in relation to Krishna, one should give up material desires. The renunciation practiced by those who desire liberation without understanding the Lord is considered superficial."  Through the development of Krishna consciousness, one can understand that everything has a purpose in the service of the Lord. Those lacking knowledge of Krishna consciousness often try to renounce material objects artificially. As a result, despite seeking liberation from material bondage, they do not achieve true renunciation. Their renunciation is deemed superficial and lacking in significance. In contrast, a person immersed in Krishna consciousness comprehends how to utilize everything in the service of the Lord, thereby avoiding becoming entangled in material consciousness.  For instance, an impersonalist believes that the Lord, being impersonal, cannot partake in eating. Consequently, the impersonalist avoids consuming delicious offerings. In contrast, a devotee recognizes Krishna as the supreme enjoyer who partakes in all offerings made to Him with devotion. After offering delicious food to the Lord, the devotee partakes in the remnants, known as prasadam. Through this act, everything becomes sanctified, eliminating the risk of spiritual downfall.  A devotee consumes prasadam in a state of Krishna consciousness, while a non-devotee dismisses it as material. The impersonalist, due to artificial renunciation, is unable to relish life fully. Therefore, even a slight disturbance of the mind can lead them back into the cycle of material existence. It is said that such a soul, despite ascending towards liberation, falls back due to the absence of a foundation in devotional service."``` Chapter 2, Text 63 ```

Chapter 2, Verse 64:
रागद्वेषविमुक्तैस्तु विषयानिन्द्रियैश्चरन् ।
आत्मवश्यैर्विधेयात्मा प्रसादमधिगच्छति ॥ ६४ ॥
Translation: But one who is liberated from attachment and aversion, and who moves among objects with the senses under control, attains the grace of the self by self-discipline.
Purport: Chapter 2, Text 64 It has been previously explained that one may externally regulate the senses through artificial means, but unless the senses are engaged in the transcendental service of the Lord, there is a risk of downfall. Although a person in complete Krishna consciousness may appear to be operating on the sensory level, his consciousness is fixed on Krishna, and he is free from attachment to sensual activities. A Krishna conscious individual is solely focused on pleasing Krishna, transcending all forms of attachment and detachment. Such a devotee can perform actions that are typically considered undesirable if it is the will of Krishna, and refrain from actions that would bring personal satisfaction if it is not Krishna's desire. Therefore, the devotee's actions, or inactions, are guided by Krishna's will. This state of consciousness is a manifestation of the causeless mercy of the Lord, attainable by the devotee despite being situated on the sensual platform.

Chapter 2, Verse 65:
प्रसादे सर्वदुःखानां हानिरस्योपजायते ।
प्रसन्नचेतसो ह्याशु बुद्धिः पर्यवतिष्ठते ॥ ६५ ॥
Translation: By being content in Krishna consciousness, one transcends the threefold miseries of material existence. In this state of contentment, one's intelligence quickly becomes firmly established.
Purport: Chapter 2, Text 65 (Purport continues from the previous page) When the mind is fixed on the lotus feet of the Lord through the practice of devotional service, the mind is purified, leading to spiritual enlightenment. This process is the path to self-realization. Attaining the brahma-bhuta stage is only possible through engaging in devotional service. Bhakti-yoga commences when one reaches the brahma-bhuta stage. Through devotional service, one ascends to the spiritual realm, enabling a deep understanding of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

Chapter 2, Verse 66:
नास्ति बुद्धिरयुक्तस्य न चायुक्तस्य भावना ।
न चाभावयतः शान्तिरशान्तस्य कुतः सुखम् ॥ ६६ ॥
Translation: One who is not connected with the Supreme (in Krishna consciousness) cannot possess transcendental intelligence or a steady mind. Without these qualities, there can be no peace. And how can there be happiness without peace?
Purport: Chapter 2, Text 66 Peace is unattainable without Krishna consciousness. As stated in the Fifth Chapter (5.29) of the Bhagavad Gita, true peace arises when one recognizes that Krishna is the ultimate enjoyer of all sacrifices and austerities, the supreme proprietor of the entire cosmic manifestation, and the true well-wisher of all living beings. Only through this understanding can one experience genuine peace. Lack of a definitive purpose leads to mental disturbances. By acknowledging Krishna as the enjoyer, proprietor, and friend of all beings and things, one can cultivate a tranquil mind and bring about inner peace. Those who lack a relationship with Krishna are perpetually in distress and devoid of peace, regardless of any outward display of serenity or spiritual progress. Krishna consciousness naturally manifests as a state of profound peace, achievable only through a deep connection with Krishna.

Chapter 2, Verse 67:
इन्द्रियाणां हि चरतां यन्मनोऽनुविधीयते । तदस्य हरति प्रज्ञां वायुर्नावमिवाम्भसि ॥
Translation: Just as a strong wind sweeps away a boat on the water, even one of the wandering senses that the mind dwells on can steal away a person's wisdom.
Purport: Unless all the senses are dedicated to serving the Lord, indulging even one of them in sense pleasures can lead a devotee astray from the path of spiritual progress. Illustrated in the life of Maharaja Ambarisha, engaging all senses in Krishna consciousness is the key to controlling the mind effectively.""" Chapter 2, Text 67 """

Chapter 2, Verse 68:
तस्माद्यस्य महाबाहो निगृहीतानि सर्वशः । इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥
Translation: Therefore, O mighty-armed one, the person who restrains the senses from their objects possesses steady intelligence.
Purport: The senses can be controlled through Krishna consciousness, where all the senses are engaged in loving service to the Lord. Just as enemies are subdued by superior force, the senses can also be controlled not by human effort, but by dedicating them to the service of the Lord. Understanding that true intelligence is established only through Krishna consciousness, and practicing this under the guidance of a genuine spiritual master, makes one a practitioner (sadhaka) suitable for liberation.``` Chapter 2, Text 68 ```

Chapter 2, Verse 69:
या निशा सर्वभूतानां तस्यां जागर्ति संयमी ।
यस्यां जाग्रति भूतानि सा निशा पश्यतो मुनेः ॥ ६९ ॥
Translation: For all beings, the night is the time of wakefulness for the self-disciplined; and for the introspective sage, the wakeful state of all beings is like night.
Purport: Chapter 2, Text 69 There are two categories of intelligent individuals: those who are intelligent in pursuing material pleasures for gratification of the senses, and those who are introspective and focused on self-realization. The activities of the introspective sage, or the contemplative individual, are like night for those engrossed in material pursuits. Materialistic individuals remain spiritually asleep in such a night due to their lack of awareness about self-realization. The introspective sage remains vigilant in the "night" of materialistic individuals. The sage experiences transcendental joy in the gradual progress of spiritual growth, while the materialistic person, who is oblivious to self-realization, dreams of various sensory pleasures, oscillating between happiness and distress in their dreamlike state. The introspective individual remains unaffected by the fleeting pleasures and pains of the material world, continuing their journey of self-realization undisturbed by material circumstances.

Chapter 2, Verse 70:
आपूर्यमाणमचलप्रतिष्ठं समुद्रमापः प्रविशन्ति यद्वत् । तद्वत्कामा यं प्रविशन्ति सर्वे स शान्तिमाप्नोति न कामकामी ॥
Translation: Just as rivers continuously flow into the ocean, yet it remains undisturbed, filled to the brim, one who is unperturbed by the constant influx of desires attains true peace; not the one who seeks to fulfill those desires.
Purport: The ocean, always brimming with water, receives even more during the rainy season, yet it remains calm and within its bounds. Similarly, a person established in Krishna consciousness is unperturbed by the ongoing demands of the material body for sense gratification. Such a devotee, content in the Lord's service, resembles the ocean, self-sufficient and undisturbed. Though desires may approach like rivers into the ocean, a Krishna conscious person remains unwavering, untouched by material cravings. This steadfastness in devotion indicates true Krishna consciousness—a state where material desires no longer hold sway. While others endlessly chase fulfillment, whether through fruitive activities, salvation, or mystic powers, they remain discontent. In contrast, a Krishna conscious soul finds joy in serving the Lord, devoid of worldly desires, even uninterested in liberation from material bondage. The devotees of Krishna, free from material longings, dwell in perfect peace.``` Chapter 2, Text 70 ```

Chapter 2, Verse 71:
विहाय कामान्यः सर्वांश्चरति निःस्पृहः ।
निर्ममो निरहङ्कारः स शान्तिमधिगच्छति ॥ ७१ ॥
Translation: One who renounces all desires for sense gratification, lives free from attachment, gives up all sense of ownership, and is free from false ego, attains true peace.
Purport: Chapter 2, Text 71 To be desireless means to not crave sense pleasures. True desirelessness is the aspiration for Krishna consciousness. Recognizing oneself as an eternal servant of Krishna, without identifying with the material body or claiming ownership of anything, signifies the pinnacle of Krishna consciousness. In this state, one understands that as Krishna is the ultimate owner, everything should be utilized for His pleasure. Arjuna exemplified this by fighting not for his own sake, but out of devotion to Krishna's will. True desirelessness is not the elimination of desires, but rather desiring to please Krishna. A spiritually mature individual recognizes that everything belongs to Krishna (isavasyam idam sarvam) and refrains from falsely claiming possession. This transcendental wisdom arises from self-realization, understanding that every living being is an eternal fragment of Krishna in essence, never equal to or greater than Him. This fundamental understanding of Krishna consciousness is the key to experiencing genuine peace.

Chapter 2, Verse 72:
एषा ब्राह्मी स्थितिः पार्थ नैनां प्राप्य विमुह्यति । स्थित्वास्यामन्तकालेऽपि ब्रह्मनिर्वाणमृच्छति ॥
Translation: This is the transcendental state, O Partha, in which one is not deluded. Even at the time of death, one who is established in this state attains the realm of Brahman.
Purport: Krishna consciousness, or divine life, can be attained in an instant or may elude one even after countless births. It all hinges on understanding and embracing this truth. King Khatvanga achieved this state moments before his passing by surrendering to Krishna. Nirvana signifies the cessation of the cycle of material existence. While Buddhist philosophy posits emptiness after worldly life, the Bhagavad-gita presents a different view. True life commences post-material existence. For a materialist, knowing that the materialistic way of life must end suffices. Yet, for those spiritually evolved, there exists a life beyond this material realm. If one becomes Krishna conscious before departing, they immediately reach the stage of brahma-nirvana. The kingdom of God and the service of the Lord are indistinguishable, as both exist on the absolute plane. Engaging in transcendental loving service of the Lord equates to entering the spiritual kingdom. Material life revolves around sense gratification, while the spiritual realm centers on Krishna consciousness. Attaining Krishna consciousness in this lifetime equates to instant realization of Brahman, and one entrenched in Krishna consciousness has already entered God's kingdom.  Brahman stands in stark contrast to matter. Thus, brahmi sthiti denotes being beyond material pursuits. Devotional service to the Lord is deemed liberation in the Bhagavad-gita (sa gunan samatityaitan brahma-bhuyaya kalpate), signifying liberation from material bondage.  Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura encapsulated the essence of the Second Chapter of the Srimad Bhagavad-gita as the crux of the entire scripture. Within the Bhagavad-gita, the topics of karma-yoga, jnana-yoga, and bhakti-yoga are expounded. The Second Chapter specifically delves into karma-yoga and jnana-yoga, offering a glimpse of bhakti-yoga as the overarching theme of the text.  Thus concludes the Bhaktivedanta Purports to the Second Chapter of the Srimad Bhagavad-gita, expounding on its central teachings. ``` Chapter 2, Text 72 ```

Chapter 3, Verse 1:
अर्जुन उवाच ज्यायसी चेत्कर्मणस्ते मता बुद्धिर्र्र्नादन । तत्किं कर्मणि घोरे मां नियोजयसि केशव ॥
Translation: Arjuna said: O Janardana, O Keshava, if You think intelligence is superior to fruitive work, then why do You want to engage me in this dreadful warfare?
Purport: In the previous chapter, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Sri Krishna, extensively explained the nature of the soul to His dear friend Arjuna, aiming to rescue him from the ocean of material sorrow. He recommended the path of realization: buddhi-yoga, or Krishna consciousness. Sometimes, Krishna consciousness is misunderstood as passivity, leading some to seclude themselves and chant the holy name of Lord Krishna without proper understanding. However, chanting the holy name of Krishna in isolation, seeking only superficial admiration from the public, is unwise without a foundation in the philosophy of Krishna consciousness. Arjuna, too, viewed Krishna consciousness, or buddhi-yoga, as a form of spiritual intelligence that involved retirement from active life, engaging in penance and austerity in seclusion. Essentially, he sought to evade the impending battle by using Krishna consciousness as an excuse. Yet, as a sincere disciple, he humbly sought guidance from his master, questioning Krishna about the best course of action. In response, Lord Krishna elaborately explained karma-yoga, or engaging in work with a consciousness centered on Krishna, in this Third Chapter.``` Chapter 3, Text 1 ```

Chapter 3, Verse 2:
व्यामिश्रेणेव वाक्येन बुद्धिं मोहयसीव मे । तदेकं वद निश्चित्य येन श्रेयोऽहमाप्नुयाम् ॥
Translation: My intellect is confused by Your mixed messages. Please clearly instruct me on the path that will bring me the highest good.
Purport: In the previous chapter, various paths were discussed, such as sankhya-yoga, buddhi-yoga, sense control through intelligence, selfless work, and the beginner's stage, presented in a scattered manner. To facilitate action and understanding, a more organized presentation of the path is essential. Arjuna sought clarification on these seemingly perplexing teachings to ensure they could be easily grasped without distortion by the common person. While Krishna did not intend to bewilder Arjuna with ambiguous words, Arjuna struggled to engage in Krishna consciousness, whether due to inertia or lack of active service. Through his inquiries, he paved the way for all earnest students seeking to unravel the mysteries of the Bhagavad-gita.""" Chapter 3, Text 2 """

Chapter 3, Verse 3:
श्रीभगवानुवाच लोकेऽस्मिन् द्विविधा निष्ठा पुरा प्रोक्ता मयानघ । ज्ञानयोगेन साङ्ख्यानां कर्मयोगेन योगिनाम् ॥
Translation: The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: O sinless Arjuna, I have already explained that there are two paths of self-realization in this world. Some seek to understand through philosophical speculation and the study of knowledge (sankhya-yoga), while others through the path of devotional service and action (karma-yoga).
Purport: In the Second Chapter, verse 39, the Lord delineated two approaches—sankhya-yoga and karma-yoga, also known as buddhi-yoga. Here, the Lord offers a clearer explanation. Sankhya-yoga involves analyzing the nature of spirit and matter, appealing to those inclined towards speculative understanding and philosophical study. The other group engages in Krishna consciousness, as mentioned in the 61st verse of the Second Chapter. The Lord also stated in verse 39 that through buddhi-yoga, or Krishna consciousness, one can free themselves from the bondage of action without any flaws in the process. This principle is further elucidated in verse 61, emphasizing complete dependence on the Supreme (specifically, Krishna), enabling easy control over the senses. Thus, both paths are interdependent, akin to religion and philosophy. Religion devoid of philosophy becomes mere sentiment or fanaticism, while philosophy without religion becomes mere mental speculation. The ultimate aim is Krishna, as sincere philosophers ultimately reach Krishna consciousness. This is also emphasized in the Bhagavad-gita. The essence lies in understanding the true nature of the self in relation to the Superself. The indirect path involves philosophical speculation leading gradually to Krishna consciousness, while the direct path involves immediate connection with everything through Krishna consciousness. Of the two, the path of Krishna consciousness is superior, as it does not rely on purifying the senses through a philosophical process. Krishna consciousness itself serves as the purifying process, making devotional service both easy and sublime simultaneously.``` Chapter 3, Text 3 ```

Chapter 3, Verse 4:
न कर्मणामनारम्भान्नैष्कर्म्यं पुरुषोऽश्नुते । न च सन्न्यसनादेव सिद्धिं समधिगच्छति ॥
Translation: Merely abstaining from work does not lead to freedom from reactions, nor does renunciation alone bring about perfection.
Purport: The renounced order of life should be embraced only after one has purified oneself through the performance of prescribed duties, which are designed to cleanse the hearts of materialistic individuals. Without purification, one cannot successfully transition to the fourth stage of life (sannyasa) abruptly. Contrary to the beliefs of some philosophers, renouncing all activities does not automatically elevate one to the status of Narayana. Lord Krishna does not endorse this notion. Sannyasa without a purified heart disrupts societal harmony. Conversely, engaging in transcendental service to the Lord, even without fulfilling one's prescribed duties, is accepted by the Lord through buddhi-yoga. As stated in the scriptures, "Even a little advancement on this path can protect one from great fear."``` Chapter 3, Text 4 ```

Chapter 3, Verse 5:
न हि कश्चित्क्षणमपि जातु तिष्ठत्यकर्मकृत् ।
कार्यते ह्यवशः कर्म सर्वः प्रकृतिजैर्गुणैः ॥ ५ ॥
Translation: No one can remain inactive even for a moment, as everyone is compelled to act by the qualities acquired from the modes of material nature.
Purport: Chapter 3, Text 5 The soul is inherently active, animating the lifeless body. It is the nature of the soul to constantly engage in action. In the absence of the soul, the body is inert. Thus, the soul is perpetually active and cannot cease its actions. When the soul interacts with material energy, it becomes influenced by material qualities. To cleanse the soul of these influences, one must perform prescribed duties as outlined in the scriptures. However, engaging in the devotional service of Krishna is the most effective means of purification. The Srimad-Bhagavatam (1.5.17) confirms this by stating that even if one does not strictly adhere to prescribed duties or devotional practices, there is no loss if they are devoted to Krishna. Conversely, meticulously following all regulations without Krishna consciousness is futile. Therefore, the process of purification, whether through renunciation or other means, is intended to facilitate the attainment of Krishna consciousness, the ultimate goal. Without this realization, all endeavors are deemed unsuccessful.

Chapter 3, Verse 6:
कर्मेन्द्रियाणि संयम्य य आस्ते मनसा स्मरन् ।
इन्द्रियार्थान्विमूढात्मा मिथ्याचारः स उच्यते ॥ ६ ॥
Translation: One who restrains the senses of action but allows the mind to dwell on sense objects deludes oneself and is known as a hypocrite.
Purport: Chapter 3, Text 6 There are many hypocrites who avoid engaging in Krishna consciousness and instead pretend to meditate, all the while indulging in thoughts of sense enjoyment. These hypocrites may also engage in dry philosophical discussions to deceive others, but as per this verse, they are the most deceitful. While one may engage in any social role for sense gratification, true progress in purifying one's existence comes from following the prescribed duties of one's station. However, someone who pretends to be a yogi while secretly seeking sensual pleasures is the ultimate deceiver, even if they speak eloquently on philosophy. Their knowledge holds no value, as the illusory energy of the Lord nullifies the effects of a sinful person's knowledge. Such a hypocrite's mind remains impure, rendering their so-called yogic meditation completely futile.

Chapter 3, Verse 7:
यस्त्विन्द्रियाणि मनसा नियभ्यारभतेsर्जुन। कर्मेन्द्रियैः कर्मयोगमसक्तः स विशिष्यते॥
Translation: On the other hand, Arjuna, one who controls the senses with the mind and engages in the yoga of action without attachment excels.
Purport: Instead of adopting a superficial spiritual persona for the sake of indulging in sense pleasures, it is far more beneficial to carry out one's duties and fulfill life's purpose, which is to break free from material entanglement and attain the spiritual realm. The ultimate self-interest is to attain Vishnu. The varna and ashrama systems are established to guide individuals towards this ultimate goal. Even householders can achieve this by engaging in regulated service in devotion to Krishna. By living a disciplined life as prescribed in the scriptures, one can progress on the path of self-realization without attachment to material pursuits. A sincere individual following this path is in a superior position compared to a deceitful spiritual pretender who uses spirituality to deceive the unsuspecting. A sincere street sweeper is more honorable than a charlatan meditator who meditates solely for personal gain.``` Chapter 3, Text 7 ```

Chapter 3, Verse 8:
नियतं कुरु कर्म त्वं कर्म ज्यायो ह्यकर्मणः । शरीरयात्रापि च ते न प्रसिद्ध्येदकर्मणः ॥
Translation: Perform your prescribed duties, for doing so is better than inaction. Even to maintain your physical body, you must engage in work.
Purport: There are many pseudo-meditators who falsely claim high birth and many professionals who pretend to have renounced everything for spiritual advancement. Lord Krishna did not want Arjuna to be a hypocrite. Instead, the Lord advised Arjuna to fulfill his duties as a warrior according to his caste. Arjuna was a householder and a warrior, so it was best for him to fulfill his duties as prescribed for a warrior-householder. These actions gradually purify the heart of a worldly person and free them from material contamination. Renunciation for mere sustenance is not approved by the Lord or any scripture. Everyone must sustain their body and soul through work. One should not abandon work whimsically without purifying their material desires. In the material world, everyone has the impure desire to control material nature for sense gratification. These impure desires must be cleansed through prescribed duties before attempting to falsely renounce work and live at the expense of others.``` Chapter 3, Text 8 ```

Chapter 3, Verse 9:
यज्ञार्थात्कर्मणोऽन्यत्र लोकोऽयं कर्मबन्धनः ।
तदर्थं कर्म कौन्तेय मुक्तसङ्गः समाचर ॥ ९ ॥
Translation: Performing work as a sacrifice for Lord Vishnu is essential, as any other type of work in this material world leads to bondage. Therefore, O son of Kunti, carry out your prescribed duties for His satisfaction, and thereby remain free from bondage.
Purport: Chapter 3, Text 9 Since work is necessary even for the basic maintenance of the body, duties prescribed according to one's social position and qualities are designed to fulfill that purpose. Yajna refers to Lord Vishnu or sacrificial performances, all of which are intended for His satisfaction. The Vedas declare: "yajno vai vishnuh." In essence, whether one performs prescribed yajnas or directly serves Lord Vishnu, the same goal is achieved. Therefore, Krishna consciousness involves the performance of yajna as outlined in this verse. The varnasrama institution also aims at pleasing Lord Vishnu. As stated in the Vishnu Purana (3.8.8): "Varnäśramäcäravatä purusenä parah puman/ vishnur aradhyate."  Hence, one must work for the satisfaction of Vishnu. Any other work undertaken in this material realm will lead to bondage, as both virtuous and sinful actions have consequences that bind the doer. Therefore, one should engage in work in Krishna consciousness to please Krishna (or Vishnu), and in doing so, one attains a liberated state. This is the art of performing work, which initially requires expert guidance. Therefore, one should diligently act under the expert guidance of a devotee of Lord Krishna, or directly under the instructions of Lord Krishna Himself (as Arjuna had the privilege to do). Actions should not be pursued for sensory gratification; rather, everything should be done for Krishna's satisfaction. This practice not only shields one from the reactions of work but also gradually elevates one to the transcendental loving service of the Lord, which leads to the realm of God.

Chapter 3, Verse 10:
सहयज्ञाः प्रजाः सृष्ट्वा पुरोवाच प्रजापतिः । अनेन प्रसविष्यध्वमेश वोऽस्त्विष्टकामधुक् ॥
Translation: In the beginning of creation, the Lord of all creatures sent forth generations of men and demigods, along with sacrifices for Vishnu, and blessed them by saying, “Be happy through this yajna [sacrifice], for its performance will bestow upon you all that is desirable for living happily and achieving liberation.”
Purport: The material creation by the Lord of creatures (Vishnu) is an opportunity offered to the conditioned souls to return home—back to Godhead. All living entities within the material creation are conditioned by material nature due to their forgetfulness of their relationship with Vishnu, or Krishna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. The Vedic principles aim to help us understand this eternal relationship, as stated in the Bhagavad-gita: vedais ca sarvair aham eva vedyah. The Lord declares that the purpose of the Vedas is to comprehend Him. The Vedic hymns proclaim: patià visvasyätmesvaram. Thus, the Lord of all living entities is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Vishnu. In the Srimad-Bhagavatam (2.4.20), Srila Sukadeva Gosvami describes the Lord as pati in various ways:  sriyah patir yajna-patih prajä-patih dhiyäà patir loka-patih dharä-patih patir gatiś candhakavrsni-sätvatäà prasidatäà me bhagavän satäà patih  The prajä-pati is Lord Vishnu, the Lord of all living creatures, worlds, beauties, and the protector of all. The Lord created this material world to teach the conditioned souls how to perform yajnas (sacrifices) for the satisfaction of Vishnu, so that they can live comfortably without anxiety in the material realm and, upon leaving the current body, enter the kingdom of God. This is the entire program for the conditioned soul. Through the performance of yajna, the conditioned souls gradually become Krishna conscious and attain godliness in all aspects. In the Age of Kali, the sankirtana-yajna (chanting the names of God) is recommended in the Vedic scriptures, and this transcendental system was introduced by Lord Caitanya for the deliverance of all beings in this age. Sankirtana-yajna and Krishna consciousness complement each other well. Lord Krishna, in His devotional form (as Lord Caitanya), is mentioned in the Srimad-Bhagavatam (11.5.32) as follows, with special reference to the sankirtana-yajna:  krsna-varnam tvisäkrstnam sangopängästrapärsadäm yajñaih sankirtanaprayair yajanti hi sumedhasah  “In this Age of Kali, people who are endowed with sufficient intelligence will worship the Lord, who is accompanied by His associates, through the performance of sankirtana-yajna.” Other yajnas prescribed in the Vedic literatures are not easy to perform in this Age of Kali, but the sankirtana-yajna is easy and sublime for all purposes, as recommended in the Bhagavad-gita (9.14).``` Chapter 3, Text 10 ```

Chapter 3, Verse 11:
देवान्भावयतानेन ते देवा भावयन्तु वः ।
परस्परं भावयन्तः श्रेयः परमवाप्स्यथ ॥ ११ ॥
Translation: By pleasing the demigods through sacrifices, the demigods will in turn please you. Through mutual cooperation, all will attain the highest welfare.
Purport: Chapter 3, Text 11 The demigods are divine administrators responsible for various aspects of material existence. They oversee the provision of air, light, water, and other blessings necessary for the sustenance of all living beings. These demigods are countless assistants within the universal form of the Supreme Lord. Their satisfaction or dissatisfaction is linked to the performance of sacrificial rituals by humans. While some rituals are specifically dedicated to appeasing certain demigods, ultimately, Lord Vishnu is the primary recipient of all offerings in sacrifices. As stated in the Bhagavad-gita, Krishna is the ultimate enjoyer of all sacrifices (bhoktäraà yajña-tapasäm). Therefore, the main goal of all sacrifices is to please the ultimate enjoyer of sacrifices. When sacrifices are performed perfectly, the demigods responsible for various aspects of material provision are pleased, resulting in an abundance of natural resources.  The performance of sacrifices brings numerous benefits, ultimately leading to liberation from material bondage. Through sacrificial acts, all actions become purified, as the Vedas affirm: "ähära-śuddhau sattva-śuddhiḥ sattva-śuddhau dhruvä smṛtiḥ smṛti-lambhe sarvagranthénäà vipramokṣaḥ." By offering sacrifices, one's food becomes sanctified, and by consuming sanctified food, one's very existence becomes purified. Through the purification of existence, subtler layers of consciousness become sanctified, leading to the remembrance of the path to liberation. This progressive purification culminates in Krishna consciousness, which is the urgent need of contemporary society.

Chapter 3, Verse 12:
इष्टान्भोगान् हि वो देवा दास्यन्ते यज्ञभाविताः । तैर्दत्तानप्रदायेभ्यो यो भुङ्क्ते स्तेन एव सः ॥
Translation: The demigods, pleased by sacrificial offerings, bestow upon you the desired necessities. One who enjoys these gifts without reciprocating with offerings to the demigods is indeed a thief.
Purport: The demigods act as intermediaries on behalf of the Supreme Lord Vishnu, providing for the material needs of living beings. Therefore, they must be satisfied through prescribed sacrifices. The Vedas prescribe various sacrifices for different demigods, yet all sacrifices ultimately reach the Supreme Lord. For those unable to comprehend the concept of the Supreme Lord, worship of the demigods is recommended. Different types of sacrifices are prescribed in the Vedas based on the material qualities of individuals. Worship of different demigods is also determined by these qualities. For instance, those with a mode of ignorance may worship the fierce goddess Kali and offer animal sacrifices. On the other hand, those in the mode of goodness are advised to worship Lord Vishnu. Regardless, all sacrifices aim at elevating one to a transcendental state. For ordinary individuals, performing the five great sacrifices (panca-maha-yajna) is essential.  It is crucial to understand that all essential needs of human society are provided by the demigods who act as agents of the Supreme Lord. Humans cannot create anything independently. Consider the various foods essential for human sustenance such as grains, fruits, vegetables, milk, and sugar for those in the mode of goodness, as well as meat for non-vegetarians—all of these are not man-made. Similarly, necessities like heat, light, water, and air are also beyond human manufacturing capabilities. Life is sustained by the benevolence of the Lord's agents, as without divine intervention, there would be no sunlight, moonlight, rain, or breeze essential for survival. Even in our industrial pursuits, raw materials like metals and minerals are provided by the Lord's agents for our well-being and for the pursuit of self-realization, leading to liberation from the cycle of material existence. This ultimate goal is achieved through sacrificial activities. When individuals forget the purpose of human life and misuse the Lord's gifts for sensual pleasure, becoming more entangled in material pursuits, they are akin to thieves and are subject to the laws of material nature. A society devoid of purpose, like a society of thieves, can never find true happiness. Materialistic individuals lack a higher goal in life and are driven solely by the pursuit of pleasure, devoid of the knowledge of sacrificial duties. However, Lord Caitanya introduced the simplest form of sacrifice—the congregational chanting of the holy names (sankirtana-yajna)—which can be performed by anyone embracing the principles of Krishna consciousness worldwide.""" ``` Chapter 3, Text 12 ```

Chapter 3, Verse 13:
यज्ञशिष्टाशिनः सन्तो मुच्यन्ते सर्वकिल्बिषैः ।
भुञ्जते ते त्वघं पापा ये पचन्त्यात्मकारणात् ॥ १३ ॥
Translation: The devotees of the Lord are released from all kinds of sins because they eat food which is offered first for sacrifice. Those who prepare food for personal sense enjoyment, indeed consume only sin.
Purport: Chapter 3, Text 13 The devotees of the Supreme Lord, known as santas, are always immersed in love for the Lord, as described in the Brahma-samhita (5.38): "premänjanacchurita-bhakti-vilocanena santah sadaiva hrdayesu vilokayanti." The santas, constantly filled with love for the Supreme Personality of Godhead—be it Govinda (the giver of all pleasures), Mukunda (the giver of liberation), or Krishna (the all-attractive person)—never partake of anything without first offering it to the Supreme Person. Therefore, these devotees consistently engage in various devotional services, such as hearing, chanting, remembering, and worshiping, which act as sacrificial offerings. Such practices keep them free from the contaminations of sinful associations in the material world.  Conversely, those who cook for their own selfish pleasure not only act as thieves but also consume the fruits of sinful actions. How can one find true happiness while being both a thief and a sinner? This is impossible. Hence, for people to attain complete happiness, they must be guided to engage in the simple process of sankirtana-yajna, with full consciousness of Krishna. Without this, there can be no peace or joy in the world.

Chapter 3, Verse 14:
अन्नाद्भवन्ति भूतानि पर्जन्यादन्नसम्भवः । यज्ञाद्भवति पर्जन्यो यज्ञः कर्मसमुद्भवः ॥
Translation: All living beings subsist on food grains, which are produced from rains. Rains are produced by the performance of sacrifice, and sacrifice is born of prescribed duties.
Purport: In his commentary on the Bhagavad-gita, Srila Baladeva Vidyabhusana writes the following: Those who worship the Supreme Lord, the yajna-purusa, through the performance of sacrifices, satisfy Him and in return receive sustenance for their bodies. These devoted souls, free from all sins accumulated over countless lifetimes, attain self-realization and liberation. The demigods, such as Indra, Candra, and Varuna, are celestial administrators who oversee material affairs. The Vedas direct offerings to these demigods to ensure the adequate supply of air, light, and water necessary for the production of food grains. When Lord Krishna is worshiped, these demigods, who are His manifestations, are automatically worshiped as well. Thus, there is no need to separately worship them. Devotees in Krishna consciousness offer food to Krishna and then partake of it, nourishing their bodies spiritually. This practice not only eradicates past sinful reactions but also immunizes the body against material contamination. Just as an antiseptic vaccine protects against epidemic diseases, partaking of food offered to Lord Vishnu immunizes us against material attachments. Those habituated to this practice are known as devotees of the Lord. A person in Krishna consciousness who consumes only food offered to Krishna can neutralize the effects of past sinful actions that hinder self-realization. Conversely, those who do not follow this practice accumulate more sinful reactions, paving the way for a future existence as hogs or dogs, suffering the consequences of their misdeeds. The material world is fraught with impurities, but partaking of prasadam (food offered to Vishnu) shields one from contamination, while neglecting this practice exposes one to impurity.  Food grains and vegetables are indeed edible. Humans consume various grains, vegetables, fruits, while animals feed on the remnants of grains, vegetables, grass, and plants. Even those who consume meat ultimately rely on plant-based production to sustain the animals they eat. Therefore, our sustenance depends on agricultural production rather than industrial manufacturing. Agricultural yields are a result of adequate rainfall, which is regulated by demigods like Indra, the sun, and the moon—all servants of the Supreme Lord. The Lord is pleased by sacrifices, and those unable to perform them will face scarcity, as per the laws of nature. In this age, the sankirtana-yajna, congregational chanting of the Lord's holy names, must be conducted to avert food shortages at the very least.""" ``` Chapter 3, Text 14 ```

Chapter 3, Verse 15:
कर्म ब्रह्मोद्भवं विद्धि ब्रह्माक्षरसमुद्भवम् । तस्मात्सर्वगतं ब्रह्म नित्यं यज्ञे प्रतिष्ठितम् ॥
Translation: Understand that all actions arise from the Supreme Brahman, and the Vedas originate from the imperishable Brahman. Therefore, the eternal Brahman pervades all sacrificial activities.
Purport: This verse emphasizes the concept of performing actions solely for the satisfaction of Lord Krishna. To work in a way that pleases the yajna-purusa, Vishnu, one must seek guidance from Brahman, the transcendental Vedas. The Vedas serve as instructions for proper conduct. Any action taken without the guidance of the Vedas is considered vikarma, unauthorized or sinful work. To avoid the negative consequences of such actions, one should always seek direction from the Vedas. Just as one follows the laws of the state in ordinary life, one should similarly follow the guidance of the Supreme Lord. The instructions in the Vedas are directly manifested from the exhalation of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. It is stated in the Brhad-aranyaka Upanishad (4.5.11), "The four Vedas—Rig Veda, Yajur Veda, Sama Veda, and Atharva Veda—emanate from the exhalation of the great Personality of Godhead." The Lord, being all-powerful, can communicate through His breath. As confirmed in the Brahma-samhita, the Lord can perform the functions of all senses through any one of His senses. He can speak through His breath and impregnate through His eyes. It is said that He impregnated material nature by His glance, giving directions in the Vedic wisdom on how conditioned souls can return to the spiritual realm. Conditioned souls in material existence are driven by desires for material enjoyment. The Vedic instructions provide a way for them to fulfill these desires and ultimately return to the spiritual abode. It is an opportunity for conditioned souls to attain liberation. Therefore, individuals should strive to follow the process of yajna by cultivating Krishna consciousness. Even those who have not followed Vedic injunctions can embrace the principles of Krishna consciousness, which will serve as a substitute for performing Vedic sacrifices or rituals.``` Chapter 3, Text 15 ```

Chapter 3, Verse 16:
एवं प्रवर्तितं चक्रं नानुवर्तयतीह यः । अघायुरिन्द्रियारामो मोघं पार्थ स जीवति ॥
Translation: My dear Arjuna, one who does not follow the cycle of sacrifice established by the Vedas in human life certainly leads a life full of sin. Living only for the satisfaction of the senses, such a person lives in vain.
Purport: The materialistic philosophy of "work hard and enjoy sense gratification" is condemned by the Lord here. Therefore, for those desiring to enjoy the material world, the prescribed cycle of performing yajnas is essential. One who neglects such regulations lives a risky life, facing condemnation. By the law of nature, the human form of life is meant for self-realization through karma-yoga, jnana-yoga, or bhakti-yoga. Transcendentalists beyond vice and virtue need not strictly adhere to yajna performances. However, those engrossed in sense gratification need purification through such yajnas. Various activities exist; those lacking Krishna consciousness are absorbed in sensory pursuits and thus must engage in virtuous deeds. The yajna system facilitates the fulfillment of desires for such individuals without entangling them in the reactions of sense enjoyment. The world's prosperity is not solely a result of personal endeavors but is orchestrated by the Supreme Lord through the demigods. Hence, yajnas are dedicated to specific demigods as mentioned in the Vedas. Ultimately, yajna practice leads to Krishna consciousness. If yajnas fail to awaken Krishna consciousness, they remain mere moral principles. Therefore, one should not confine spiritual progress to moral codes but should transcend them to attain Krishna consciousness.``` Chapter 3, Text 16 ```

Chapter 3, Verse 17:
यस्त्वात्मरतिरेव स्यादात्मतृप्तश्च मानवः ।
आत्मन्येव च सन्तुष्टस्तस्य कार्यं न विद्यते ॥ १७ ॥
Translation: But for one who delights in the self, whose human life is dedicated to self-realization, and who finds contentment within the self alone, completely fulfilled—such a person has no prescribed duties.
Purport: Chapter 3, Text 17 A person who is completely absorbed in Krishna consciousness, and finds deep satisfaction in acts performed in that consciousness, is freed from the necessity of further duties. Through Krishna consciousness, all impurities within are immediately purified, a result equivalent to many thousands of sacrificial rituals. This purification of consciousness leads to unwavering confidence in one's eternal relationship with the Supreme. By the Lord's grace, his path becomes illuminated, and he transcends the need to adhere to Vedic injunctions. Such a Krishna conscious individual loses interest in material pursuits and no longer seeks pleasure in worldly distractions like alcohol, relationships, and other material entanglements.

Chapter 3, Verse 18:
नैव तस्य कृतेनार्थो नाकतेनेह कश्चन । न चास्य सर्वभूतेषु कश्चिदर्थव्यपाश्रयः ॥
Translation: A self-realized person has no specific purpose to achieve in the performance of their prescribed duties, nor do they have any reason to abstain from such duties. They do not rely on anyone else for their needs.
Purport: A self-realized individual is no longer bound to carry out any prescribed duties, except those done in Krishna consciousness. It should be noted that being in Krishna consciousness does not imply inactivity, as elaborated in the upcoming verses. A person in Krishna consciousness does not seek refuge in any being, whether human or demigod. Their actions in Krishna consciousness alone suffice to fulfill their responsibilities.""" Chapter 3, Text 18 """

Chapter 3, Verse 19:
तस्मादसक्तः सततं कार्यं कर्म समाचर । असक्तो ह्याचरन् कर्म परमाप्नोति पूरुषः ॥
Translation: Therefore, one should perform their prescribed duties without attachment to the results. By acting in this way, one attains the Supreme.
Purport: For devotees, the Supreme is the Personality of Godhead, and for impersonalists, it is liberation. Acting in Krishna consciousness, under proper guidance and without attachment to the results, leads one towards the ultimate goal of life. Arjuna is instructed to fight in the Battle of Kurukshetra for Krishna's cause, as Krishna desired it. Being a good or nonviolent person is a form of personal attachment, but acting on behalf of the Supreme without attachment to outcomes is the highest level of action, as guided by the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Sri Krishna.  Vedic rituals, such as prescribed sacrifices, are performed to purify impious activities done for sense gratification. However, actions performed in Krishna consciousness transcend the reactions of good and evil deeds. A Krishna conscious individual acts solely for Krishna, without attachment to the results. They engage in various activities, yet remain completely detached.``` Chapter 3, Text 19 ```

Chapter 3, Verse 20:
कर्मणैव हि संसिद्धिमास्थिता जनकादयः । लोकसंग्रहमेवापि संपश्यन् कर्तुमर्हसि ॥
Translation: Kings like Janaka attained perfection by performing their prescribed duties alone. Therefore, for the sake of guiding the people, you too should engage in your duties.
Purport: Self-realized kings like Janaka were not bound by the duties prescribed in the Vedas, yet they dutifully performed them to set an example for society. Janaka, the father of Sita and father-in-law of Lord Sri Rama, was a devoted soul beyond material desires. Despite his enlightened state, as the ruler of Mithila, he demonstrated the importance of fulfilling one's responsibilities. Lord Krishna and Arjuna, His eternal companion, did not need to partake in the Kurukshetra War. However, they engaged in battle to teach the necessity of righteous violence when all peaceful means fail. Even though those in Krishna consciousness may be detached from worldly affairs, they actively engage to educate others on righteous living. Through their actions, seasoned practitioners of Krishna consciousness inspire others to follow suit, as elaborated in the subsequent verse.""" Chapter 3, Text 20 """

Chapter 3, Verse 21:
यद्यदाचरति श्रेष्ठस्तत्तदेवेतरो जनः ।
स यत् प्रमाणं कुरुते लोकस्तदनुवर्तते ॥ २१ ॥
Translation: Whatever actions a noble person performs, common people follow suit. The standards they establish through their exemplary conduct, the rest of the world adopts.
Purport: Chapter 3, Text 21 In general, people look up to leaders who can guide them through their actions. A leader cannot effectively teach others to refrain from certain behaviors if they themselves engage in those very actions. Lord Caitanya emphasized the importance of a teacher demonstrating proper behavior before imparting knowledge. Such a teacher, known as an acarya, embodies the ideal example. Thus, a teacher must adhere to the principles outlined in scriptures to effectively guide others. It is inappropriate for a teacher to create rules that contradict the teachings of the revealed scriptures, such as the Manu-samhita and similar texts, which are considered authoritative guides for society. Therefore, a leader's instructions should be rooted in the principles of these standard scriptures.  Those seeking self-improvement must follow the established guidelines practiced by great teachers. The Srimad-Bhagavatam also stresses the importance of following in the footsteps of exemplary devotees as a means of advancing on the spiritual path. Whether it be the king, a governmental leader, a father, or a teacher, all natural leaders have a significant responsibility towards those under their care. Hence, they should be well-versed in the moral and spiritual codes outlined in standard texts.

Chapter 3, Verse 22:

The Srimad-Bhagavatam (10.33.30–31) emphasizes this point:  "One should simply follow the instructions of the Lord and His empowered servants. Some misguided devotees of Lord Shiva engage in smoking marijuana and other intoxicants, mistakenly imitating his actions and unknowingly inviting danger. Similarly, there are pseudo-devotees of Lord Krishna who seek to imitate His divine dance of love (räsa-lila) without realizing their limitations in comparison to His ability to lift Govardhana Hill. By elevating the mode of passion to goodness through prescribed spiritual practices, one can avoid descending into anger through spiritual attachment. Though possessing partial independence, when this independence is misused and the inclination for service transforms into a desire for sense gratification, individuals fall under the sway of lust. Consequently, the mind and senses become reservoirs of lust. Subsequently, the intelligence becomes the stronghold of these lustful tendencies. Intelligence resides in close proximity to the soul. When influenced by lust, the intelligence leads the soul to falsely identify with material elements, the mind, and the senses. The soul becomes ensnared in material sense gratification, mistaking it for true happiness. This misidentification of the soul is eloquently described in the Srimad-Bhagavatam (10.84.13):  yasyätma-buddhih kunape tridhätuke sva-dhih kalaträdisu bhauma ijyädhih yat-tirthabuddhih salile na karhicij janesv abhijñesu sa eva go-kharah  "A person who considers the body, composed of three elements, as the self, who regards the bodily by-products as family members, who worships the land of birth, and who visits holy places merely to bathe rather than associate with enlightened beings, is likened to an ass or a cow."``` Chapter 3, Text 40 ```

Chapter 3, Verse 41:
तस्मात्त्वमिन्द्रियाण्यादौ नियम्य भरतर्षभ ।
पाप्मानं प्रजहि ह्येनं ज्ञानविज्ञाननाशनम् ॥ ४१ ॥
Translation: Therefore, O Arjuna, best of the Bharatas, in the very beginning, control the senses and conquer this great symbol of sin [lust]. Destroy this enemy that annihilates knowledge and self-realization.
Purport: Chapter 3, Text 41 The Lord advised Arjuna to regulate his senses right from the start to overcome the greatest sinful adversary, lust, which obstructs the desire for self-realization and understanding of the true self. "Jnana" refers to the knowledge of the self in contrast to the non-self, recognizing that the spirit soul is distinct from the body. "Vijnana" denotes the specific understanding of the spirit soul's inherent nature and its relationship with the Supreme Soul. As elucidated in the Srimad-Bhagavatam (2.9.31):  jñānam parama-guhyam me yad vijñāna-samanvitam sa-rahasyam tad-aṅgam ca grhāṇa gaditam mayā  "The knowledge about the self and the Supreme Self is profoundly confidential and mysterious. Yet, this knowledge and its specific realization can be comprehended when explained in its various aspects by the Lord Himself." The Bhagavad-gita imparts both general and specific knowledge about the self. Living entities are integral parts of the Lord and are meant to serve Him. This awareness is known as Krishna consciousness. Therefore, one must imbibe Krishna consciousness right from the outset of life to develop full Krishna consciousness and act accordingly.  Lust is merely a distorted reflection of the natural love for God inherent in every living being. However, when one is educated in Krishna consciousness from an early age, that innate love for God cannot degrade into lust. If love for God transforms into lust, it becomes arduous to revert to the original state. Nevertheless, Krishna consciousness is so potent that even a latecomer can cultivate love for God by adhering to the prescribed principles of devotional service. Hence, at any phase of life or upon realizing its importance, one can commence regulating the senses in Krishna consciousness, engaging in devotional service to the Lord, and transform lust into divine love—the pinnacle of human perfection.

Chapter 3, Verse 42:
इन्द्रियाणि पराण्याहुरिन्द्रियेभ्यः परं मनः ।
मनसस्तु परा बुद्धिर्र्यो बुद्धेः परतस्तु सः ॥ ४२ ॥
Translation: The senses are considered higher than the physical body; the mind is superior to the senses; intelligence is above the mind; and the soul is even higher than intelligence.
Purport: Chapter 3, Text 42 The senses are channels through which desires manifest. Desires are contained within the body but are expressed through the senses. Therefore, the senses are considered more powerful than the body as a whole. When one is in a state of higher consciousness, or Krishna consciousness, these sensory outlets are not active. In Krishna consciousness, the soul establishes a direct connection with the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Thus, the hierarchy of bodily functions described here ultimately leads to the Supreme Soul. Bodily actions are carried out through the senses, and when the senses are restrained, all bodily activities cease. However, if the mind is active, even when the body is still, the mind continues to function, as in dreams. Above the mind is the discernment of the intelligence, and above the intelligence lies the essence of the soul. When the soul is directly engaged with the Supreme, all other faculties—intelligence, mind, and senses—automatically align. In the Katha Upanishad, a similar concept is explained: sense objects are superior to the senses, and the mind is superior to sense objects. By engaging the mind in constant service to the Lord, the senses are prevented from engaging in other distractions. This mindset has been elucidated as paraà dṛṣṭvä nivartate. When the mind is absorbed in the transcendental service of the Lord, lower tendencies are naturally subdued. The soul, described as mahän, the great, in the Katha Upanishad, transcends all—sense objects, senses, mind, and intelligence. Thus, comprehending the soul's inherent nature is the key to resolving all dilemmas.  One must utilize intelligence to ascertain the soul's constitutional position and consistently immerse the mind in Krishna consciousness. This approach resolves all challenges. Novice spiritual aspirants are typically advised to distance themselves from sensory temptations. Additionally, one must fortify the mind through intelligent discernment. By engaging the mind in Krishna consciousness through complete surrender to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the mind grows stronger. Even if the senses are potent like serpents, they lose their influence when their fangs are broken. Though the soul governs intelligence, mind, and senses, without the reinforcement of Krishna consciousness, the restless mind is susceptible to downfall.

Chapter 4, Verse 1:
श्रीभगवानुवाच इमं विवस्वते योगं प्रोक्तवानहमव्ययम् । विवस्वान् मनवे प्राह मनुरिक्ष्वाकवेऽब्रवीत् ॥
Translation: The Supreme Lord, Sri Krishna, said: I imparted this eternal science of yoga to the sun-god, Vivasvan, who then passed it on to Manu, the progenitor of mankind, and Manu in turn instructed it to Ikshvaku.
Purport: This verse reveals the ancient lineage of the Bhagavad-gita, originally imparted to the royal rulers of all planetary systems, beginning with the sun planet. The duty of kings on all planets is to safeguard their subjects, and therefore, it is essential for the royal order to comprehend the teachings of Bhagavad-gita to govern wisely and shield the citizens from the entanglement of material desires. Human life is intended for the pursuit of spiritual wisdom, establishing an eternal connection with the Supreme Personality of Godhead. It is the responsibility of rulers across all realms to educate, cultivate, and inspire their citizens in this divine knowledge. Essentially, leaders are tasked with disseminating the science of Krishna consciousness, enabling people to embrace this profound wisdom and tread a successful path while utilizing the precious opportunity of human existence.  In the current era, the sun-god is known as Vivasvan, the ruler of the sun, which serves as the source of all planets within the solar system. In the Brahma-samhita (5.52), it is stated:  yac-cakṣur esa savitä sakalagrahänām rājā samasta-sūramūrtir aseṣatejāḥ yasyājñayā bhramati sambhūta-kāla-cakro govindam ādi-puruṣaṁ tam aham bhajāmi  “Let me worship,” Lord Brahma said, “the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Govinda [Krishna], who is the original person and under whose order the sun, which is the king of all planets, is assuming immense power and heat. The sun represents the eye of the Lord and traverses its orbit in obedience to His order.”  The sun is the chief among planets, and the sun-god (currently known as Vivasvan) governs the sun planet, which regulates all other planets by providing warmth and light. He revolves according to the command of Krishna, who initially instructed Vivasvan in the science of Bhagavad-gita. Hence, the Gita is not merely a speculative text for ordinary scholars but a timeless repository of knowledge passed down through generations.  In the Mahabharata (Shanti-parva 348.51–52), the historical lineage of the Gita is traced as follows:  tretā-yugādau ca tato vivasvān manave dadou manuś ca loka-bhṛtyarthaṁ sutāyeksavave dadou  īkṣvākunā ca kathito vyāpya lokān avasthitaḥ  “At the beginning of Treta-yuga, this wisdom of the Supreme was imparted by Vivasvan to Manu. Manu, the progenitor of mankind, passed it on to his son Maharaja Ikshvaku, the ruler of this earth and the forefather of the Raghu dynasty, in which Lord Ramachandra appeared.” Thus, the Bhagavad-gita has been present in human society since the time of Maharaja Ikshvaku.  Currently, we have crossed five thousand years of the Kali-yuga, which spans 432,000 years. Prior to this, there was the Dvapara-yuga (800,000 years), and before that, the Treta-yuga (1,200,000 years). Hence, approximately 2,005,000 years ago, Manu imparted the teachings of the Gita to his disciple and son Maharaja Ikshvaku, the ruler of the Earth. The reign of the current Manu is estimated to last for about 305,300,000 years, of which 120,400,000 have elapsed. Considering that the Gita was spoken by the Lord to the sun-god Vivasvan before the birth of Manu, it can be approximated that the Gita was revealed at least 120,400,000 years ago, and it has been accessible to human society for two million years. The Lord reiterated these teachings to Arjuna around five thousand years ago. This historical account of the Gita, as per its own verses and the words of Lord Sri Krishna, emphasizes that it was originally conveyed to the sun-god, who then passed it to his son Manu, and Manu further transmitted it to Ikshvaku.""" Chapter 4, Verse 5:
Translation: The Supreme Lord said: Many births have passed for both you and me, O Arjuna. I remember them all, but you do not, O vanquisher of foes.
Purport: Chapter 4, Text 5 In the Brahma-samhita (5.33), it is revealed that the Supreme Lord, Govinda (Krishna), is the original, absolute, and eternal person.
