Chapter 4, Verse 6:
अजोऽपि सन्नव्ययात्मा भूतानामीश्वरोऽपि सन् ।
प्रकृतिं स्वामधिष्ठाय सम्भवाम्यात्ममायया ॥ ६ ॥
Translation: Although I am unborn and My transcendental body never deteriorates, and although I am the Lord of all living entities, I still appear in every millennium in My original transcendental form.
Purport: Chapter 4, Text 6 The Lord has spoken about the peculiarity of His birth: although He may appear like an ordinary person, He remembers everything of His many, many past “births,” whereas a common man cannot remember what he has done even a few hours before. If someone is asked what he did exactly at the same time one day earlier, it would be very difficult for a common man to answer immediately. He would surely have to dredge his memory to recall what he was doing exactly at the same time one day before. And yet, men often dare claim to be God, or Krishna. One should not be misled by such meaningless claims.  Then again, the Lord explains His prakriti, or His form. Prakriti means “nature,” as well as svarūpa, or “one’s own form.” The Lord says that He appears in His own body. He does not change His body, as the common living entity changes from one body to another. The conditioned soul may have one kind of body in the present birth, but he has a different body in the next birth. In the material world, the living entity has no fixed body but transmigrates from one body to another. The Lord, however, does not do so. Whenever He appears, He does so in the same original body, by His internal potency. In other words, Krishna appears in this material world in His original eternal form, with two hands, holding a flute. He appears exactly in His eternal body, uncontaminated by this material world.  Although He appears in the same transcendental body and is Lord of the universe, it still appears that He takes His birth like an ordinary living entity. And although His body does not deteriorate like a material body, it still appears that Lord Krishna grows from childhood to boyhood and from boyhood to youth. But astonishingly enough He never ages beyond youth. At the time of the Battle of Kurukshetra, He had many grandchildren at home; or, in other words, He had sufficiently aged by material calculations. Still He looked just like a young man twenty or twenty-five years old. We never see a picture of Krishna in old age because He never grows old like us, although He is the oldest person in the whole creation—past, present, and future. Neither His body nor His intelligence ever deteriorates or changes. Therefore, it is clear that in spite of His being in the material world, He is the same unborn, eternal form of bliss and knowledge, changeless in His transcendental body and intelligence.  Factually, His appearance and disappearance is like the sun’s rising, moving before us, and then disappearing from our eyesight. When the sun is out of sight, we think that the sun is set, and when the sun is before our eyes, we think that the sun is on the horizon. Actually, the sun is always in its fixed position, but owing to our defective, insufficient senses, we calculate the appearance and disappearance of the sun in the sky. And because Lord Krishna’s appearance and disappearance are completely different from that of any ordinary, common living entity, it is evident that He is eternal, blissful knowledge by His internal potency—and He is never contaminated by material nature.  The Vedas also confirm that the Supreme Personality of Godhead is unborn yet He still appears to take His birth in multimanifestations. The Vedic supplementary literatures also confirm that even though the Lord appears to be taking His birth, He is still without change of body. In the Bhagavatam, He appears before His mother as Narayana, with four hands and the decorations of the six kinds of full opulences. His appearance in His original eternal form is His causeless mercy, bestowed upon the living entities so that they can concentrate on the Supreme Lord as He is, and not on mental concoctions or imaginations, which the impersonalist wrongly thinks the Lord’s forms to be. The word maya, or ätma-mäyä, refers to the Lord’s causeless mercy, according to the Visva-kosa dictionary.  The Lord is conscious of all of His previous appearances and disappearances, but a common living entity forgets everything about his past body as soon as he gets another body. He is the Lord of all living entities because He performs wonderful and superhuman activities while He is on this earth. Therefore, the Lord is always the same Absolute Truth and is without differentiation between His form and self, or between His quality and body.  A question may now be raised as to why the Lord appears and disappears in this world. This is explained in the next verse.

Chapter 4, Verse 7:

अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥ ७ ॥

"Srjämi" means that the Lord manifests Himself as He is. Although the Lord appears at the end of the Dväpara-yuga of the twenty-eighth millennium of the seventh Manu, He is not bound by rules and regulations. He appears by His own will whenever there is a predominance of irreligiosity and a decline of true religion. The principles of religion are laid down in the Vedas, and any deviation from them makes one irreligious. The Vedas are considered the direct orders of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. The purpose of the Vedas is to establish principles under the order of the Supreme Lord. The highest principle of religion is to surrender unto Him only. The Lord appears when such principles are disturbed by the demoniac. Each incarnation of the Lord has a specific mission, described in the scriptures. The mission is to lead people to God consciousness and obedience to the principles of religion.  The teachings of the Bhagavad Gita were imparted to Arjuna, who was highly advanced compared to ordinary persons. In all incarnations of the Lord, the same principles are taught, but they may appear differently in varied circumstances. The purpose of incarnations is to awaken Krishna consciousness everywhere.

Chapter 4, Verse 8:
परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् ।
धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे ॥ ८ ॥
Translation: To protect the righteous, to annihilate the wicked, and to reestablish the principles of righteousness, I manifest myself in every age.
Purport: Chapter 4, Text 8 In the Bhagavad-gita, a holy person, known as a sädhu, is one who is completely absorbed in Krishna consciousness. Even if someone appears to be lacking in religious principles, if they are fully devoted to Krishna consciousness, they should be recognized as a sädhu. The term "miscreants," or duskritam, refers to those who do not value Krishna consciousness. These individuals are considered foolish and of low character, despite any worldly knowledge or accomplishments they may possess. On the other hand, a person who is wholeheartedly dedicated to Krishna consciousness is esteemed as a sädhu, regardless of their level of education or social refinement.  The Supreme Lord does not need to personally appear to destroy atheists; He has capable agents who can handle such tasks, as seen in the past with the demons Ravana and Kamsa. However, the Lord descends specifically to console His devoted followers who are constantly troubled by demonic forces. Sometimes, these demons even target their own relatives, as seen with Hiranyakashipu's persecution of his son Prahlada and Kamsa's harassment of his sister Devaki and her husband Vasudeva, who were parents of Krishna. While Krishna's primary purpose was to protect Devaki, His birth also led to the demise of Kamsa. Thus, the Lord's incarnations serve the dual purpose of safeguarding His devotees and vanquishing evil forces.  In the Caitanya-caritamrita by Krishnadasa Kaviraja, the verses (Madhya 20.263–264) summarize the concept of divine incarnations:  "The avatära, or incarnation of Godhead, descends from the kingdom of God for material manifestation. And the particular form of the Personality of Godhead who so descends is called an incarnation, or avatära. Such incarnations are situated in the spiritual world, the kingdom of God. When they descend to the material creation, they assume the name avatära."  Various types of avatäras exist, including purusavatäras, gunavatäras, lilavatäras, sakty-äveśa avatäras, manvantara-avatäras, and yugavatäras, appearing according to divine schedules across the universe. However, Lord Krishna is the original Lord, the source of all incarnations. He descends specifically to alleviate the anxieties of His pure devotees who yearn to witness His divine pastimes in Vrindavana. Therefore, the primary purpose of Krishna's incarnation is to satisfy His devoted followers.  The Lord affirms that He manifests Himself in every millennium, including the Age of Kali. As mentioned in the Srimad-Bhagavatam, Lord Caitanya Mahäprabhu is the incarnation for the Age of Kali. He propagated Krishna worship through the congregational chanting of holy names, spreading Krishna consciousness throughout India. Lord Caitanya predicted the global dissemination of this sankirtana movement, reaching every town and village. Though not explicitly mentioned, Lord Caitanya, as the incarnation of Krishna, is subtly described in confidential scriptures like the Upanishads, Mahabharata, and Bhagavatam. Devotees of Lord Krishna are deeply drawn to Lord Caitanya's sankirtana movement, which, unlike other avatäras, delivers miscreants through His boundless mercy.

Chapter 4, Verse 9:
जन्म कर्म च मे दिव्यमेवं यो वेत्ति तत्त्वतः ।
त्यक्त्वा देहं पुनर्जन्म नैति मामेति सोऽर्जुन ॥ ९ ॥
Translation: One who understands the divine nature of My birth and activities in truth, upon leaving the body, does not take birth again in this material world, but attains Me, O Arjuna.
Purport: Chapter 4, Text 9 The Lord’s descent from His transcendental abode has been explained earlier (in verse 6). One who comprehends the truth of the appearance of the Supreme Personality of Godhead is already liberated from material bondage. Such a soul returns to the spiritual realm immediately upon leaving the current material body. This liberation from material entanglement is not easily attained. Impersonalists and yogis achieve liberation after much effort and many lifetimes. Yet, the liberation they attain—merging into the impersonal effulgence of the Lord—is only partial, with the risk of returning to the material world. However, a devotee, by simply understanding the transcendental nature of the Lord's form and activities, reaches the Lord's abode after leaving the body, without the risk of returning to the material world.  In the Brahma-samhita (5.33), it is stated that the Lord has innumerable forms and incarnations: advaitam acyutam anadi ananta-rūpam. Although the Lord manifests in many transcendental forms, they are all one and the same Supreme Personality of Godhead. One must firmly grasp this truth, even though it may be beyond the grasp of mundane scholars and empirical philosophers. As the Vedas (Puruṣa-bodhiné Upanishad) affirm:  eko devo nitya-lilänurakto bhakta-vyäpi hṛdy antarätmä  “The one Supreme Personality of Godhead is eternally engaged in many, many transcendental forms in relationships with His unalloyed devotees.” This Vedic statement is corroborated in this verse of the Gita by the Lord Himself.  One who accepts this truth based on the authority of the Vedas and the Supreme Personality of Godhead, without wasting time in speculative philosophy, attains the highest stage of liberation. By embracing this truth with faith, one can undoubtedly attain liberation. The Vedic declaration tat tvam asi is perfectly applicable in this context. Anyone who recognizes Lord Krishna as the Supreme, or who declares to the Lord, “You are the same Supreme Brahman, the Personality of Godhead,” is immediately liberated and assured of entering into the Lord's transcendental association.  In essence, such a faithful devotee of the Lord achieves perfection, as confirmed by the Vedic proclamation:  tam eva viditväti mrtyum eti nänyaḥ panthā vidyate ’yanäya  “One can attain the perfect stage of liberation from birth and death simply by knowing the Lord, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and there is no other way to achieve this perfection.” (Svetasvatara Upanishad 3.8)  The absence of an alternative means that anyone who does not recognize Lord Krishna as the Supreme Personality of Godhead is certainly in ignorance and will not attain salvation by superficially engaging with spiritual truths or interpreting the Bhagavad-gita through mundane scholarship. Such empirical philosophers may hold significant positions in the material world, but they are not necessarily eligible for liberation. These proud scholars must await the causeless mercy of a devotee of the Lord. Therefore, one should nurture Krishna consciousness with faith and knowledge to attain perfection.

Chapter 4, Verse 10:
Translation: Freed from attachment, fear, and anger, fully absorbed in Me, and seeking refuge in Me, many individuals in the past purified themselves through knowledge of Me. As a result, they all attained transcendental love for Me.
Purport: Chapter 4, Text 10 For those heavily influenced by materialism, grasping the personal nature of the Supreme Absolute Truth is challenging. Their attachment to the bodily concept of life makes it nearly impossible for them to comprehend the Supreme as a person. They struggle to fathom the existence of a transcendental, imperishable, knowledgeable, and eternally blissful form. In their materialistic view, the body is perishable, ignorant, and miserable. Hence, when informed about the personal form of the Lord, they project their bodily limitations onto the Supreme Being.  Materialists often perceive the gigantic material manifestation as supreme, leading them to view the Supreme as impersonal. Due to their intense material absorption, the idea of retaining personality post-liberation from matter terrifies them. The concept of individual and personal spiritual life frightens them, prompting a preference for merging into the impersonal void. They liken living entities to bubbles merging into the ocean, considering it the highest spiritual perfection attainable without individual personality. This fear-driven state lacks a complete understanding of spiritual existence.  Moreover, some individuals fail to grasp spiritual existence altogether. Confounded by various philosophical speculations and contradictions, they grow disillusioned and may deny the existence of a supreme cause, embracing nihilism. Such individuals are spiritually diseased. Some are so attached to material pursuits that they neglect spiritual life, while others seek union with the supreme spiritual cause. There are also those who reject all spiritual notions out of frustration, resorting to intoxication and mistaking their hallucinations for spiritual visions.  To transcend these material attachments and misconceptions—neglect of spiritual life, fear of a spiritual personal identity, and the void concept born of life's disappointments—one must fully surrender to the Lord under the guidance of a genuine spiritual master. Following the disciplines and principles of devotional life leads to the pinnacle of devotional service known as bhäva, or transcendental love of Godhead.  As stated in Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu (1.4.15–16), the science of devotional service progresses through stages: - Initial faith leads to association with spiritually elevated individuals. - Association with a spiritual master initiates devotional service, leading to freedom from material attachments. - Through steadfast self-realization, one develops a taste for hearing about the Absolute Personality of Godhead, Sri Krishna. - This taste fosters attachment to Krishna consciousness, culminating in bhäva, the preliminary stage of transcendental love of God. - The highest stage, prema, is characterized by constant engagement in transcendental loving service of the Lord.  Thus, through the gradual process of devotional service under a bona fide spiritual master's guidance, one can attain the highest stage, free from material attachments, fear of individual spiritual identity, and the disillusionment that fuels nihilistic philosophies. Ultimately, one can reach the abode of the Supreme Lord.

Chapter 4, Verse 11:
ये यथा मां प्रपद्यन्ते तांस्तथैव भजाम्यहम् ।
मम वर्त्मानुवर्तन्ते मनुष्याः पार्थ सर्वशः ॥ ११ ॥
Translation: As individuals surrender unto Me, I reciprocate accordingly. O son of Pritha, all people follow My path in various ways.
Purport: Chapter 4, Text 11 People seek to connect with Krishna in different forms of His manifestations. While some may perceive Krishna in His impersonal spiritual radiance (brahmajyoti) or as the universal Supersoul residing within all beings, true realization of Krishna is attained only by His sincere devotees. Krishna is the ultimate goal of everyone's pursuit, and thus He fulfills the desires of each individual seeking Him. In the spiritual realm, Krishna reciprocates with His pure devotees in a manner that aligns with their heartfelt desires. Some may desire Krishna as their master, friend, child, or beloved, and Krishna lovingly reciprocates with all devotees based on the depth of their love for Him.  In the material world, similar exchanges of emotions occur, and the Lord responds accordingly to the diverse types of worshipers. Pure devotees, both in this world and in the spiritual abode, engage in personal service to Krishna and derive transcendental joy from lovingly serving Him. On the other hand, those who are impersonalists and seek to merge into the effulgence of the Lord are also accommodated by Krishna. However, by rejecting the eternal blissful Personality of Godhead, they miss out on the sublime joy of engaging in personal service to the Lord and lose their individuality in the process.  Some impersonalists, unable to maintain their impersonal realization, return to the material realm to fulfill their latent desires for activities. They are not granted access to the spiritual realms but are given another chance to engage in material pursuits. The Lord bestows upon fruitive workers the results of their prescribed duties, acting as the bestower of the fruits of sacrifices (yajñesvara), and grants mystic powers to yogis seeking such abilities. Ultimately, all individuals are reliant on the mercy of the Supreme Lord for success, and various spiritual paths represent different stages of advancement toward the same ultimate goal.  Therefore, unless one attains the pinnacle of Krishna consciousness, all endeavors remain incomplete, as emphasized in the Srimad-Bhagavatam (2.3.10):  "Whether one is devoid of desires like the devotees, or harbors desires for material gains, or aspires for liberation, one should diligently worship the Supreme Personality of Godhead with intense devotion, leading to the perfection of Krishna consciousness."

Chapter 4, Verse 12:
काङ्क्षन्तः कर्मणां सिद्धिं यजन्ते इह देवताः । क्षिप्रं हि मानुषे लोके सिद्धिर्भवति कर्मजा ॥
Translation: Men in this world desire success in fruitive activities, and therefore they worship the demigods. Indeed, results from fruitive work in this world come quickly.
Purport: There is a common misconception about the gods or demigods of this material world. Men of lesser intelligence, despite being considered great scholars, often mistake these demigods for various forms of the Supreme Lord. In reality, the demigods are not different forms of God; rather, they are His distinct parts and parcels. God is singular, while His parts and parcels are numerous. The Vedas affirm, "nityo nityänäm": God is one. İsvaraḥ paramah kṛṣṇah. The Supreme God is one—Krishna—and the demigods are empowered beings tasked with managing the material world. These demigods are all living entities (nityānām) possessing varying degrees of material power. They cannot be equated with the Supreme God—Narayana, Vishnu, or Krishna. Anyone equating God and the demigods is deemed an atheist or pasandi. Even revered demigods like Brahma and Shiva cannot be compared to the Supreme Lord. In truth, the demigods themselves worship the Lord, such as Brahma and Shiva (śiva-viriñci-nutam). Yet, intriguingly, many human leaders are worshipped by foolish individuals due to a misconception of anthropomorphism or zoomorphism. Iha devatäh refers to a powerful man or demigod in this material world. However, Narayana, Vishnu, or Krishna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, transcends this world. He exists above and beyond material creation. Even Sripada Shankaracarya, the leader of the impersonalists, acknowledges that Narayana or Krishna transcends this material realm. Nevertheless, misled individuals (hṛtajñänah) venerate demigods seeking immediate results. They obtain these results, unaware that they are temporary and meant for the less intelligent. The demigods of this material world and their worshippers will vanish with the destruction of this material realm. The blessings of the demigods are material and fleeting. Both the material worlds and their inhabitants, including the demigods and their devotees, are mere bubbles in the cosmic ocean. In this world, society is fixated on transient pursuits such as material wealth, family, and pleasures. To attain such ephemeral goals, people worship demigods or influential figures in society. If someone secures a government position by venerating a political leader, they perceive it as a significant boon. Hence, they bow down to these so-called leaders or "big guns" to secure temporary favors, which they indeed obtain. Such misguided individuals lack interest in Krishna consciousness, the enduring solution to the tribulations of material existence. They are driven by sensual pleasures and are drawn to worshipping empowered beings known as demigods for a fleeting taste of enjoyment. This verse underscores the rarity of people's inclination towards Krishna consciousness, as they are predominantly engrossed in material pleasures and hence revere potent living entities.``` Chapter 4, Text 12 ```

Chapter 4, Verse 14:
न मां कर्माणि लिम्पन्ति न मे कर्मफले स्पृहा ।
इति मां योऽभिजानाति कर्मभिर्न स बध्यते ॥ १४ ॥
Translation: Actions do not bind Me, nor do I have any desire for the fruits of actions. One who realizes this truth about Me is not bound by the reactions of work.
Purport: Chapter 4, Text 14 Just as in the material world there are laws that exempt the king from wrongdoing and make the king not subject to ordinary laws, similarly, although the Lord is the creator of this material world, He remains unaffected by the activities within it. He creates and remains detached from the creation, while living beings become entangled in the results of their actions due to their desire to control material resources. The owner of a business is not held responsible for the actions of the workers; the workers themselves are accountable. Living beings pursue sense gratification, which is not ordained by the Lord. They engage in worldly activities to fulfill their desires and seek heavenly pleasures after death. However, the Lord, being complete in Himself, is not attracted to such temporary pleasures. The celestial demigods are merely His servants. The Lord does not seek the inferior pleasures that the workers desire; He remains aloof from material actions and their consequences.  For instance, the rain is not responsible for the diverse vegetation that grows on earth, even though without rain, plant life would not thrive. The Vedic scriptures confirm this principle, stating that in material creation, the Lord is the ultimate cause, while the immediate cause is material nature that makes the cosmic manifestation visible. Various beings, such as demigods, humans, and animals, exist as a result of their past actions, good or bad. The Lord provides them with suitable conditions and regulations based on the modes of nature, but He is not accountable for their past or present deeds.  The Vedanta-sutra (2.1.34) affirms that the Lord is impartial and does not favor any living entity. Each individual is responsible for their own actions, with the Lord granting opportunities through the external energy of material nature. One who comprehends the intricacies of karma, or actions and their consequences, remains unaffected by the outcomes of their deeds. Such a person, well-versed in the transcendental nature of the Lord, is established in Krishna consciousness and is not subject to karmic laws.  On the other hand, someone ignorant of the transcendental nature of the Lord and who perceives His actions as aimed at achieving material results, like ordinary beings, becomes entangled in karmic reactions. A liberated soul, who understands the Supreme Truth and is firmly rooted in Krishna consciousness, transcends the cycle of karma and remains unaffected by its entanglements.

Therefore, it is imperative to follow the footsteps of the revered authorities in the spiritual lineage. Otherwise, even the most intelligent individuals may become perplexed regarding the prescribed actions in Krishna consciousness. Hence, the Lord chose to personally enlighten Arjuna in the path of Krishna consciousness. By following Arjuna's example under the direct guidance of the Lord, one can avoid confusion.  It is said that the principles of religion cannot be fully understood through mere speculative knowledge. True religious principles can only be established by the Supreme Lord Himself. Dharmäà tu säkṣäd bhagavat-praṇétam (Bhag. 6.3.19). No one can concoct religious principles through imperfect speculation. Chapter 4, Verse 24:
ब्रह्मार्पणं ब्रह्म हविर्ब्रह्माग्नौ ब्रह्मणा हुतम् ।
ब्रह्मैव तेन गन्तव्यं ब्रह्मकर्मसमाधिना ॥ २४ ॥
Translation: Offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, offered by Brahman in the fire of Brahman; Brahman alone is to be reached by one absorbed in Brahman through the performance of Brahman-like actions.
Purport: Chapter 4, Text 24 This verse elucidates how engaging in activities in Krishna consciousness leads one to the ultimate spiritual goal. There are various activities in Krishna consciousness, which will be elaborated upon in subsequent verses. For now, the fundamental principle of Krishna consciousness is being explained. A conditioned soul, bound by material influences, naturally acts within the material realm but must strive to transcend it. The process through which a conditioned soul can rise above the material environment is Krishna consciousness. Just as a person suffering from a digestive ailment caused by excessive milk consumption can be cured by consuming yogurt, similarly, one absorbed in material pursuits can be healed by embracing Krishna consciousness as outlined in the Gita. This process is commonly known as yajna, or sacrificial activities performed solely for the satisfaction of Vishnu, or Krishna. The more one engages in worldly activities with Krishna consciousness or for Vishnu's pleasure, the more the environment becomes spiritually charged through complete absorption. The term "brahma" denotes the spiritual realm. The Lord is spiritual, and the effulgence emanating from His transcendental form is known as brahmajyoti. Everything exists within this brahmajyoti, but when it is obscured by illusion (maya) or material desires, it is perceived as material. By embracing Krishna consciousness, this material covering can be swiftly removed. Thus, an offering made in the spirit of Krishna consciousness, the one who consumes such an offering, the act of consumption, the contributor, and the outcome—all merge into Brahman, the Absolute Truth. When the Absolute Truth is veiled by maya, it is referred to as matter. Matter, when utilized in service of the Absolute Truth, regains its spiritual essence. Krishna consciousness is the process of transforming illusory consciousness into Brahman, the Supreme Reality. When the mind is completely absorbed in Krishna consciousness, it enters a state of samadhi, or deep meditation. Any action performed in this elevated state of consciousness is considered a yajna, a sacrifice for the Supreme. In this state of spiritual awareness, the giver, the gift, the act of giving, the one who performs the offering, and the ultimate result—all merge into the Absolute, the Supreme Brahman. This is the essence of Krishna consciousness.

Translation: Some yogis worship the demigods by offering sacrifices to them, while others offer sacrifices in the fire of the Supreme Brahman.
Purport: Chapter 4, Text 25 In the practice of Krishna consciousness, a person is considered a perfect yogi or a first-class mystic. However, there are others who perform similar sacrifices in the worship of demigods, as well as those who sacrifice to the Supreme Brahman, the impersonal aspect of the Supreme Lord. These different types of sacrifices represent various categories, but ultimately, the essence of sacrifice is to please the Supreme Lord, Vishnu, also known as Yajna.  There are essentially two primary divisions of sacrifice: sacrificing worldly possessions and sacrificing for transcendental knowledge. Those in Krishna consciousness offer all material possessions to please the Supreme Lord, while others seek temporary material gains by sacrificing to demigods like Indra or the sun-god. Impersonalists sacrifice their individual identity to merge into the impersonal Brahman.  The demigods are powerful beings appointed by the Supreme Lord to oversee various material functions in the universe. Those seeking material benefits worship these demigods through Vedic rituals. They are known as bahv-isvara-vädi, believers in multiple gods. On the other hand, those who worship the impersonal aspect of the Absolute Truth view the forms of demigods as temporary and sacrifice their individual selves in the supreme fire, thus merging into the Supreme existence.  Impersonalists dedicate their time to philosophical contemplation in order to understand the transcendental nature of the Supreme. Fruitive workers sacrifice their material possessions for material enjoyment, while impersonalists renounce their material designations to merge into the Supreme existence. For impersonalists, the fire altar of sacrifice is the Supreme Brahman, with the self being the offering consumed by the fire of Brahman.  In contrast, a Krishna conscious person like Arjuna sacrifices everything for the satisfaction of Krishna. Such an individual offers all material possessions and even the self entirely to Krishna. This complete surrender to Krishna makes one a first-class yogi, without losing one's individual existence.

Chapter 4, Verse 26:
श्रोत्रादीनीन्द्रियाण्यन्ये संयमाग्निषु जुह्वति । शब्दादीन्विषयानन्य इन्द्रियाग्निषु जुह्वति ॥
Translation: Some offer the hearing process and other senses into the fire of self-control, while others offer the objects of the senses into the fire of the senses.
Purport: The four divisions of human life—brahmacari (celibate student), grihastha (householder), vanaprastha (retired), and sannyasi (renunciant)—are all meant to cultivate perfection in yoga and transcendental realization. Human life is not meant for mere sense gratification like that of animals; hence, these divisions are designed to facilitate spiritual progress. Brahmacaris, guided by a genuine spiritual teacher, discipline their minds by refraining from sensual indulgence. A brahmacari focuses on hearing topics related to Krishna consciousness, as hearing is fundamental for spiritual understanding. Thus, a sincere brahmacari wholeheartedly engages in harer nämānukīrtanam—chanting and hearing the glories of the Lord. By avoiding materialistic sounds, the brahmacari's hearing is immersed in the transcendental vibrations of the Hare Krishna mantra. Similarly, householders, who have some scope for sense enjoyment, exercise moderation in such activities. While sex, intoxication, and meat-eating are prevalent in society, a regulated householder does not succumb to unrestrained indulgence in these pleasures. Marriage based on religious principles is a norm in civilized societies, as it provides a framework for controlled sensual activities. This disciplined, detached approach to marital relations can be considered a form of sacrifice (yajna), as the regulated householder sacrifices the inclination towards sense pleasure for a higher, spiritual life.``` Chapter 4, Text 26 ```

Chapter 4, Verse 27:
सर्वाणीन्द्रियकर्माणि प्राणकर्माणि चापरे । आत्मसंयमयोगाग्नौ जुह्वति ज्ञानदीपिते ॥
Translation: Others, who seek self-realization through controlling the mind and senses, offer the functions of all the senses and the life breath into the fire of self-discipline.
Purport: This verse refers to the yoga system as expounded by Patanjali. In Patanjali's Yoga-sutras, the soul is described as pratyag-ätmä and paräg-ätmä. When the soul is attached to sense enjoyment, it is known as paräg-ätmä; however, when it becomes detached from such enjoyment, it transforms into pratyag-ätmä. The soul is influenced by ten types of air functioning within the body, which can be observed through the breath. The Patanjali yoga system teaches how to regulate the body's air functions in a precise manner, so that they ultimately aid in purifying the soul from material attachments. The ultimate aim of this yoga system is to attain pratyag-ätmä, which involves disengaging from material activities. The senses interact with external objects—such as the ear for hearing, eyes for seeing, nose for smelling, tongue for tasting, and hand for touching—these activities are considered functions of präëa-väyu. The apäna-väyu moves downward, vyäna-väyu expands and contracts, samäna-väyu maintains balance, and udäna-väyu ascends. When one is enlightened, all these functions are directed towards seeking self-realization.``` Chapter 4, Text 27 ```

Chapter 4, Verse 28:

स्वाध्यायज्ञानयज्ञाश्च यतयः संशितव्रताः ॥ २८ ॥

Purport: Chapter 4, Text 28 Various forms of sacrifice are practiced by individuals seeking spiritual advancement. Similarly, in other countries, there are hospitals, retirement homes, and charitable organizations providing free education and medical aid to the less fortunate. These acts of charity are known as sacrifices of wealth. Others pursue spiritual elevation or desire to ascend to higher celestial realms by voluntarily undertaking rigorous austerities such as the candrāyaṇa or cäturmäsya vows. These practices involve strict adherence to rules governing one's conduct, such as refraining from shaving, specific dietary restrictions, limited meals, or staying away from home. Such sacrifices of material comforts are termed as sacrifices of austerity. Some individuals delve into various forms of mystic yogas like the Patanjali system (aimed at merging with the Absolute), hatha-yoga, or astanga-yoga (focused on specific attainments). Others embark on pilgrimages to sacred sites seeking spiritual perfection. These endeavors are categorized as sacrifices for achieving specific material goals. There are also those who dedicate themselves to the study of Vedic scriptures, particularly the Upanishads, Vedanta-sutras, or Sankhya philosophy. These practices are known as sacrifices of study. All these practitioners are earnestly engaged in different forms of sacrifice, aspiring for elevated states of being. However, Krishna consciousness stands apart as it entails direct service to the Supreme Lord. Attaining Krishna consciousness is not possible through any of the aforementioned sacrifices but is achievable solely through the grace of the Lord and His genuine devotees. Therefore, Krishna consciousness transcends all other forms of sacrifice.

Chapter 4, Verse 29:

Translation: Some others, dedicated to the practice of breath control for entering into deep meditation, regulate their breath by offering the outgoing breath into the incoming, and the incoming breath into the outgoing. By mastering this technique, they achieve a state of trance where all breathing ceases. Yet others, disciplined in their eating habits, offer their outgoing breath as a sacrifice to the incoming breath.
Purport: This technique of controlling the breath is known as pranayama. Initially, it is practiced in hatha yoga through various seated postures. These methods are recommended for sense control and spiritual progress. Pranayama involves manipulating the internal air currents to reverse their flow. The apana air moves downward, while the prana air moves upward. The pranayama practitioner breathes in the opposite direction until both currents are balanced in equilibrium. Exhaling into the inhaled breath is called recaka. When both air flows are completely halted, it is known as kumbhaka yoga. Through consistent practice of kumbhaka yoga, one can prolong life and advance in spiritual realization. A wise yogi seeks perfection in the current life, without waiting for future incarnations. By practicing kumbhaka yoga, yogis can extend their lifespan significantly. A devotee of Krishna, absorbed in loving service to the Lord, naturally gains mastery over the senses. Engaged in Krishna's service, the senses remain pure and unaffected. At the end of life, such a devotee transcends to the spiritual realm of Lord Krishna without striving for longevity. He attains liberation swiftly, as mentioned in the Bhagavad-gita (14.26):  mäm ca yo ’vyabhicāreṇa bhakti-yogena sevate sa guṇān samatityaitän brahma-bhūyäya kalpate  "One who engages in unwavering devotional service to the Lord transcends the material modes and is elevated to the spiritual realm." A Krishna-conscious individual begins from a transcendent state and remains in that consciousness consistently, ensuring no regression. Such a devotee swiftly enters the abode of the Lord. Restricting one's diet naturally occurs when consuming only krsna-prasadam, food offered to the Lord first. Moderating food intake greatly aids in controlling the senses, crucial for liberation from material entanglements.``` Chapter 4, Text 29 ```

Chapter 4, Verse 31:
नायं लोकोऽस्त्ययज्ञस्य कुतोऽन्यः कुरुसत्तम ॥ ३१ ॥
Translation: O best of the Kuru dynasty, without sacrifice, one cannot live happily in this world, nor in the next. What then to speak of another life?
Purport: Chapter 4, Text 31 Regardless of the form of material existence one finds oneself in, there is a pervasive ignorance about one's true spiritual nature. This ignorance leads to a cycle of reactions to past sinful actions, binding one to continued material existence. The root cause of this cycle is ignorance, and the consequence is a life entangled in sin and suffering. The human form of life offers a unique opportunity to break free from this entanglement. The Vedas provide guidance for liberation by outlining the paths of righteous living, economic stability, regulated enjoyment, and ultimately, liberation from material suffering.  Following the path of righteousness and engaging in prescribed sacrifices can address our material needs and challenges. Through sacrificial offerings, such as yajna, we can ensure an abundance of food, milk, and other necessities, even in times of population growth. Once our physical needs are met, the natural progression is towards satisfying our senses. The Vedas recommend the institution of marriage for the regulated enjoyment of the senses, leading to gradual elevation towards liberation from material bondage. The pinnacle of spiritual perfection is to establish a deep connection with the Supreme Lord.  By faithfully performing sacrifices as prescribed, one can attain perfection. If one disregards the Vedic injunctions regarding sacrifice, it is impossible to find true happiness in this life, let alone in future lives on other planets. Different heavenly realms offer varying degrees of material pleasures to those engaged in diverse forms of sacrifice. However, the supreme happiness is attained by aspiring for the spiritual planets through the practice of Krishna consciousness. Embracing a life centered on Krishna consciousness is the ultimate solution to all material tribulations and the key to eternal blissful existence.

उपदेक्ष्यन्ति ते ज्ञानं ज्ञानिनस्तत्त्वदर्शिनः ॥ ३४ ॥

The Lord is the original spiritual master, and those in the disciplic succession can transmit His teachings directly to their disciples. Spiritual realization cannot be attained through self-made methods, as adopted by misguided individuals. The Bhagavatam (6.3.19) proclaims, "Religion is the direct command of the Lord." Therefore, mere mental speculation or intellectual debates cannot guide one on the right path. Progress in spiritual life is not achieved through independent study of scriptures alone; one must approach a genuine spiritual master to receive true knowledge. Surrendering completely to the spiritual master and serving him like a humble servant, without any false pride, is crucial. A genuine spiritual master is inherently compassionate towards his disciple. When the disciple is submissive and eager to serve, the exchange of knowledge and inquiries becomes perfect.

Chapter 4, Verse 35:
यज्ज्ञात्वा न पुनर्मोहमेवं यास्यसि पाण्डव ।
येन भूतान्यशेषेण द्रक्ष्यस्यात्मन्यथो मयि ॥ ३५ ॥
Translation: Having acquired true knowledge from a self-realized soul, O Arjuna, you will not fall into such delusion again. By this knowledge, you will see that all living beings are inseparable parts of the Supreme, or in other words, they belong to Me.
Purport: Chapter 4, Text 35 Receiving knowledge from a self-realized soul, one who perceives things as they are, leads to understanding that all living entities are integral aspects of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Lord Sri Krishna. The notion of existence separate from Krishna is termed maya (mā—not, yā—this). Some may believe that they have no connection with Krishna, viewing Him solely as a significant historical figure and regarding the Absolute as the impersonal Brahman. However, as elucidated in the Bhagavad-gita, this impersonal Brahman is the radiant manifestation of Krishna's personal form. Krishna, as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, is the origin of everything. The Brahma-samhita explicitly states that Krishna is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the origin of all causes. Even the countless incarnations are merely His diverse expansions. Similarly, the living entities are also expansions of Krishna. The Mayavadi philosophers incorrectly assume that Krishna loses His distinct existence in His numerous expansions. This notion is materialistic. In the material realm, we observe that when something is fragmented, it loses its original identity. Yet, the Mayavadi philosophers fail to grasp that in the absolute realm, one plus one equals one, and one minus one also equals one. This is the nature of the absolute truth.  Due to a lack of comprehensive knowledge in the science of the absolute, we are currently enveloped in illusion, perceiving ourselves as separate from Krishna. Although we are distinct parts of Krishna, we are fundamentally not different from Him. The physical distinctions among living entities are products of maya and not actual realities. Our ultimate purpose is to please Krishna. Driven by maya, Arjuna mistakenly prioritized his temporary bodily relationships over his eternal spiritual bond with Krishna. The core teaching of the Gita revolves around this concept: as eternal servants of Krishna, living beings cannot be disconnected from Him, and their sense of individuality apart from Krishna is termed maya. As separate components of the Supreme, living entities have a specific role to play. Having forgotten this purpose since time immemorial, they inhabit various bodies, such as humans, animals, and demigods. These bodily distinctions arise from a lapse in remembering the transcendental service of the Lord. Yet, when one engages in transcendental service through Krishna consciousness, they are instantly liberated from this illusion. Such pure knowledge can only be acquired from an authentic spiritual master, enabling one to discern that the living entity is not equal to Krishna. True wisdom dictates that the Supreme Soul, Krishna, is the ultimate refuge for all living beings. When living entities forsake this refuge, they are ensnared by material energy, deluded into believing they possess a separate identity. Consequently, under various material identities, they forget Krishna. However, when these deluded entities embrace Krishna consciousness, it signifies their journey toward liberation, as affirmed in the Bhagavatam (2.10.6): muktir hitvänyathärūpaṁ svarūpeṇa vyavasthitiḥ. Liberation entails being established in one's inherent position as an eternal servitor of Krishna (Krishna consciousness).

Chapter 4, Verse 42:
तस्मादज्ञानसम्भूतं हृत्स्थं ज्ञानासिनात्मनः ।
छित्वैनं संशयं योगमातिष्ठोत्तिष्ठ भारत ॥ ४२ ॥
Translation: Therefore, O Bharata, with the sword of knowledge, cut asunder the doubts born of ignorance residing in your heart. Stand up and engage in the practice of yoga.
Purport: Chapter 4, Text 42 The yoga system elucidated in this chapter is known as sanatana-yoga, the eternal duties performed by the living entity. This yoga consists of two aspects of sacrificial activities: sacrifice of material possessions and self-realization, which is a pure spiritual endeavor. If the sacrifice of material possessions is not aimed at spiritual realization, it remains material in nature. However, when such sacrifices are performed with a spiritual purpose or in devotional service, they become perfect sacrifices. Spiritual activities are further divided into understanding one's own self, or one's inherent nature, and comprehending the truth about the Supreme Personality of Godhead. By following the teachings of Bhagavad-gita, one can easily grasp these two crucial aspects of spiritual knowledge. Such a person faces no difficulty in attaining complete understanding of the self as an integral part of the Lord. This understanding is beneficial as it enables one to comprehend the transcendental activities of the Lord.  At the beginning of this chapter, the Supreme Lord Himself discussed His transcendental activities. One who fails to comprehend the teachings of the Gita is faithless and misuses the independence granted by the Lord. Such a person, who lacks understanding of the eternal, blissful, all-knowing nature of the Lord, is indeed ignorant. Ignorance can be dispelled through gradual acceptance of the principles of Krishna consciousness. Different types of sacrifices, such as offerings to demigods, sacrifices to Brahman, celibacy, household duties, sense control, mystic yoga, penance, renunciation of material possessions, Vedic study, and adherence to varnasrama-dharma, all lead to the awakening of Krishna consciousness. These sacrifices are forms of regulated actions, with self-realization being the primary objective.  A genuine seeker of self-realization is a true student of Bhagavad-gita, while those who doubt the authority of Krishna regress. It is advised to study Bhagavad-gita, or any scripture, under a bona fide spiritual master with humility and surrender. A bona fide spiritual master belongs to an eternal lineage and faithfully follows the instructions of the Supreme Lord, passed down through the sun-god millions of years ago, from whom the teachings of Bhagavad-gita have descended to the earthly realm. Therefore, one should adhere to the path of Bhagavad-gita as instructed in the scripture itself and be cautious of those who seek personal gain and mislead others from the true path. The Supreme Lord is indeed the ultimate personality, and His activities are transcendental. One who realizes this truth is liberated from the very outset of studying Bhagavad-gita.  Thus conclude the Bhaktivedanta Purports to the Fourth Chapter of the Srimad Bhagavad-gita, in the matter of Transcendental Knowledge.

Chapter 5, Verse 1:
अर्जुन उवाच संन्यासं कर्मणां कृष्ण पुनर्योगं च शंससि । यत् श्रेय एतयोरेकं तन्मे ब्रूहि सुनिश्चितम् ॥
Translation: Arjuna asked: O Krishna, first You advise renunciation of work, and then You recommend working with devotion. Kindly tell me decisively which path is more beneficial.
Purport: In this Fifth Chapter of the Bhagavad-gita, the Lord emphasizes that engaging in work with devotion is superior to mere speculative thinking. Devotional service is more accessible as it transcends the material realm, freeing one from karmic reactions. The Second Chapter introduced the concept of the soul and its entanglement in the material body, along with the method of liberation through buddhi-yoga, or devotional service. The Third Chapter explained that a person established in knowledge is released from obligatory duties. In the Fourth Chapter, the Lord informed Arjuna that all forms of sacrificial activities lead to wisdom. However, towards the chapter's end, the Lord urged Arjuna to awaken and fight, embodying perfect knowledge. By emphasizing the significance of both work with devotion and knowledge-based renunciation, Krishna perplexed Arjuna and clouded his resolve. Arjuna believed renunciation through knowledge necessitated complete cessation of sense-driven activities. He questioned how engaging in devotional service could lead to cessation of work. Essentially, he perceived renunciation through knowledge as devoid of any activity, viewing work and renunciation as incompatible. Arjuna failed to grasp that work performed with complete understanding is devoid of reactions and is equivalent to inaction. Hence, he sought clarification on whether to renounce all activities or to engage in work with full awareness.``` Chapter 5, Text 1 ```

Chapter 5, Verse 2:
Purport: Chapter 5, Text 2 **Translation:** The Supreme Lord said: Renunciation of work and working in devotion are both pathways to spiritual elevation. However, between the two, working in devotion is superior to renunciation of work.  **Purport:** Engaging in activities solely for material enjoyment leads to bondage. Pursuing bodily comforts perpetuates the cycle of transmigration, binding the soul to material existence. The Srimad-Bhagavatam (5.5.4–6) illustrates this concept:  "Engrossed in sense gratification, people unknowingly endure the miseries of their temporary bodies, a result of past actions. Failing to inquire about their true identity, they remain entangled in fruitive pursuits, transmigrating from one body to another. To break free from this cycle, one must cultivate a love for devotional service to Vasudeva."  Mere theoretical knowledge that one is not the body is insufficient for liberation. Action in alignment with one's spiritual identity is essential to transcend material bondage. Acting in Krishna consciousness is not ordinary action driven by material desires. Actions performed with full awareness contribute to spiritual progress. Renunciation of material activities alone cannot purify the heart of a conditioned soul. Without Krishna consciousness, renunciation lacks completeness. As Srila Rupa Gosvami explains in Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu (1.2.258):  "When those desiring liberation renounce objects related to the Supreme Lord, mistaking them as material, their renunciation is deemed incomplete."  True renunciation is rooted in the understanding that everything belongs to the Supreme Lord, and no one can claim ownership. Recognizing that all is Krishna's property leads to true renunciation. Everything should be utilized in Krishna's service. This genuine practice of Krishna consciousness surpasses artificial renunciation advocated by impersonalist renunciants.

Chapter 5, Verse 3:
ज्ञेयः स नित्यसंन्यासी यो न द्वेष्टि न काङ्क्षति ।
निद्वन्द्वो हि महाबाहो सुखं बन्धात्प्रमुच्यते ॥ ३ ॥
Translation: One who neither hates nor desires the fruits of their actions is known to be always renounced. Such a person, free from all dualities, easily overcomes material bondage and is completely liberated, O mighty-armed Arjuna.
Purport: Chapter 5, Text 3 A person fully absorbed in Krishna consciousness is naturally a renunciant because they harbor neither aversion nor attachment towards the outcomes of their deeds. Such a renunciant, devoted to the divine service of the Lord, is profoundly wise as they comprehend their inherent connection with Krishna. They are fully aware that Krishna is the Supreme Absolute Truth and that they are His eternal fragment. This understanding is flawless, both in essence and in quantity. The notion of merging with Krishna is erroneous, for a part can never be equal to the whole. True transcendental knowledge lies in recognizing one's unity in quality with Krishna while acknowledging the distinction in quantity. This realization leads to inner fulfillment, devoid of any desires or regrets. Their mind is free from dualities, as every action is performed solely for the pleasure of Krishna. Liberated from the oscillations of opposing forces, such a soul attains liberation, even while existing in this material realm.

Chapter 5, Verse 4:
साङ्ख्ययोगौ पृथग्बालाः प्रवदन्ति न पण्डिताः । एकमप्यास्थितः सम्यगुभयोर्विन्दते फलम् ॥
Translation: The ignorant claim that devotional service (karma-yoga) and the analytical study of the material world (Sankhya) are separate paths. However, the truly wise understand that one who diligently follows either path attains the benefits of both.
Purport: The purpose of analyzing the material world is to discover the essence of existence, which is the soul of all creation - Vishnu, the Supersoul. Engaging in devotional service means serving the Supersoul. It is akin to either locating the root of a tree or nourishing that root. A genuine student of Sankhya philosophy identifies Vishnu as the root of the material world and, with profound understanding, dedicates oneself to serving the Lord. In essence, both paths converge in the worship of Vishnu. Those lacking deep insight may perceive Sankhya and karma-yoga as divergent, but the truly knowledgeable recognize the shared goal of these diverse practices.``` Chapter 5, Text 4 ```

Chapter 5, Verse 5:
यत् साङ्ख्यैः प्राप्यते स्थानं तद्योगैरपि गम्यते । एकं साङ्ख्यं च योगं च यः पश्यति स पश्यति ॥
Translation: One who understands that the spiritual realization achieved through analytical study can also be attained through devotional service, and thus perceives analytical study and devotional service to be equally valuable, truly perceives reality.
Purport: The essence of philosophical inquiry is to discover the ultimate purpose of life. As the ultimate aim of life is self-realization, the conclusions derived from both analytical study and devotional service are essentially the same. Through Sankhya philosophy, one comprehends that the individual soul is not a fragment of the material world but an integral part of the Supreme Spirit. Therefore, the soul is not connected to the material realm; its actions should be directed towards the Supreme. Acting in Krishna consciousness signifies being in one's natural state. In the Sankhya process, detachment from materialism is essential, while in devotional yoga, attachment to Krishna's work is pivotal. In truth, both methods are identical, despite the apparent contrast of detachment in one and attachment in the other. Detachment from materialism and attachment to Krishna are fundamentally synonymous. One who grasps this truth perceives reality as it is.``` Chapter 5, Text 5 ```

Chapter 5, Verse 6:
संन्यासस्तु महाबाहो दुःखमाप्तुमयोगतः ।
योगयुक्तो मुनिर्ब्रह्म न चिरेणाधिगच्छति ॥ ६ ॥
Translation: O mighty-armed Arjuna, renunciation alone is insufficient to attain true happiness without engaging in devotional service. However, a wise person dedicated to devotional service can swiftly attain the Supreme.
Purport: Chapter 5, Text 6 Within the renounced order of life, there exist two distinct classes of sannyasis. The Mayavadi sannyasis delve into the study of Sankhya philosophy, whereas the Vaishnava sannyasis immerse themselves in the teachings of Bhagavatam, which offer a comprehensive commentary on the Vedanta-sutras. While Mayavadi sannyasis also study the Vedanta-sutras, they rely on their own interpretation known as Sariraka-bhasya, authored by Shankaracharya. On the other hand, followers of the Bhagavata school engage in devotional service to the Lord in accordance with pancaratriki regulations. As a result, Vaishnava sannyasis are occupied with various transcendental activities in service to the Lord and are untouched by material pursuits. In contrast, Mayavadi sannyasis, absorbed in Sankhya, Vedanta, and speculative endeavors, struggle to appreciate the essence of devotional service. Their intellectual pursuits often become wearisome, prompting them to turn to the Bhagavatam without a proper understanding, leading to a cumbersome study of the Srimad-Bhagavatam.  The dry speculations and impersonal interpretations through artificial means adopted by Mayavadi sannyasis prove futile. In contrast, Vaishnava sannyasis engaged in devotional service find joy in carrying out their transcendental duties and are assured of eventual entry into the spiritual realm. At times, Mayavadi sannyasis deviate from the path of self-realization and revert to engaging in materialistic activities under the guise of philanthropy and altruism, which are merely worldly pursuits. Hence, it is evident that those immersed in Krishna consciousness are in a superior position compared to sannyasis engrossed in mere philosophical speculations about Brahman, as eventually even the latter gravitate towards Krishna consciousness after numerous lifetimes.

Chapter 5, Verse 7:
योगयुक्तो विशुद्धात्मा विजितात्मा जितेन्द्रियः ।
सर्वभूतात्मभूतात्मा कुर्वन्नपि न लिप्यते ॥ ७ ॥
Translation: One who is engaged in devotion, possesses a pure soul, and has mastered the mind and senses is beloved by all and loves all. Despite being active, such a person remains untainted.
Purport: Chapter 5, Text 7 A person walking the path of liberation through Krishna consciousness is cherished by all living beings, and in turn, holds affection for all. This mutual regard arises from their Krishna consciousness. Such an individual does not perceive any living being as separate from Krishna, much like how the leaves and branches of a tree are integral to the tree itself. Understanding that watering the tree's root nourishes all its parts, or that feeding the stomach sustains the entire body, the Krishna-conscious servant treats all beings with care, earning their love. Satisfied by his selfless service, others hold him in high esteem. His pure consciousness enables complete control over the mind and senses. With his mind steadfast on Krishna, he remains unwavering and free from distractions from the Lord. He is averse to anything unrelated to Krishna—be it in speech, food, or activity. His senses are thus regulated. A person with disciplined senses does not cause harm to others. One might question, "Was Arjuna not in Krishna consciousness when he engaged in battle and seemingly acted aggressively?" However, as explained earlier, the soul is eternal and cannot be destroyed; hence, no one truly perished on the battlefield. By Krishna's will, only their physical forms were altered. Arjuna, fighting on Kurukshetra, was essentially executing Krishna's commands in full consciousness of the Lord. Such a person remains unentangled in the consequences of his actions.

Chapter 5, Verse 10:
ब्रह्मण्याधाय कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा करोति यः ।
लिप्यते न स पापेन पद्मपत्रमिवाम्भसा ॥ १० ॥
Translation: One who performs their duties without attachment, surrendering the results unto the Supreme Lord, is unaffected by sinful actions, like a lotus leaf untouched by water.
Purport: Chapter 5, Text 10 In this context, "brahmaëi" refers to being in Krishna consciousness. The material world is a manifestation of the three modes of material nature, known as pradhana. Vedic hymns such as "sarvam hy etad brahma" (Mäṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 2), "tasmäd etad brahma näma-rūpam annaṁ ca jäyate" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.10), and the Bhagavad-gita (14.3) affirm that everything in the material world is a manifestation of Brahman. Although the effects manifest differently, they are inseparable from the cause. The İsopanisad teaches that everything is connected to the Supreme Brahman, Krishna, and therefore all things belong to Him alone. One who fully comprehends that everything belongs to Krishna, that He is the ultimate proprietor, and that everything is meant for His service, naturally remains detached from the outcomes of their actions, whether good or bad. Even one's physical body, given by the Lord for specific actions, can be engaged in Krishna consciousness. In this state, it remains untainted by sinful reactions, just as a lotus leaf, though in water, remains dry. The Gita (3.30) also instructs, "mayi sarväṇi karmäṇi sannyasya": "Offer all works unto Me [Krishna]." In essence, a person lacking Krishna consciousness acts based on the body and senses, while one in Krishna consciousness acts with the understanding that the body belongs to Krishna and should be utilized in His service.

Chapter 5, Verse 11:
कायेन मनसा बुद्ध्या केवलैरिन्द्रियैरपि ।
योगिनः कर्म कुर्वन्ति सङ्गं त्यक्त्वात्मशुद्धये ॥ ११ ॥
Translation: The yogis, renouncing attachment, perform actions with their body, mind, and intellect, and even through their senses, solely for the purification of the self.
Purport: Chapter 5, Text 11 When one engages in activities in Krishna consciousness to please the senses of Krishna, all actions, whether physical, mental, intellectual, or sensory, become free from material contamination. A Krishna conscious person faces no material repercussions from their actions. Thus, purified actions, known as sad-äcära, can be effortlessly carried out by those acting in Krishna consciousness. Sri Rupa Gosvami, in his Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu (1.2.187), explains this concept as follows:  "ihä yasya harer däsye karmaṇā manasā girā nikhilāsv apy avasthāsu jīvanmuktaḥ sa ucyate"  A person who acts in Krishna consciousness, serving Krishna with their body, mind, intellect, and speech, is considered liberated even while living in the material world, despite engaging in various activities. Such a person is free from false ego because they do not identify themselves with their material body or claim ownership over it. They understand that they are not the body but belong to Krishna, and that the body also belongs to Krishna. By dedicating everything—whether it be physical, mental, intellectual, verbal, or material possessions—to the service of Krishna, they become completely aligned with Him. They merge with Krishna, transcending the misconception that they are the body. This state represents the pinnacle of Krishna consciousness.

Chapter 5, Verse 12:
युक्तः कर्मफलम् त्यक्त्वा शान्तिमाप्नोति नैष्ठिकीम् ।
अयुक्तः कामका रेण फले सक्तो निबध्यते ॥ १२ ॥
Translation: The steadfastly devoted soul attains unadulterated peace by relinquishing the fruits of actions to Me; whereas a person not united with the Divine, who is attached to desires and the results of their labor, becomes ensnared.
Purport: Chapter 5, Text 12 The distinction between a person in Krishna consciousness and one in bodily consciousness lies in their attachment. The former is devoted to Krishna, while the latter is fixated on the outcomes of their endeavors. The individual who is dedicated to Krishna and serves Him exclusively is truly liberated, devoid of anxieties about the results of their actions. In the Bhagavatam, anxiety over outcomes is attributed to perceiving duality, lacking knowledge of the Absolute Truth. Krishna is the Supreme Absolute Truth, the Personification of Godhead. In Krishna consciousness, duality dissolves. Everything emanates from Krishna’s energy, and He is supremely benevolent. Thus, actions in Krishna consciousness are transcendent, beyond material repercussions. One experiences profound peace in Krishna consciousness. Conversely, those entangled in calculating profits for sensory gratification cannot attain such peace. The essence of Krishna consciousness lies in realizing that nothing exists apart from Krishna, leading to a state of tranquility and fearlessness.

Chapter 5, Verse 13:
सर्वकर्माणि मनसा संन्यस्यास्ते सुखं वशी ।
नवद्वारे पुरे देही नैव कुर्वन् न कारयन् ॥ १३ ॥
Translation: When the embodied being renounces all actions in the mind, they reside contentedly, mastering happiness. Dwelling within the city with nine gates, they neither act themselves nor cause others to act.
Purport: Chapter 5, Text 13 The embodied soul resides in the city with nine gates, symbolizing the physical body. The body's functions are automated by its inherent modes of nature. Despite being influenced by the body's conditions, the soul can transcend them through will. Due to forgetting their divine essence, the soul identifies solely with the material body, leading to suffering. Through Krishna consciousness, one can reawaken their true nature and transcend bodily entrapment. Thus, embracing Krishna consciousness enables one to detach from bodily engagements. In this state of control, where one's perspectives shift, they find joy within the city of nine gates. The nine gates are described as follows:  nava-dväre pure dehi haṁso leläyate bahiḥ vasī sarvasya lokasya sthävarasya carasya ca  "The Supreme Personality of Godhead, residing within every living being, governs all entities across the universe. The body comprises nine gates—two eyes, two nostrils, two ears, one mouth, the anus, and the genitals. In the conditioned state, the living being identifies themselves with the body. However, upon recognizing the Lord within, they attain the same freedom as the Lord, even while in the body." (Svetasvatara Upanishad 3.18)  Therefore, a Krishna-conscious individual transcends both external and internal bodily activities.

Chapter 5, Verse 14:
न कर्तृत्वं न कर्माणि लोकस्य सृजति प्रभुः ।
न कर्मफलसंयोगं स्वभावस्तु प्रवर्तते ॥ १४ ॥
Translation: The embodied soul, the master of the body, does not create actions, nor does he induce people to act, nor does he create the fruits of actions. All these are carried out by the modes of material nature.
Purport: Chapter 5, Text 14 As explained in the Seventh Chapter, the living entity is one of the energies of the Supreme Lord, distinct from the material nature, which is another energy, considered inferior. The soul, the superior nature, has been entangled with material nature since time immemorial. The temporary material body he acquires becomes the platform for various activities and their consequences. Dwelling in this conditional state, one experiences the reactions of bodily actions by mistakenly identifying with the body. This ignorance, accumulated over countless lifetimes, is the root cause of suffering and distress. By disassociating from bodily activities, the soul transcends the reactions. While seemingly the master of the body while residing within it, in reality, the soul is neither the owner nor the controller of its actions and consequences. Like a person struggling in an ocean, tossed by its waves beyond his control, the soul in the material world is buffeted by circumstances. The ultimate solution lies in attaining transcendental Krishna consciousness, which liberates the soul from all turmoil.

Chapter 5, Verse 15:
नादत्ते कस्यचित् पापं न चैव सुकृतं विभुः ।
ज्ञानेनावृतं ज्ञानं तेन मुह्यन्ति जन्तवः ॥ १५ ॥
Translation: The Supreme Lord does not take on anyone's sins or merits. However, due to ignorance that covers their true knowledge, beings become deluded.
Purport: Chapter 5, Text 15 The term "vibhu" in Sanskrit refers to the Supreme Lord who possesses boundless knowledge, wealth, strength, fame, beauty, and renunciation. He remains content within Himself, unperturbed by sinful or virtuous deeds. The Lord does not orchestrate specific circumstances for any living being. It is the living being, clouded by ignorance, who desires to experience certain life situations, thus initiating a cycle of actions and reactions. By nature, the living being is endowed with knowledge, yet due to limited power, they are susceptible to ignorance. While the Lord is all-powerful, the living being is minute in comparison. The Lord is omniscient, whereas the living being is atomic. As a living soul, the being has the ability to willfully desire. Only the omnipotent Lord can fulfill these desires. When a being is ensnared by their desires, the Lord allows them to manifest, yet the Lord is not accountable for the ensuing actions and reactions. In a state of confusion, the embodied soul identifies with the temporary material body and becomes subject to fleeting joys and sorrows in life. The Lord, as the Paramatma or Supersoul, constantly accompanies the living being and comprehends their desires, akin to sensing the fragrance of a flower in proximity. Desire serves as a subtle form of conditioning for the living being. The Lord fulfills desires according to deserving: man proposes, God disposes. The individual lacks omnipotence in fulfilling their desires, while the Lord can fulfill all desires. Being impartial, the Lord does not interfere with the desires of the independent living entities. However, when one desires Krishna, the Lord provides special care and encourages a path towards Him for eternal happiness. The Vedic hymns affirm, "The Lord engages the living entity in virtuous acts for elevation and in sinful acts for descent to hell." (Kausitaki Upanishad 3.8)  ajño jantur anīśo ’yam ätmanaḥ sukha-duḥkhayoḥ īśvara-prerito gacchet svargaṁ väśv abhram eva ca  “The living entity is completely dependent in his distress and happiness. By the will of the Supreme, he can ascend to heaven or descend to hell, as a cloud is moved by the wind.”  Hence, the embodied soul, due to an ancient aversion to Krishna consciousness, deludes themselves. Though inherently eternal, blissful, and aware, due to their limited existence, they forget their natural state of serving the Lord and become ensnared by ignorance. Under the veil of ignorance, the living being falsely attributes their conditional existence to the Lord. This is also affirmed in the Vedanta-sutras (2.1.34), stating, “The Lord neither favors nor disfavors anyone, though it may seem so.”

Chapter 5, Verse 16:
ज्ञानेन तु तदज्ञानं येषां नाशितमात्मनः । तेषामादित्यवज्ज्ञानं प्रकाशयति तत् परम् ॥
Translation: But for those whose ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge, that knowledge reveals the Supreme, like the sun illuminating all things.
Purport: Those who have forgotten Krishna may be bewildered, but those in Krishna consciousness are not. In the Bhagavad-gita, it is said that knowledge is like a boat to cross the ocean of material existence, and that the fire of knowledge burns all reactions to work. True knowledge is attained by surrendering to Krishna, as stated in Chapter Seven, Verse 19: "After many births and deaths, one who is in full knowledge surrenders to Me." When one attains Krishna consciousness, everything is revealed, just as the sun reveals all in the daytime. The living entity is often misled; for example, claiming to be God is a grave mistake. If one were truly God, how could they be deluded by ignorance? This would imply that ignorance is more powerful than God, which is absurd. True knowledge can be gained from a bona fide spiritual master who is in perfect Krishna consciousness. Therefore, one must seek out such a guru to learn the path of Krishna consciousness. This divine knowledge will dispel all ignorance, just as the sun dispels darkness. Even if one understands they are not the body but a spiritual being, they may still struggle to differentiate between the soul and the Supreme Soul. By taking shelter of a genuine Krishna conscious spiritual master, one can attain complete understanding. To truly know God and one's relationship with Him, one must meet a representative of God. A genuine spiritual guide never claims to be God, but is honored as such due to their deep knowledge of God. It is essential to discern the difference between God and the individual soul. Lord Sri Krishna emphasizes in the Second Chapter that every living being and the Lord are distinct individuals, both in the past, present, and future, even after liberation. In the darkness of night, everything appears as one, but in the light of day, each entity is seen in its true form. Recognizing individuality within spiritual existence is true wisdom.``` Chapter 5, Text 16 ```

Chapter 5, Verse 17:
तद्बुद्धयस्तदात्मानस्तन्निष्ठास्तत्परायणाः । गच्छन्त्यपुनरावृत्तिं ज्ञाननिर्धूतकल्मषाः ॥
Translation: When one's intelligence, mind, faith, and devotion are all fixed on the Supreme, they are completely purified of doubts through true knowledge. Such individuals proceed directly on the path of liberation.
Purport: The Supreme Transcendental Truth is Lord Krishna, as declared in the Bhagavad-gita. This truth is the essence of all Vedic literature. Para-tattva refers to the Supreme Reality, known to the enlightened as Brahman, Paramatma, and Bhagavän. Bhagavän, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, represents the pinnacle of the Absolute Truth. As Lord Krishna affirms, "There is nothing superior to Me, O Arjuna." The impersonal Brahman is also upheld by Krishna. Thus, in every aspect, Krishna embodies the Supreme Reality. One who constantly directs their mind, intellect, faith, and devotion towards Krishna, or in other words, one who is fully absorbed in Krishna consciousness, is cleansed of all doubts and attains comprehensive knowledge of the transcendental realm. A Krishna conscious individual comprehends the dual nature of Krishna—simultaneously as the Supreme and as an individual. Armed with this transcendental wisdom, one can steadily progress on the path to liberation.``` Chapter 5, Text 17 ```

Chapter 5, Verse 18:
विद्याविनयसम्पन्ने ब्राह्मणे गवि हस्तिनि । शुनि चैव श्वपाके च पण्डिताः समदर्शिनः ॥
Translation: The wise, endowed with true knowledge and humility, see with equal vision a learned and gentle brahmana, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and even an outcaste.
Purport: A person devoted to Krishna consciousness does not discriminate based on species or caste. While society may differentiate between a brahmana and an outcaste, or between a dog, a cow, and an elephant based on their species, a spiritually enlightened person views these distinctions as insignificant. This is because such a person recognizes the presence of the Supreme Lord in all beings. The Lord, in His aspect as the Supersoul, resides within the heart of every living being. Understanding this connection to the Supreme is true wisdom.  Regardless of one's social status or species, the Lord shows equal compassion to all, as He considers every living being as a friend while maintaining His position as the Supersoul. The Supersoul exists within both the outcaste and the brahmana, even though their physical bodies differ. Bodies are products of material nature influenced by various modes, but the soul and the Supersoul within them are of the same spiritual essence. Although the soul and the Supersoul share similar qualities of consciousness, eternity, and bliss, they differ in their scope: the individual soul is aware only within its own body, whereas the Supersoul is aware of all bodies.  A person dedicated to Krishna consciousness comprehends this truth fully, possessing true wisdom and an impartial perspective. Both the soul and the Supersoul share the qualities of consciousness, eternity, and bliss, but the Supersoul's awareness extends to all bodies, transcending distinctions.``` Chapter 5, Text 18 ```

Chapter 5, Verse 19:
इहैव तैर्जितः सर्गो येषां साम्ये स्थितं मनः । निर्दोषं हि समं ब्रह्म तस्माद् ब्रह्मणि ते स्थिताः ॥
Translation: Those whose minds are steadfast in equanimity have already conquered the cycle of birth and death. They are pure like Brahman, and thus they abide in Brahman.
Purport: Equanimity of mind, as mentioned above, is a hallmark of self-realization. Those who have truly reached this state are considered to have transcended material existence, particularly the cycle of birth and death. As long as one identifies with the physical body, they are bound by material limitations. However, upon attaining equanimity through self-realization, one is liberated from worldly bondage. This signifies freedom from repeated births in the material realm and the ability to enter the spiritual realm after death. Just as the Lord is faultless due to being free from attachment and aversion, an individual who is devoid of such dualities also becomes faultless and qualified to enter the spiritual realm. Such individuals are already liberated, and their characteristics are further elaborated below.""" Chapter 5, Text 19 """

Chapter 5, Verse 20:
न प्रहृष्येत् प्रियं प्राप्य नोद्विजेत् प्राप्य चाप्रियम् ।
स्थिरबुद्धिरसम्मूढो ब्रह्मविद् ब्रह्मणि स्थितः ॥ २० ॥
Translation: One who neither exults on attaining something pleasant nor despairs when encountering the unpleasant, who possesses unwavering intellect, is free from delusion, and is well-versed in the knowledge of the Supreme, is established in the Absolute Truth.
Purport: Chapter 5, Text 20 The characteristics of a self-realized individual are delineated here. Firstly, such a person is not deceived by the false identification of the body with the true self. He fully comprehends that he is not the physical body but an infinitesimal part of the Supreme Lord. Consequently, he does not find joy in material gains nor sorrow in material losses related to the body. This mental composure is known as sthira-buddhi, or self-intelligence. He remains unperplexed, recognizing the distinction between the gross body and the soul, and does not mistake the impermanent body for the eternal soul. This understanding enables him to grasp the complete understanding of the Absolute Truth, encompassing Brahman, Paramatma, and Bhagavän. He accurately discerns his inherent position without attempting to merge entirely with the Supreme. This realization is known as Brahman realization or self-realization. Such unwavering awareness is termed Krishna consciousness.
