Chapter 7, Verse 14:
दैवी ह्येषा गुणमयी मम माया दुरत्यया ।
मामेव ये प्रपद्यन्ते मायामेतां तरन्ति ते ॥ १४ ॥
Translation: This divine energy of Mine, consisting of the three modes of material nature, is difficult to overcome. However, those who surrender unto Me can easily transcend it.
Purport: Chapter 7, Text 14 The Supreme Personality of Godhead possesses innumerable energies, all of which are divine. Although living entities are part of His energies and are therefore divine, their original superior power is obscured by contact with material energy. This covering by material energy makes it impossible to overcome its influence. As previously mentioned, both material and spiritual natures, being emanations from the Supreme Personality of Godhead, are eternal. Living entities belong to the eternal superior nature of the Lord, but due to contamination by the inferior nature of matter, their illusion is also eternal. The conditioned soul is hence termed nityabaddha, or eternally conditioned. No one can trace the history of how they became conditioned at a certain point in material history. Therefore, liberation from the clutches of material nature is very challenging, even though material nature is an inferior energy, as it is ultimately governed by the supreme will, which the living entity cannot overcome. Despite being inferior, material nature is termed divine nature due to its divine connection and movement by divine will. Operated by divine will, material nature, although inferior, acts marvelously in the creation and destruction of the cosmic manifestation. The Vedas affirm this, stating, "māyāṁ tu prakṛtiṁ vidyān māyinam tu maheśvaram," meaning, "Although illusion is false or temporary, the background of illusion is the supreme magician, the Personality of Godhead, who is Maheśvara, the supreme controller" (Svetasvatara Upanishad 4.10).  Another interpretation of guṇa is rope; it signifies that the conditioned soul is tightly bound by the ropes of illusion. Just as a person bound by hands and feet cannot free themselves and requires assistance from someone unbound, the conditioned soul needs help from a liberated person. Since the bound cannot help themselves, the rescuer must be liberated. Therefore, only Lord Krishna or His authorized representative, the spiritual master, can liberate the conditioned soul. Without such superior assistance, one cannot break free from the bondage of material nature. Devotional service, or Krishna consciousness, facilitates such liberation. Krishna, as the Lord of illusory energy, can command this insurmountable energy to release the conditioned soul out of His causeless mercy towards the surrendered soul and His paternal affection for the living entity, who is originally a beloved son of the Lord. Thus, surrendering unto the lotus feet of the Lord is the sole means to escape the clutches of stringent material nature.  The phrase "māṁ eva" is also significant, where "māṁ" refers specifically to Krishna (Vishnu) and not Brahma or Shiva. Although Brahma and Shiva are highly exalted and nearly on the level of Vishnu, incarnations influenced by rajo-guṇa (passion) and tamo-guṇa (ignorance) cannot deliver the conditioned soul from maya's grip. In other words, both Brahma and Shiva are also under the sway of maya. Only Vishnu is the master of maya and thus the sole bestower of release to the conditioned soul. The Vedas confirm this in the phrase "tam eva viditvā," signifying that "Freedom is attainable only through understanding Krishna." Even Lord Shiva acknowledges that liberation can only be granted through the mercy of Vishnu, affirming, "mukti-pradātā sarveṣāṁ viṣṇur eva na saṁśayaḥ," meaning, "There is no doubt that Vishnu is the deliverer of liberation for everyone."

Chapter 7, Verse 15:
न मां दुष्कृतिनो मूढाः प्रपद्यन्ते नराधमाः ।
माययापहृतज्ञाना आसुरं भावमाश्रिताः ॥ १५ ॥
Translation: Those who are miscreants, grossly foolish, lowest among mankind, whose knowledge is stolen by illusion, and who embrace the atheistic nature of demons, do not surrender unto Me.
Purport: Chapter 7, Text 15 In the Bhagavad-gita, it is stated that by surrendering to the lotus feet of the Supreme Personality Krishna, one can transcend the stringent laws of material nature. This raises a question: Why do educated philosophers, scientists, businessmen, administrators, and leaders not surrender to Sri Krishna, the all-powerful Personality of Godhead? These leaders of society strive for liberation from material nature through various methods and endeavors over many lifetimes. Yet, if liberation can be attained simply by surrendering to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, why do these intelligent and hard-working individuals not choose this straightforward path?  The Gita provides a candid response. Truly learned leaders like Brahma, Shiva, Kapila, the Kumaras, Manu, Vyasa, Devala, Asita, Janaka, Prahlada, Bali, and later personalities such as Madhvacarya, Ramanujacarya, and Sri Caitanya, who are philosophers, politicians, educators, and scientists, surrender to the lotus feet of the all-powerful Supreme Person. On the contrary, those who falsely claim to be philosophers, scientists, educators, or administrators for material gain reject the path of the Supreme Lord. Lacking knowledge of God, they devise their own worldly plans, only complicating the problems of material existence in their futile attempts to solve them. Due to the immense power of material energy, it thwarts the unauthorized schemes of atheists and bewilders their knowledge.  The atheistic schemers are referred to as duṣkṛtinaḥ, or "miscreants." Kṛtī denotes one who has performed virtuous deeds. The atheist planner may indeed be intelligent and accomplished, as executing any grand plan, whether good or bad, demands intelligence. However, since the atheist's intellect is misdirected in opposition to the Supreme Lord's plan, they are termed duṣkṛtī, signifying that their intelligence and efforts are misguided.  The Gita unequivocally states that material energy operates under the direction of the Supreme Lord and possesses no independent authority. It functions akin to how a shadow moves in accordance with the object's movements. Nonetheless, material energy is potent, and due to their godless disposition, atheists cannot comprehend its workings or the plan of the Supreme Lord. Ensnared by illusion and the modes of passion and ignorance, their plans are thwarted, as seen in the cases of Hiranyakashipu and Ravana—despite their material erudition as scientists, philosophers, administrators, and educators. These miscreants, known as duskritinah, manifest in four distinct types, as delineated below.  (1) The mūḍhas, or grossly foolish individuals, resemble hardworking beasts of burden. They seek to enjoy the fruits of their labor exclusively and are unwilling to part with them for the Supreme. An apt analogy is the ass, toiling tirelessly for its master without understanding the purpose. Similarly, the foolish fruitive worker remains content with meager material gains, engrossed in relentless labor for illusory masters, oblivious to the true purpose of karma (action).  Often, those engrossed in ceaseless labor claim they lack time to contemplate the eternal nature of the soul. Material acquisitions, though transient, become their sole focus, even though they enjoy only a fraction of the fruits of their labor. They endure sleepless nights pursuing material gains, neglecting their health, and subsisting on minimal sustenance, all while tirelessly serving illusory masters. Ignorant of the ultimate master, these foolish workers squander their time serving material wealth, failing to surrender to the supreme master of all masters or to seek knowledge from authentic sources. Just as swine prefer filth over delectable sweets, the foolish workers incessantly pursue transient pleasures of the material world, neglecting the eternal spiritual essence that governs material existence.  (2) Another category of duṣkṛtī, or miscreants, are termed narādhama, the lowest among mankind. Nara signifies human beings, and adhama denotes the lowest. Among the 8,400,000 species of life, there are 400,000 human species, with some existing in primitive states. Civilized individuals adhere to societal, political, and religious regulations. However, those socially and politically advanced yet devoid of religious principles fall into the narādhama category. Religion devoid of acknowledgment of God's supremacy lacks true essence, as religious principles aim to unveil the Supreme Truth and man's relationship with Him.  The civilized human existence aims to rekindle consciousness of the eternal bond with the Supreme Truth, the all-powerful Personality of Godhead Sri Krishna. Those who squander this opportunity are deemed narādhama. Scriptures reveal that even in the womb, a distressed infant implores God for deliverance, promising devotion upon birth. Seeking divine consciousness in children is the duty of guardians. The reformatory ceremonies prescribed in the Manu-smṛti aim to revive God consciousness within the varnasrama system. Regrettably, these practices are largely abandoned worldwide today, resulting in a predominance of narādhama in society.  When the majority descends to narādhama status, their education holds no value against the overpowering force of nature. According to the Gita's standard, true erudition lies in viewing the learned brahmana, the dog, the cow, the elephant, and the outcaste on equal footing—a perspective embraced by genuine devotees. Sri Nityananda Prabhu, the divine master and incarnation of Godhead, exemplified mercy by uplifting the typical narādhama, the brothers Jagai and Madhai. Thus, condemned narādhama can revive their spiritual consciousness solely through the grace of a devotee.  (3) The mäyayāpahṛta-jñānāḥ represent another class of miscreants, individuals whose erudition is nullified by illusory material energy. Often highly learned—be it philosophers, poets, scholars, or scientists—they are misled by illusion, disobeying the Supreme Lord.  Even among scholars of the Bhagavad-gita, many fall into the mäyayāpahṛta-jñānāḥ category today. The Gita straightforwardly proclaims Sri Krishna as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, unequalled and supreme, the father of Brahma and all beings. Sri Krishna is not merely Brahma's father but the progenitor of all life forms, the source of the impersonal Brahman and Paramatma. Surrendering to His lotus feet is advised to all, yet the mäyayāpahṛta-jñānāḥ mock the Supreme Lord, perceiving Him as a mere mortal. Unaware that human life's blessed form mirrors the eternal, transcendental aspect of the Supreme Lord, they deviate from the truth.  The unauthorized interpretations of the Gita by mäyayāpahṛta-jñānāḥ, outside the paramparā system, obstruct spiritual understanding. These deluded interpreters neither surrender to Sri Krishna's lotus feet nor guide others to do so.  (4) The final category of miscreants, äsuraṁ bhāvam āśritāḥ, openly embrace atheistic principles. Some argue that the Supreme Lord cannot descend into the material realm without providing substantial reasoning. Others subordinate Him to the impersonal aspect, contrary to the Gita's teachings. Envious of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, atheists concoct numerous illicit incarnations in their minds, dismissing Sri Krishna's lotus feet.  Sri Yamunacharya Albandaru of South India aptly expressed, "O my Lord! Despite Your extraordinary qualities, features, and activities, despite confirmation of Your divine nature in sacred scriptures and recognition by eminent authorities renowned for their profound knowledge in transcendental science and divine qualities, those entrenched in atheistic ideologies remain oblivious to You."  Hence, individuals who are (1) grossly foolish, (2) the lowest of mankind, (3) deluded speculators, and (4) professed atheists, as described above, fail to surrender to the Personality of Godhead, disregarding all scriptural and authoritative counsel.

Chapter 7, Verse 16:
Translation: O best among the Bharatas, four types of virtuous individuals worship Me, O Arjuna. They are the distressed, the seekers of wealth, the curious, and those in pursuit of knowledge of the Absolute Truth.
Purport: Chapter 7, Text 16 Unlike the wicked, these individuals adhere to the principles outlined in scriptures. They are known as sukritinah, meaning they follow the rules and regulations of the scriptures, moral and social laws, and are somewhat devoted to the Supreme Lord. Among them, there are four categories of people—those who experience distress, those in need of material wealth, the curious, and those seeking knowledge of the Absolute Truth. They approach the Supreme Lord for devotional service under various circumstances. However, they are not pure devotees as they have personal aspirations while engaging in devotional service. Pure devotion is selfless, without any material desires or expectations of gain. The Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu (1.1.11) defines pure devotion as follows:  "One should render transcendental loving service to the Supreme Lord Krishna favorably and without desire for material profit or gain through fruitive activities or philosophical speculation. That is called pure devotional service."  When these four types of individuals seek devotional service from the Supreme Lord and are purified through association with a genuine devotee, they too become pure devotees. For the wicked, engaging in devotional service is challenging due to their self-centered lives devoid of spiritual goals. Nevertheless, some of them, by chance, may encounter a pure devotee and also become pure devotees.  Those engrossed in material activities approach the Lord in times of distress and, in the company of pure devotees, become devotees of the Lord. Those who are disheartened also seek the association of pure devotees out of curiosity to learn about God. Similarly, when rationalists face failures in their pursuit of knowledge, they may develop a desire to learn about God. They then turn to the Supreme Lord for devotional service, transcending their knowledge of the impersonal Brahman and the localized Paramatma, and embracing the personal conception of Godhead through the grace of the Supreme Lord or His pure devotee. Ultimately, when the distressed, the curious, the seekers of knowledge, and those in need of wealth are free from all material desires and realize that material gains do not contribute to spiritual progress, they become pure devotees. Until they reach this purified state, devotees engaged in transcendental service may be tainted by fruitive activities and the pursuit of worldly knowledge. Thus, one must transcend these before attaining the stage of pure devotional service.

Chapter 7, Verse 17:
तेषां ज्ञानी नित्ययुक्त एकभक्तिर्विशिष्यते ।
प्रियो हि ज्ञानिनोऽत्यर्थमहं स च मम प्रियः ॥ १७ ॥
Translation: Among them, the one who is constantly united with knowledge and singular devotion is exceptional. For I am exceedingly dear to the wise, and he is dear to Me.
Purport: Chapter 7, Text 17 Those free from material desires—be they distressed, curious, destitute, or seekers of ultimate truth—can all become pure devotees. Yet, among them, the individual who comprehends the Absolute Truth and is devoid of material attachments truly becomes a pure devotee of the Supreme Lord. According to the Lord, among the four categories, the devotee who possesses complete knowledge and simultaneously engages in devotional service is considered the most superior. Through the pursuit of knowledge, one realizes the distinction between the self and the material body. As one progresses further, one attains knowledge of the impersonal Brahman and the Supersoul. Upon complete purification, one recognizes their inherent position as the eternal servant of God. By associating with pure devotees, the curious, distressed, seekers of material gain, and the knowledgeable all transform into pure beings. However, in the preliminary stage, the individual who possesses full awareness of the Supreme Lord and actively practices devotional service holds a special place in the Lord's heart. Those situated in profound knowledge of the transcendental nature of the Supreme Personality of God are so safeguarded in their devotion that material contamination cannot affect them.

Chapter 7, Verse 18:
उदाराः सर्व एवैते ज्ञानी त्वात्मैव मे मतम् ।
आस्थितः स हि युक्तात्मा मामेवानुत्तमां गतिम् ॥ १८ ॥
Translation: All these devotees are certainly generous souls, but the one who is established in knowledge of Me is considered by Me as My very self. Engaged in My transcendental service, such a devotee is certain to attain Me, the ultimate and highest destination.
Purport: Chapter 7, Text 18 It is not that devotees with less knowledge are not beloved to the Lord. The Lord considers all to be generous because anyone who approaches the Lord for any reason is deemed a mahätmä, a great soul. Those devotees who seek material gains through their devotional service are also accepted by the Lord due to the exchange of affection. They ask the Lord for material benefits out of love, and upon receiving them, they become satisfied and progress in their devotion. However, a devotee with complete knowledge is especially dear to the Lord because their sole purpose is to lovingly serve the Supreme Lord. Such a devotee cannot bear to be away from the Lord even for a moment. Likewise, the Supreme Lord holds great affection for His devotee and is inseparable from them.  In the Srimad-Bhagavatam (9.4.68), the Lord states:  sädhavo hṛdayaṁ mahyaṁ sädhūnāṁ hṛdayaṁ tv aham madanyat te na jänanti nähaṁ tebhyo manäg api  “The devotees reside in My heart, and I reside in the hearts of the devotees. The devotee knows nothing beyond Me, and I cannot forget the devotee. There exists an intimate bond between Me and the pure devotees. Pure devotees, possessing complete knowledge, are always in spiritual communion with Me, and therefore, they are extremely dear to Me.”

Chapter 7, Verse 19:
Translation: At the end of many births and deaths, the wise one surrenders to Me, knowing Me as the ultimate cause of all beings. Such a great soul is rare to find.
Purport: Chapter 7, Text 19 Through many lifetimes of devotion and spiritual practices, a soul may come to realize that the Supreme Lord is the ultimate goal of spiritual attainment. Initially, there may be a tendency towards impersonalism as one tries to detach from material desires. However, as one progresses, they understand that true spiritual life involves devotional activities. Recognizing this, the soul becomes devoted to the Supreme Lord and surrenders completely. At this stage, one comprehends that Lord Krishna's mercy is paramount, He is the origin of everything, and the material world is not separate from Him. The soul perceives the material realm as a distorted reflection of the spiritual reality and sees everything in relation to Lord Krishna. This universal vision leads to complete surrender to Lord Krishna as the highest aspiration. Such surrendered souls are exceedingly rare.  This verse is elaborated upon beautifully in the Svetasvatara Upanishad (3.14-15) and the Chandogya Upanishad (5.1.15), emphasizing the central importance of the Supreme Lord in all aspects of existence. Just as life is the essence of all bodily functions, Lord Vasudeva (Sri Krishna) is the essence of all creation. The powers of speech, sight, hearing, and thought hold significance only when connected to the Supreme Lord. Recognizing the all-pervasive nature of Vasudeva, the devotee surrenders with full understanding, as highlighted in the Bhagavad Gita (7.17, 11.40).

Chapter 7, Verse 20:
कामैस्तैस्तैर्हृतज्ञानाः प्रपद्यन्तेsन्यदेवताः । तं तं नियममास्थाय प्रकृत्या नियताः स्वया ॥
Translation: Those whose wisdom is overtaken by material desires surrender to various demigods and adhere to specific rituals and worship practices based on their individual natures.
Purport: Individuals who have transcended material attachments surrender to the Supreme Lord and engage in devotional service to Him. Until one is completely purified of material influences, they naturally tend towards non-devotional activities. However, even those with material desires who turn to the Supreme Lord are not deeply entangled in external attractions; by pursuing the right path, they swiftly overcome material lust. The Srimad-Bhagavatam advises that whether one is a pure devotee free from material desires, filled with material aspirations, or seeking liberation from material entanglements, they should all surrender to Vasudeva and worship Him. As stated in the Bhagavatam (2.3.10):  akāmaḥ sarvakāmo vä mokṣakāma udäradhih tivreṇa bhakti-yogena yajeta puruṣaṁ param  Those lacking spiritual insight often seek refuge in demigods to promptly fulfill material desires. Typically, such individuals do not turn to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, as they are influenced by the lower modes of nature (ignorance and passion) and therefore worship various demigods. Adhering to the prescribed rites and rituals, they find contentment. Worshippers of demigods are driven by petty desires and lack awareness of the ultimate goal, unlike a devotee of the Supreme Lord who is guided on the right path. The Vedic scriptures recommend worshipping different deities for specific purposes (e.g., the sun for healing ailing individuals), leading non-devotees to believe that demigods are superior to the Supreme Lord for certain needs. However, a true devotee recognizes Lord Krishna as the master of all. As affirmed in Caitanya-caritamrita (Adi 5.142), "ekale isvara krsna, ära saba bhrtya": only the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krishna, is the master, while all others are His servants. Hence, a sincere devotee does not turn to demigods for material fulfillment but relies solely on the Supreme Lord, finding contentment in whatever He bestows upon them.``` Chapter 7, Text 20 ```

Chapter 7, Verse 21:
यो यो यां यां तनुं भक्तः श्रद्धयार्चितुमिच्छति ।
तस्य तस्याचलां श्रद्धां तामेव विदधाम्यहम् ॥ २१ ॥
Translation: I am present in the heart of all beings as the Supersoul. Whenever someone wishes to worship a particular deity with faith, I make their faith unwavering towards that deity.
Purport: Chapter 7, Text 21 The Supreme Lord has granted free will to all beings. When an individual earnestly desires material pleasures and seeks the favor of material demigods, the Supreme Lord, as the Supersoul within everyone's heart, recognizes their intentions and facilitates their desires. As the ultimate father of all beings, He respects their independence and provides opportunities for them to fulfill their material aspirations. One may question why the all-powerful God allows living beings to indulge in material enjoyment and become ensnared by illusion. The answer lies in preserving their independence. By granting complete autonomy to individuals to pursue their desires, the Supreme Lord conveys His ultimate instruction as revealed in the Bhagavad Gita: renounce all other pursuits and surrender completely unto Him. This surrender leads to true happiness.  Both living beings and demigods are subservient to the will of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Hence, an individual cannot worship a demigod solely based on personal desire, nor can a demigod bestow blessings without the Supreme Will. It is said that not even a blade of grass moves without the consent of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Typically, those distressed in the material world turn to demigods as advised in Vedic scriptures. For specific desires, individuals may worship particular demigods. For instance, a sick person may venerate the sun-god, a seeker of knowledge may worship the goddess of learning, Sarasvati, and one seeking a beautiful spouse may worship Uma, the consort of Lord Shiva. The scriptures offer various recommendations for worshipping different demigods based on specific material desires. When an individual yearns for a particular material benefit, the Supreme Lord instills a strong desire to seek that boon from the corresponding demigod, leading to its fulfillment. The inclination of a living being towards a specific demigod is orchestrated by the Supreme Lord. Demigods themselves cannot influence individuals in this manner, but since the Supreme Lord, as the Supersoul residing in all beings, inspires them to worship certain demigods. Demigods are integral components of the universal body of the Supreme Lord and lack independent will. The Vedic texts affirm, "The Supreme Personality of Godhead, as the Supersoul, also resides within the demigod's heart, and through the demigod, fulfills the desires of living beings. However, both the demigod and the living being are subject to the supreme will and are not independent."

Chapter 7, Verse 22:
स तया श्रद्धया युक्तस् तस्याराधनम् ईहते ।
लभते च ततः कामान् मयैव विहितान् हि तान् ॥ २२ ॥
Translation: Endowed with such faith, one worships a specific demigod and attains his desires. However, in reality, these blessings are granted by Me alone.
Purport: Chapter 7, Text 22 The demigods cannot bestow blessings on their devotees without the consent of the Supreme Lord. While a living being may forget that everything belongs to the Supreme Lord, the demigods never forget this fact. Therefore, the worship of demigods and the fulfillment of desires are not the work of the demigods themselves, but rather orchestrated by the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Those lacking in wisdom may not realize this and thus seek material benefits from the demigods. However, a true devotee, when in need, solely seeks the grace of the Supreme Lord. Requesting material gains is not characteristic of a genuine devotee. Typically, individuals turn to the demigods out of a sense of desperation to satisfy their desires. This occurs when a being seeks something inappropriate and the Supreme Lord does not fulfill that desire. In the Caitanya-caritamrita, it is stated that one who worships the Supreme Lord while simultaneously desiring material pleasures is conflicted in their aspirations. The worship of the Supreme Lord through devotional service and the worship of demigods are not equivalent, as the latter is materialistic, whereas the former is entirely spiritual.  For a soul aspiring to return to the divine abode, material desires act as obstacles. A sincere devotee of the Lord does not receive the material rewards sought by less discerning individuals, who, therefore, opt to venerate the demigods of the material realm instead of engaging in the devotional worship of the Supreme Lord.

Chapter 7, Verse 23:
अन्तवत्तु फलं तेषां तद्भवत्यल्पमेधसाम् ।
देवान् देवयजो यान्ति मद्भक्ता यान्ति मामपि ॥ २३ ॥
Translation: Men of small intelligence worship the demigods, and their fruits are limited and temporary. Those who worship the demigods go to the planets of the demigods, but My devotees ultimately reach My supreme planet.
Purport: Chapter 7, Text 23 Some commentators on the Bhagavad-gita suggest that worshiping a demigod can lead one to the Supreme Lord. However, it is clearly stated here that worshipers of demigods ascend to various planetary systems where these celestial beings reside. Just as a worshiper of the sun reaches the sun or a worshiper of the moon attains the moon, those who worship specific demigods reach their respective planets. It is important to understand that not all worshipers of demigods reach the Supreme Personality of Godhead. The devotees of the Supreme Lord directly attain His supreme abode.  One may question why worshiping the demigods, who are considered parts of the Supreme Lord, does not lead to the same ultimate destination. The answer lies in the intelligence of the worshipers, as some are unaware of where to direct their offerings. This ignorance results in the misconception that each demigod is a separate deity and a rival to the Supreme Lord. In reality, demigods are integral parts of the universal body of the Supreme Lord.  According to the Srimad-Bhagavatam, the brahmanas represent the head, the kshatriyas the arms, the vaisyas the waist, and the sudras the legs of the Supreme Lord. Understanding that both demigods and ordinary beings are fragments of the Supreme Lord leads to perfect knowledge. Those who fail to grasp this concept attain different planets where demigods reside, unlike the destination of the devotees.  The rewards obtained through worshiping demigods are impermanent, as everything within the material realm, including the planets, demigods, and their devotees, is temporary. Hence, worshiping demigods is considered a pursuit of the less intelligent. In contrast, the pure devotee immersed in Krishna consciousness experiences eternal, blissful existence filled with knowledge. The achievements of such a devotee differ from those of ordinary worshipers of demigods. The Supreme Lord, with His unlimited favor and mercy, bestows boundless grace upon His pure devotees.

Chapter 7, Verse 24:
अव्यक्तं व्यक्तिमापन्नं मन्यन्ते मामबुद्धयः ।
परं भावमजानन्तो ममाव्ययमनुत्तमम् ॥ २४ ॥
Translation: Unintelligent individuals, lacking full knowledge of Me, mistakenly believe that I, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krishna, was previously impersonal and have now taken on this personality. Due to their limited understanding, they fail to grasp My superior, imperishable, and supreme nature.
Purport: Chapter 7, Text 24 Those who worship demigods are considered less intelligent, and similarly, impersonalists are also deemed as such. Here, Lord Krishna, in His personal form, addresses Arjuna. Yet, due to ignorance, impersonalists argue that the Supreme Lord is ultimately formless. Yamunacarya, a devoted follower in the lineage of Ramanujacarya, penned two fitting verses on this matter. He writes,  "O Lord, those like Vyasadeva and Narada recognize You as the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Through studying various Vedic texts, one can comprehend Your attributes, form, and deeds, and thus realize You as the Supreme Personality of Godhead. However, those in the modes of passion and ignorance, the demons and non-devotees, cannot fathom You. Despite their expertise in Vedanta, Upanishads, and other Vedic texts, they cannot grasp the Personality of Godhead." (Stotra-ratna 12)  The Brahma-samhita affirms that the Personality of Godhead cannot be comprehended solely through Vedanta study. Only by the grace of the Supreme Lord can one know the Supreme Personality. Hence, this verse clearly states that not only are demigod worshippers less intelligent, but non-devotees engrossed in Vedanta and Vedic speculation devoid of genuine Krishna consciousness are also lacking in intelligence. For them, understanding God's personal nature is unattainable. Those who believe the Absolute Truth is impersonal are labeled as abuddhayah, signifying their ignorance of the ultimate aspect of the Absolute Truth. The Srimad-Bhagavatam asserts that supreme realization begins from the impersonal Brahman and progresses to the localized Supersoul, yet the ultimate realization in the Absolute Truth is the Personality of Godhead. Modern impersonalists are even less wise, as they disregard the declaration of their predecessor Shankaracharya, who explicitly stated that Krishna is the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Thus, impersonalists, being unaware of the Supreme Truth, perceive Krishna as merely the son of Devaki and Vasudeva, a prince, or a potent being. This misperception is also condemned in the Bhagavad-gita (9.11): "Only fools view Me as an ordinary person."  In truth, understanding Krishna necessitates engaging in devotional service and cultivating Krishna consciousness. The Bhagavatam (10.14.29) confirms this:  "My Lord, with even a slight trace of the mercy of Your lotus feet, one can grasp the greatness of Your personality. However, those who speculate to comprehend the Supreme Personality of Godhead, despite years of Vedic study, remain unaware of You." Understanding the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krishna, His form, qualities, or names cannot be achieved through mental speculation or scholarly discussions on Vedic literature. He can only be understood through devotional service. When one wholeheartedly practices Krishna consciousness, starting with chanting the maha-mantra—Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare/ Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare—only then can one grasp the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Impersonalist non-devotees perceive Krishna as possessing a material body and consider His activities, form, and everything else as illusory. These impersonalists are known as Mayavadis, who are ignorant of the ultimate truth.  The twentieth verse clearly states, "Those whose knowledge is stolen by desires surrender to various demigods." Apart from the Supreme Personality of Godhead, there exist demigods with their respective abodes, just as the Lord has His own planet. As mentioned in the twenty-third verse, "The worshipers of the demigods reach the planets of those demigods, whereas My devotees reach Me." Worshipers of demigods attain different planetary systems where various demigods reside, akin to how a sun worshiper attains the sun or a moon worshiper attains the moon. It is not that worshiping any demigod will lead one to the Supreme Personality of Godhead; this is explicitly denied here. It is stated that demigod worshipers reach different material planets, while devotees of the Supreme Lord directly reach His supreme abode.  The monistic belief that the ultimate truth is formless and that form is a construct is unfounded. Here, it is explicitly stated that form is not a construct. From the teachings of the Gita, can one infer that the demigods and their realms are impersonal? Clearly, both the demigods and Krishna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, are personal entities; Lord Krishna is the Supreme Personality of Godhead with His own abode, just as the demigods have theirs.  The monistic notion that the ultimate truth is formless and that form is a fabrication is baseless. As per the Bhagavad-gita, it is evident that the forms of the demigods and the form of the Supreme Lord coexist, and Lord Krishna is sac-cid-ananda—eternal, blissful, and knowledgeable. The Vedas affirm that the Supreme Absolute Truth is ānanda-mayo ’bhyäsät, inherently filled with joyous pleasure, and is the reservoir of limitless auspicious qualities. In the Gita, the Lord states that despite being aja (unborn), He manifests. These are the truths to be gleaned from the Bhagavad-gita. The concept of the Supreme Personality of Godhead being impersonal is incomprehensible; the imposition theory posited by impersonalist monists is refuted by the Gita's teachings. Here, it is evident that the Supreme Absolute Truth, Lord Krishna, possesses both form and personality.

Chapter 7, Verse 25:
नाहं प्रकाशः सर्वस्य योगमायासमावृतः । मूढोऽयं नाभिजानाति लोको मामजमव्ययम् ॥
Translation: I am never manifest to the foolish and unintelligent. Covered by My internal potency, they do not recognize Me as unborn and infallible.
Purport: It may be argued that since Krishna was visibly present on earth, why isn't He manifest to everyone now? However, during His presence, only a few recognized Him as the Supreme Personality of Godhead. For instance, in the assembly of Kurus, Bhishma and the Pandavas acknowledged Him as the Supreme God. Similarly, only His pure devotees could perceive Him as the source of all pleasure. To non-devotees and the common man, He remained concealed by His internal potency.  In the prayers of Kunti in Srimad-Bhagavatam (1.8.19), it is stated that the Lord is veiled by the curtain of yoga-maya, making Him incomprehensible to ordinary people. This yoga-maya curtain is also mentioned in the Isopanishad (mantra 15), where the devotee prays:  hiraṇmayena pātreṇa satyasyäpihitaṁ mukham tat tvaṁ pūṣann apāvṛṇu satyadharmāya dṛṣṭaye  “O my Lord, You are the maintainer of the entire universe, and devotional service to You is the highest religious principle. Therefore, I pray that You will also maintain me. Your transcendental form is covered by the yoga-maya. The brahmajyoti is the covering of the internal potency. May You kindly remove this glowing effulgence that impedes my seeing Your sac-cid-ananda-vigrahah [Bs. 5.1], Your eternal form of bliss and knowledge.” The Supreme Personality of Godhead, in His transcendental form of bliss and knowledge, is concealed by the internal potency of the brahmajyoti, making it impossible for less intelligent impersonalists to perceive Him.  In Srimad-Bhagavatam (10.14.7), Brahma offers this prayer: “O Supreme Personality of Godhead, O Supersoul, O master of all mystery, who can calculate Your potency and pastimes in this world? You are always expanding Your internal potency, and therefore no one can understand You. Learned scientists and scholars can examine the atomic constitution of the material world and planets, yet they are unable to fathom Your energy and potency, even in Your presence.” The Supreme Personality of Godhead, Lord Krishna, is not just unborn but also avyaya, inexhaustible. His eternal form is bliss and knowledge, and His energies are boundless and unfathomable.""" ``` Chapter 7, Text 25 ```

Chapter 7, Verse 26:
वेदाहं समतीतानि वर्तमानानि चार्जुन ।
भविष्याणि च भूतानि मां तु वेद न कश्चन ॥ २६ ॥
Translation: O Arjuna, as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, I know everything that has happened in the past, all that is happening in the present, and all things that are yet to come. I also know all living entities; but Me no one knows.
Purport: Chapter 7, Text 26 This verse clearly distinguishes between personality and impersonality. If Krishna, as the form of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, were considered material by impersonalists, then like ordinary beings, He would change His body, forget His past life, and lack knowledge of the future. Material beings cannot recall past lives, foresee the future, or comprehend the present. Only when one is liberated from material influences can they understand past, present, and future.  Contrary to ordinary humans, Lord Krishna asserts that He comprehends the past, present, and future entirely. In the Fourth Chapter, He recalls instructing Vivasvan, the sun-god, millions of years ago. Krishna's omniscience extends to every living entity as the Supersoul residing in their hearts. Despite manifesting as the Supreme Personality of Godhead and dwelling as the Supersoul within every being, those lacking insight, even if recognizing the impersonal Brahman, fail to perceive Sri Krishna as the Supreme Person. Sri Krishna's transcendental form is imperishable, akin to the sun, with maya as a passing cloud. In the material realm, the sun, clouds, stars, and planets coexist. Clouds may momentarily obscure them from our limited vision, but the sun, moon, and stars remain unaffected. Similarly, maya cannot veil the Supreme Lord. His internal potency conceals Him from those lacking understanding. As noted in the third verse of this chapter, among countless individuals striving for perfection in human life, only a rare few grasp the essence of Lord Krishna. Even one perfected in realizing the impersonal Brahman or localized Paramatma cannot fathom the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Sri Krishna, without embracing Krishna consciousness.

Chapter 7, Verse 27:
इच्छाद्वेषसमुत्थेन द्वन्द्वमोहेन भारत ।
सर्वभूतानि सम्मोहं सर्गे यान्ति परन्तप ॥ २७ ॥
Translation: O scion of Bharata, O conqueror of the foe, all living entities are born into delusion, bewildered by dualities arising from desire and hate.
Purport: Chapter 7, Text 27 The true nature of the living entity is one of subordination to the Supreme Lord, who embodies pure knowledge. When one becomes separated from this pure knowledge, they fall under the influence of illusory energy and are unable to comprehend the Supreme Personality of Godhead. This illusory energy manifests in the form of dualities stemming from desire and hatred. Driven by desire and aversion, the ignorant individual aspires to merge with the Supreme Lord and begrudges Krishna as the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Pure devotees, untainted by desire and hatred, recognize that Lord Sri Krishna manifests through His internal potencies. Conversely, those ensnared by duality and ignorance mistakenly believe that the Supreme Personality of Godhead is a creation of material energies, leading to their unfortunate state. Such deluded individuals are characterized by their immersion in dualities such as dishonor and honor, sorrow and joy, female and male, good and bad, pleasure and pain. They identify with labels like "This is my wife," "This is my home," "I am the master of this house," "I am the husband of this wife," succumbing to the illusions of duality. Those consumed by such dualities are profoundly misguided and thus unable to grasp the essence of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

Chapter 7, Verse 28:
येषां त्वन्तगतं पापं जनानां पुण्यकर्मणाम् ।
ते द्वन्द्वमोहा निर्मुक्ता भजन्ते मां दृढव्रताः ॥ २८ ॥
Translation: Those individuals whose past and present actions are virtuous, and whose sins have been completely eradicated, are liberated from the dualities of delusion. They worship Me with unwavering determination.
Purport: Chapter 7, Text 28 This verse highlights those who are qualified for transcending to a higher spiritual realm. It is extremely challenging for those who are sinful, atheistic, ignorant, or deceptive to rise above the conflicting emotions of desire and aversion. Only those who have diligently followed religious principles, performed virtuous deeds, and overcome the consequences of their past misdeeds can embrace devotional service. Through this, they gradually attain a deep understanding of the Supreme Personality of Godhead and can meditate on Him in a state of trance. This process leads to a spiritual elevation where one is firmly established on the path of spiritual realization. Chapter 8, Verse 3:
श्रीभगवानुवाच अक्षरं ब्रह्म परमं स्वभावोऽध्यात्ममुच्यते । भूतभावोद्भवकरो विसर्गः कर्मसंज्ञितः ॥
Translation: The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: The indestructible, transcendental living entity is called Brahman, and his eternal nature is called adhyatma, the self. Action pertaining to the development of the material bodies of the living entities is called karma, or fruitive activities.
Purport: Brahman is indestructible and eternally existing, and its constitution is not changed at any time. Beyond Brahman lies Parabrahman, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Brahman refers to the individual living entity, while Parabrahman refers to the Supreme Lord. The inherent nature of the living entity differs from the role it assumes in the material realm. In material consciousness, the living entity seeks dominion over matter, but in spiritual consciousness, specifically Krishna consciousness, its role is to serve the Supreme. The material consciousness prompts the living entity to assume various material bodies, which is known as karma or the manifestation of diverse forms due to material consciousness.  In Vedic scriptures, the living entity is referred to as jīvātmā and Brahman, but never as Parabrahman. The jīvātmā assumes different states—it may merge into the dark material nature and identify with matter, or identify with the superior spiritual nature. Hence, it is known as the Supreme Lord's marginal energy. Depending on its identification with material or spiritual nature, the living entity acquires a material or spiritual body. In material realm, it may take on any of the 8,400,000 species of life, while in the spiritual realm it has only one form. In the material realm, the living entity may manifest as a human, demigod, animal, bird, etc., in accordance with its karma. To attain material heavenly realms and enjoy their pleasures, sacrifices (yajna) are performed, and upon depletion of merits, the entity returns to earth in human form. This cycle is known as karma.  The Chandogya Upanishad elucidates the Vedic sacrificial process, where five kinds of offerings are made into five kinds of fire on the sacrificial altar. These fires symbolize the heavenly planets, clouds, earth, man and woman, while the offerings represent faith, the enjoyer on the moon, rain, grains, and semen.  Through sacrifice, the living entity aims for specific heavenly realms and eventually reaches them. Once the merit from the sacrifice is exhausted, the entity descends to earth in the form of rain, transforms into grains, consumed by humans, and ultimately transformed into semen, leading to rebirth as a human to continue the cycle of sacrifice. In contrast, a Krishna conscious individual bypasses such sacrifices, embracing Krishna consciousness directly to prepare for the return to the Supreme Lord.  Certain impersonalist commentators on the Bhagavad Gita mistakenly suggest that Brahman assumes the form of the jiva in the material world, citing Chapter Fifteen, verse 7, of the Gita to support their claim. However, in this verse, the Lord also refers to the living entity as “an eternal fragment of Myself.” The fragment of God, the living entity, may descend into the material realm, but the Supreme Lord (Acyuta) never does. Hence, the notion that the Supreme Brahman transforms into the jiva is unfounded. It is crucial to recognize the distinction between Brahman (the individual living entity) and Parabrahman (the Supreme Lord) in Vedic teachings.``` Chapter 8, Text 3 ```

Purport: Chapter 8, Text 4 The physical nature is in a constant state of flux. It arises at a certain point and will cease at a certain point. The universal form of the Supreme Lord, encompassing all demigods and their respective realms, is called adhidaivata. Coexisting within the individual soul's body is the Supersoul, a complete representation of Lord Krishna. This Supersoul, known as Paramatma or adhiyajña, resides within the heart. The word 'eva' in this verse is significant, emphasizing that the Paramatma is inseparable from the Supreme Lord. The Supersoul, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, positioned alongside the individual soul, observes the soul's actions and is the source of its various forms of consciousness. Chapter 8, Verse 14:
Translation: For one who constantly remembers Me without deviation, I am easily attainable, O son of Pritha, due to their unwavering engagement in devotional service.
Purport: Chapter 8, Text 14 This verse elucidates the ultimate destination achieved by pure devotees who wholeheartedly serve the Supreme Personality of Godhead through bhakti-yoga. Earlier verses discussed different types of devotees—those in distress, the curious, seekers of material gain, and speculative philosophers. Various paths to liberation were also mentioned: karma-yoga, jnana-yoga, and hatha-yoga. While these yoga systems incorporate elements of bhakti, this verse emphasizes pure bhakti-yoga devoid of jnana, karma, or hatha. Ananyacetäḥ signifies that in pure bhakti-yoga, the devotee desires only Krishna. A pure devotee seeks neither heavenly realms, merging into the brahmajyoti, nor salvation from material entanglement. Such a devotee harbors no desires. In Caitanya-caritamrita, the pure devotee is termed niṣkäma, signifying a lack of self-interest. True peace is attained solely by such a devotee, not by those pursuing personal gain. While jnanayogis, karmayogis, and hathayogis are motivated by personal interests, a perfect devotee's sole desire is to please the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Thus, the Lord affirms that He is easily accessible to unwaveringly devoted souls.  A pure devotee perpetually engages in devotional service to Krishna in His various divine forms. Krishna manifests in multiple expansions and incarnations like Rama and Nrisimha, allowing a devotee to lovingly serve any of these transcendental forms. Such a devotee remains free from the challenges faced by practitioners of other yogas. Bhakti-yoga is straightforward, pure, and easily practiced—beginning with the simple chanting of Hare Krishna. While the Lord is merciful to all, He exhibits special favor towards those who serve Him steadfastly. The Lord assists such devotees in diverse ways. As per the Vedas (Katha Upanishad 1.2.23), one fully surrendered in the devotional service of the Supreme Lord can comprehend Him as He is. Also, in Bhagavad-gita (10.10), the Lord imparts intelligence to such a devotee, enabling them to ultimately attain Him in His spiritual abode.  The distinctive trait of a pure devotee is their unwavering remembrance of Krishna, irrespective of time or place. No obstacles should hinder their service, as they should be capable of serving anywhere and anytime. While some advocate for devotees to reside in holy places like Vrindavana, a pure devotee can reside anywhere and create a Vrindavana-like atmosphere through their devotional service. Sri Advaita once told Lord Caitanya, "Wherever You are, O Lord—there is Vrindavana."  The terms satatam and nityaśaḥ, meaning "always" or "regularly," highlight that a pure devotee consistently remembers and meditates upon Krishna. These qualities make the Lord most easily attainable for a pure devotee. Bhakti-yoga is the foremost system recommended in the Gita. Typically, bhakti-yogis engage in five ways: (1) śänta-bhakta, neutral devotion; (2) däsya-bhakta, servitude; (3) säkhya-bhakta, friendship; (4) vätsalya-bhakta, parenthood; and (5) mādhurya-bhakta, conjugal love for the Supreme Lord. In any of these relationships, a pure devotee remains consistently engrossed in the transcendental loving service of the Supreme Lord, never forgetting Him, making the Lord easily accessible. A pure devotee never forgets the Supreme Lord for a moment, and reciprocally, the Supreme Lord never forgets His pure devotee. This mutual remembrance is the profound blessing of the Krishna conscious practice of chanting the maha-mantra—Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare/ Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare.

Even those who attain the highest material planets, the abodes of demigods, are still bound by the cycle of repeated birth and death. Chapter 8, Verse 17:
सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तम् अहर यद् ब्रह्मणो विदुः ।
रात्रिम् युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ १७ ॥
Translation: According to human calculation, a thousand ages constitute a day of Brahma, and the same duration is his night.
Purport: Chapter 8, Text 17 The material universe exists within a finite time frame, manifested in cycles known as kalpas. A kalpa represents a day in the life of Brahma, each day consisting of a thousand cycles of four yugas or ages: Satya, Treta, Dvapara, and Kali. The Satya yuga is characterized by virtue, wisdom, and righteousness, with minimal ignorance and vice, lasting for 1,728,000 years. In the Treta yuga, vice begins to emerge, lasting for 1,296,000 years. The Dvapara yuga witnesses a further decline in virtue and righteousness, with vice prevailing, lasting for 864,000 years. Finally, in the current age of Kali (which has been ongoing for the past 5,000 years), there is a prevalence of conflict, ignorance, irreligion, and vice, with true virtue being scarce, lasting for 432,000 years. In Kali yuga, vice reaches such an extreme that at its conclusion, the Supreme Lord appears in the form of Kalki Avatar, to defeat the forces of darkness, protect His devotees, and initiate a new Satya yuga. This cycle then repeats itself. A thousand such cycles of the four yugas constitute a day and a night of Brahma. Brahma lives for one hundred such "years," after which he passes away. By earthly calculations, these "hundred years" amount to 311 trillion and 40 billion years. While this may seem vast and endless from a temporal perspective, in the context of eternity, it is as fleeting as a flash of lightning. In the Causal Ocean, countless Brahma beings emerge and vanish like bubbles in the ocean. Brahma and his creation are all part of the material universe, subject to constant change.  Even Brahma, the creator, is not exempt from the cycle of birth, aging, disease, and death. However, due to his direct service to the Supreme Lord in managing the universe, Brahma attains liberation instantly. Esteemed sannyasis are elevated to Brahma's abode, Brahmaloka, the highest planet in the material realm, surpassing all other celestial realms. Eventually, Brahma and all residents of Brahmaloka undergo dissolution in accordance with the laws of the material world.

Chapter 8, Verse 21:
अव्यक्तोऽक्षर इत्य् उक्तस् तम् आहुः परमाम् गतिम् ।
यम् प्राप्य न निवर्तन्ते तद् धाम परमम् मम ॥ २१ ॥
Translation: That which the Vedantists describe as unmanifest and infallible, that which is known as the supreme destination, that place from which, having attained it, one never returns—that is My supreme abode.
Purport: Chapter 8, Text 21 The supreme abode of the Personality of Godhead, Krishna—which is known as Krishnaloka, Goloka Vrindavana—is described here. In the spiritual sky, there is no need for sunshine, moonshine, fire, or electricity, as all the planets are self-luminous. In this universe, we have only one self-luminous planet, the sun, but in the spiritual sky, all planets are self-luminous. The shining effulgence of all those planets, known as Vaikunthas, forms the radiant sky called brahmajyoti. This effulgence emanates from the planet of Krishna, Goloka Vrindavana. A part of this radiant sky is covered by the mahat-tattva, the material world. The majority of this shining sky is filled with spiritual planets known as Vaikunthas, with Goloka Vrindavana being the chief among them. When a living entity is in the dark material world, they are in a conditioned state, but upon reaching the spiritual sky by transcending the illusory tree of the material world, they attain liberation. Once liberated, there is no possibility of returning to the material world. In the conditioned state, the living entity sees themselves as the master of the material world, but in the liberated state, they enter the spiritual realm and become an associate of the Supreme Lord, where they enjoy eternal bliss, eternal life, and complete knowledge.  One should be deeply moved by this knowledge and aspire to transfer themselves to that eternal world, freeing themselves from the false reflection of reality. For those overly attached to the material world, it is challenging to detach themselves, but by embracing Krishna consciousness, gradual detachment is possible. Associating with devotees who are in Krishna consciousness and engaging in devotional service is crucial. By seeking out a community dedicated to Krishna consciousness and learning the ways of devotional service, one can sever their attachment to the material world. Mere external renunciation, like wearing saffron robes, is not enough to break free from material allurements; one must cultivate attachment to the devotional service of the Lord. Therefore, one should earnestly understand that devotional service, as explained in the Twelfth Chapter, is the sole means to transcend the illusory representation of the material world. In the Fourteenth Chapter, the contamination of all processes by material nature is discussed, highlighting devotional service as the purest transcendental path.  The phrase "paramäm mama" is significant. In reality, every corner belongs to the Supreme Lord, but the spiritual world, being "paramam," is replete with six opulences. The Katha Upanishad (2.2.15) also confirms that in the spiritual world, there is no need for sunshine, moonshine, or stars, as the entire spiritual sky is illuminated by the internal potency of the Supreme Lord. This supreme abode can only be attained through surrender and no other means.

Translation: O Partha, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is greater than all, is attainable only by unalloyed devotion. Although He resides in His abode, He pervades everything, and all beings are situated within Him.
Purport: This verse clearly reveals that the ultimate destination, beyond which there is no return, is the divine abode of Lord Krishna, the Supreme Person. The Brahma-samhita describes this supreme abode as cintamani-dhama, a realm where all desires are fulfilled. In the transcendental land of Goloka Vrindavana, the abode of Lord Krishna, there are palaces crafted from touchstone, desire trees that provide any desired food, and surabhi cows that yield unlimited milk. Hundreds of thousands of goddesses of fortune (Lakshmis) serve the Lord there, who is known as Govinda, the primeval Lord and the root cause of all causes. The Lord plays His flute melodiously (veṇuṁ kvaṇantam) and possesses a form that is supremely attractive—His eyes resemble lotus petals, and His complexion is like that of rain clouds. His beauty surpasses that of countless Cupids. He adorns saffron garments, a garland around His neck, and a peacock feather in His hair. In the Bhagavad-gita, Lord Krishna briefly mentions His personal abode, Goloka Vrindavana, the highest planet in the spiritual domain. A detailed description is provided in the Brahma-samhita. The Vedic scriptures (Katha Upanishad 1.3.11) affirm that there is nothing superior to the abode of the Supreme Lord, which is the ultimate destination (puruṣän na paraṁ kiñcit sä käṣṭhä paramä gatiḥ). Once one attains this abode, there is no return to the material world. The supreme abode of Krishna and Krishna Himself are identical in quality. On this earth, Vrindavana, situated ninety miles southeast of Delhi, mirrors the divine Goloka Vrindavana in the spiritual sky. When Krishna descended to earth, He performed His pastimes in Vrindavana, an area of about eighty-four square miles in the Mathura district of India.  The Brahma-samhita (5.37) further confirms that although the Lord always resides in His supreme abode, Goloka Vrindavana, He pervades everything, ensuring the smooth functioning of the universe (goloka eva nivasaty akhilātma-bhūtaḥ). As mentioned in the Vedas (Svetasvatara Upanishad 6.8), paräsya śaktir vividhaiva śrūyate/ sväbhäviki jñänakriyä ca: His energies are so vast that they govern the cosmic manifestation flawlessly, even though the Supreme Lord is infinitely distant.``` Chapter 8, Text 22 ```

Purport: Chapter 8, Text 28 This verse encapsulates the essence of the Seventh and Eighth chapters of the Bhagavad Gita, which focus on Krishna consciousness and devotional service. A brahmacari, or celibate student, lives under the care of the spiritual master like a servant, begging for alms and following strict discipline. After years of Vedic study, a brahmacari develops a virtuous character and transitions into household life.  Householders must perform sacrifices and acts of charity to progress spiritually. Following retirement, one enters the stage of vanaprastha, living in seclusion and practicing severe penances. By diligently following the prescribed stages of life – brahmacarya, household life, vanaprastha, and finally sannyasa – one attains spiritual perfection. This understanding is not attained through mere scholarship or speculation but by hearing and contemplating in the association of devoted practitioners.  Those with even a flicker of faith in the Bhagavad Gita should seek guidance from a sincere devotee, as only devotees can grasp its true essence. By associating with devotees, one delves deeper into devotional service, dispelling doubts and misconceptions about Krishna and His divine activities. As one's doubts dissipate, a deep sense of Krishna consciousness emerges, leading to profound love for the Supreme Lord. This pinnacle of spiritual realization allows the devotee to reside eternally in Krishna's divine abode, Goloka Vrindavana, experiencing eternal bliss.  This concludes the Bhaktivedanta Purports to the Eighth Chapter of the Srimad Bhagavad-gita on Attaining the Supreme.

Chapter 9, Verse 1:
श्रीभगवानुवाच इदं तु ते गुह्यतमं प्रवक्ष्याम्यनसूयवे । ज्ञानं विज्ञानसहितं यज्ज्ञात्वा मोक्ष्यसेऽशुभात् ॥
Translation: The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: My dear Arjuna, because you are never envious of Me, I shall impart to you this most confidential knowledge and realization, knowing which you shall be relieved of the miseries of material existence.
Purport: As a devotee hears more and more about the Supreme Lord, he becomes enlightened. This hearing process is recommended in the Srimad-Bhagavatam: “The messages of the Supreme Personality of Godhead are full of potencies, and these potencies can be realized if topics regarding the Supreme Godhead are discussed amongst devotees. This cannot be achieved by the association of mental speculators or academic scholars, for it is realized knowledge.”  Devotees are constantly engaged in the service of the Supreme Lord. The Lord understands the mentality and sincerity of a particular living entity engaged in Krishna consciousness and gives him the intelligence to understand the science of Krishna in the association of devotees. Discussion of Krishna is potent, and if a fortunate person has such association and tries to assimilate the knowledge, then he will surely advance toward spiritual realization. Lord Krishna, to encourage Arjuna to higher elevation in His potent service, describes in this Ninth Chapter matters more confidential than any He has already disclosed.  The very beginning of Bhagavad-gita, the First Chapter, serves as an introduction to the rest of the book; and in the Second and Third chapters, the spiritual knowledge described is considered confidential. Topics discussed in the Seventh and Eighth chapters are specifically related to devotional service and are referred to as more confidential due to their enlightening nature in Krishna consciousness. However, the matters described in the Ninth Chapter pertain to unalloyed, pure devotion, making it the most confidential. One who is situated in the most confidential knowledge of Krishna is naturally transcendental and experiences no material distress, even while in the material world. In the Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu, it is stated that one with a sincere desire to render loving service to the Supreme Lord, despite being in the material realm, is considered liberated. Similarly, the Tenth Chapter of the Bhagavad-gita explains that anyone engaged in such service is a liberated soul.  The first verse holds specific significance. The words idaṁ jñānam (“this knowledge”) refer to pure devotional service, comprising nine activities: hearing, chanting, remembering, serving, worshiping, praying, obeying, maintaining friendship, and surrendering everything. By practicing these nine elements of devotional service, one attains spiritual consciousness, Krishna consciousness. When one's heart is purified from material contamination, one can comprehend the science of Krishna. Merely understanding that a living entity is not material is not enough; it may mark the beginning of spiritual realization, but one must discern the distinction between bodily activities and the spiritual activities of someone who recognizes they are not the body.  In the Seventh Chapter, we have already explored the opulent potency of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, His diverse energies, the inferior and superior natures, and the entirety of this material manifestation. Now, in Chapter Nine, the glories of the Lord will be delineated.  The Sanskrit word anasūyave in this verse is also significant. Generally, commentators, even if highly scholarly, are envious of Krishna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Even the most erudite scholars often write inaccurately about the Bhagavad-gita due to their envy of Krishna. The commentaries provided by devotees of the Lord are authentic. No one can explain Bhagavad-gita or impart perfect knowledge of Krishna if they harbor envy. Criticizing the character of Krishna without knowing Him reflects foolishness. Therefore, such commentaries should be approached with caution. For those who understand that Krishna is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, pure and transcendental, these chapters will be immensely beneficial.""" Chapter 9, Text 1 """

Chapter 9, Verse 2:
Translation: This knowledge is the king of education, the most secret of all secrets. It is the purest knowledge, and because it gives direct perception of the self by realization, it is the perfection of religion. It is everlasting, and it is joyfully performed.
Purport: Chapter 9, Text 2 This chapter of Bhagavad-gita is considered the pinnacle of education as it encapsulates the essence of all doctrines and philosophies discussed prior. Throughout Indian history, prominent philosophers like Gautama, Kanada, Kapila, Yajnavalkya, Sandilya, Vaishvanara, and Vyasadeva, the author of Vedanta-sutra, have contributed to the vast field of knowledge in philosophy and spirituality. The Lord now emphasizes that this Ninth Chapter is the apex of all such knowledge, encompassing the core teachings derived from the study of Vedas and various philosophical traditions. It is deemed the most confidential because it involves understanding the distinction between the soul and the body. The ultimate confidential knowledge culminates in devotional service.  Typically, people are educated in external knowledge rather than this confidential spiritual knowledge. While various fields like politics, sociology, sciences, and engineering are extensively studied worldwide, unfortunately, there are no educational institutions explicitly teaching the science of the spirit soul. Yet, the soul is the essence of the body; without the soul, the body holds no value. Despite this, emphasis is placed on material needs, neglecting the vital soul.  The Bhagavad-gita, especially from the Second Chapter onwards, underscores the significance of the soul. Initially, the Lord clarifies that the body is perishable while the soul is imperishable. This confidential knowledge reveals the soul's distinct nature as immutable, indestructible, and eternal. However, mere awareness of the soul's difference from the body does not provide comprehensive information about the soul. Some may mistakenly believe that upon liberation, the soul remains inactive or impersonal. Yet, the soul, inherently active within the body, remains eternally active, particularly in the spiritual realm. The activities of the spirit soul, the most confidential aspect of spiritual knowledge, are highlighted as the pinnacle of all knowledge.  This knowledge represents the purest form of all actions, as elucidated in Vedic scriptures. The Padma Purana analyzes man's sinful deeds, illustrating how sins lead to successive sinful reactions. Just as a seed takes time to grow into a tree, sinful actions also undergo stages before bearing fruit, which individuals eventually experience as distress and pain. In contrast, those fully engaged in devotional service to Lord Krishna are liberated from all sinful reactions, as confirmed in the Padma Purana.  Devotional service's purifying influence is potent, termed as "pavitram uttamam," the purest. Devotional activities transcend material considerations, untouched by material qualities. Engaging in devotional service yields direct perceptible results. Chanting the holy names of Krishna without offenses brings transcendental pleasure and purification. Additionally, actively sharing and participating in Krishna consciousness missionary activities fosters spiritual progress, independent of prior education or qualifications. Engaging in devotional service enlightens one unequivocally, as affirmed in the Vedanta-sutra.  The story of Narada exemplifies how association with great devotees and engaging in devotional service can lead to spiritual enlightenment, regardless of educational background. By simply participating in devotional activities, one gains profound insights, as evidenced by Narada's transformation. Devotional service is a joyful process, facilitating spiritual advancement and purification. The Lord graciously accepts even simple offerings made with love, emphasizing the eternal nature of devotional service beyond temporary, self-serving motives.  Devotional service continues even after liberation, unlike the Mayavadi philosophy's notion of merging with God post-liberation. Genuine devotional service persists in the spiritual realm, where devotees joyfully serve the Supreme Lord. True devotional service commences post-liberation, as emphasized in the Bhagavad-gita. Understanding the Supreme Personality of Godhead necessitates devotional service, surpassing other yogic practices. Purification through devotional service enables one to comprehend the science of God, as expounded in the Srimad-Bhagavatam. The process of devotional service, or Krishna consciousness, stands as the pinnacle of education and the most confidential knowledge, offering the purest form of religion to be joyfully embraced without difficulty.

This unwavering conviction is genuine faith. As mentioned in the Srimad-Bhagavatam (4.31.14):  "By watering the root of a tree, all its branches, twigs, and leaves are nourished; similarly, by feeding the stomach, all the senses of the body are satisfied. Upon studying the Bhagavad-gita, one should promptly realize its essence: renounce all other pursuits and embrace the service of the Supreme Lord, Krishna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. This conviction signifies faith.  The cultivation of such faith is the path of Krishna consciousness. There are three categories of individuals in Krishna consciousness. The third category comprises those lacking faith. Even if they engage in devotional activities outwardly, they struggle to attain the highest spiritual realization. The first-class practitioners steadily progress and achieve the desired outcome. Individuals in the third category may have faith in the goodness of devotional service to Krishna but lack comprehensive knowledge of Krishna as revealed in scriptures like Srimad-Bhagavatam and Bhagavad-gita. At times, these third-category practitioners exhibit inclinations towards karma-yoga or jnana-yoga and may face disturbances. Once they overcome these tendencies, they advance to the second or first category in Krishna consciousness. Those who, despite hearing about Krishna and the merits of devotional service, lack faith and dismiss it as mere praise, find the path arduous, even if they superficially engage in devotional activities. Translation: Just as the mighty wind, ever-present and pervasive, remains in the sky, similarly all beings exist within Me.
Purport: Chapter 9, Text 6 For an ordinary person, it may be challenging to comprehend how the vast material creation rests within the Supreme Lord. To aid our understanding, the Lord provides an analogy. Consider the sky, the largest entity we can conceive. Within this sky, the wind or air represents a significant cosmic force, influencing the movements of all things. Despite its magnitude, the wind remains situated within the sky; it does not transcend it. Likewise, all the magnificent cosmic phenomena exist by the supreme will of God and are subservient to that divine will. As the saying goes, not even a blade of grass moves without the will of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Therefore, everything unfolds according to His will: creation, sustenance, and dissolution. Yet, He remains detached from these activities, akin to how the sky remains unaffected by the wind's actions.  The Upanishads affirm, "It is out of fear of the Supreme Lord that the wind blows." (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8.1) The Brhad-aranyaka Upanishad (3.8.9) states, "Under the supreme order and the supervision of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the moon, the sun, and the other celestial bodies move." The Brahma-samhita (5.52) further elucidates:  yac-cakṣur eṣa savitä sakalagrahāṇāṁ räjä samasta-sūramūrtir aseṣatejāḥ yasyäjñayä bhramati sambhūtakälacakro govindam ädi-puruṣaṁ tam ahaṁ bhajāmi  This verse describes the sun's movement as one of the eyes of the Supreme Lord, possessing immense heat and light. Yet, it orbits as ordained by Govinda's supreme will. Thus, Vedic texts provide evidence that this awe-inspiring material world is entirely under the control of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Further elaboration on this subject will be presented in subsequent verses of this chapter.

When the time comes for creation once again, it is His divine desire that initiates the process.
