Chapter 9, Verse 11:
अवजानन्ति मां मूढा मानुषीं तनुम् आश्रितम् ।
परं भावम् अजानन्तो मम भूत महेश्वरम् ॥ ११ ॥
Translation: Fools deride Me when I descend in the human form. They do not know My transcendental nature as the Supreme Lord of all that be.
Purport: Chapter 9, Text 11 The previous verses in this chapter make it clear that the Supreme Personality of Godhead, despite appearing as a human being, is not an ordinary man. The Personality of Godhead, who oversees the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire cosmic manifestation, cannot be a mere mortal. Yet, there are many ignorant individuals who view Krishna as just a powerful human and nothing more. In truth, He is the original Supreme Personality, as affirmed in the Brahma-samhita (isvaraḥ paramah kṛṣṇaḥ); He is the Supreme Lord.  While there are various controllers (isvaras), with one seeming greater than the other, Krishna is the supreme controller. In the material world's typical hierarchy, we observe officials, directors, secretaries, ministers, and presidents, each exerting control but also being subject to another's authority. However, Krishna is the ultimate controller, as stated in the Brahma-samhita (isvaraḥ paramah kṛṣṇaḥ), and His form is sac-cid-ananda, nonmaterial.  Material bodies cannot perform the extraordinary acts described in earlier verses. His body is eternal, blissful, and filled with knowledge. Although He is not an ordinary man, the foolish ridicule Him and perceive Him as human. His body is referred to as mänuṣīṁ because He behaves like a man - a friend of Arjuna's, a participant in the political dynamics of the Kurukshetra War. In many ways, He appears like an ordinary man, but in reality, His body is sac-cid-ananda-vigrahah [Bs. 5.1] - eternally blissful and possessing absolute knowledge. This is also confirmed in Vedic literature. Sac-cid-ananda-rūpāya kṛṣṇāya: "I offer my obeisances unto the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krishna, who embodies eternal blissful knowledge." (Gopala-tapani Upanishad 1.1) Additional Vedic descriptions include Tam ekaṁ govindam: "You are Govinda, the pleasure of the senses and the cows." Sac-cidänanda-vigraham: "Your form is transcendental, full of knowledge, bliss, and eternality." (Gopala-tapani Upanishad 1.35)  Despite the transcendental qualities of Lord Krishna's body - full of bliss and knowledge, there exist many self-proclaimed scholars and commentators of the Bhagavad-gita who belittle Krishna as an ordinary man. While a scholar may be exceptional due to past good deeds, perceiving Sri Krishna in this manner stems from a lack of true knowledge. Hence, they are termed mūḍha, as only the ignorant consider Krishna an average human being. These individuals are unaware of the confidential activities of the Supreme Lord and His various energies. They fail to recognize that Krishna's body symbolizes complete knowledge and bliss, that He is the ultimate proprietor, and that He can grant liberation to all. Due to their ignorance of Krishna's numerous transcendental attributes, they mock Him.  Furthermore, they are unaware that the Supreme Personality of Godhead's appearance in this material world is a manifestation of His internal energy. He is the master of the material energy, as reiterated in various places (mama mäyä duratyayä). He asserts that the material energy, though potent, is under His control, and those who surrender to Him can transcend its influence. If a soul surrendered to Krishna can escape the grip of material energy, how can the Supreme Lord, overseeing the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire cosmic nature, possess a material body like ours? This perception of Krishna is utterly nonsensical. The foolish cannot fathom how Krishna, resembling a human, can govern both the infinite and the minute simultaneously. Though He controls the infinite and the finite, He remains distinct from this entire manifestation. His inconceivable transcendental energy, yogam aiśvaram, enables Him to control the infinite and the finite concurrently and to remain detached from them. While the ignorant struggle to grasp how Krishna, appearing as a human, can govern the infinite and the finite, pure devotees accept this truth, recognizing Krishna as the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Therefore, they wholeheartedly surrender to Him and engage in Krishna consciousness, the devotional service of the Lord.  There are ongoing debates between impersonalists and personalists regarding the Lord's human-like appearance. However, consulting the Bhagavad-gita and Srimad-Bhagavatam, the authoritative texts for understanding Krishna's science, reveals that Krishna is the Supreme Personality of Godhead. He is not an ordinary man, even though He manifested on earth in human form. In the Srimad-Bhagavatam, First Canto, First Chapter, when sages led by Shaunaka inquired about Krishna's activities, they stated:  kṛtavän kila karmäṇi saha rämeṇa keçavaḥ ati-martyäni bhagavän gūḍhaḥ kapaṭamāṇuṣaḥ  "Lord Sri Krishna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, along with Balarama, played like a human being, and thus disguised, He performed many superhuman acts." (Bhag. 1.1.20) The Lord's human-like appearance bewilders the ignorant. No ordinary human could perform the miraculous feats that Krishna did while present on earth. When Krishna appeared before His parents, Vasudeva and Devaki, He initially showed four arms, but upon their prayers, He transformed into an ordinary child. As described in the Bhagavatam (10.3.46), babhūva präkṛtaḥ śiśuḥ: He assumed the form of a regular child, an ordinary human. This once more highlights that the Lord's human-like manifestation is a feature of His transcendental form. In the Eleventh Chapter of the Bhagavad-gita, Arjuna prayed to behold Krishna's four-handed form (tenaiva rūpeṇa caturbhujena). After revealing this form, Krishna, upon Arjuna's request, resumed His original human-like form (mānuṣaṁ rūpam). These distinct features of the Supreme Lord certainly do not belong to an ordinary human being.  Some who ridicule Krishna and are influenced by Mayavadi philosophy cite a verse from the Srimad-Bhagavatam (3.29.21) to argue that Krishna is merely an ordinary man. Ahaṁ sarveṣu bhūteṣu bhūtātmävasthitaḥ sadā: "The Supreme is present in every living entity." It is advisable to heed the interpretations of Vaishnava acharyas like Jiva Gosvami and Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura regarding this specific verse rather than following the opinions of unauthorized individuals who mock Krishna. Jiva Gosvami, commenting on this verse, explains that Krishna, in His expansion as Paramatma, resides within all living and non-living entities as the Supersoul. Therefore, a novice devotee who solely focuses on the Deity in the temple and disregards other living beings is essentially worshiping the form of the Lord in vain. There exist three types of Lord's devotees, with the neophyte being at the lowest stage. The novice devotee may prioritize the Deity in the temple over fellow devotees, prompting Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura to caution against such a mindset. A devotee should recognize that since Krishna resides in everyone's heart as Paramatma, each body is a vessel or temple of the Supreme Lord. Hence, just as one reveres the Lord's temple, one should similarly honor every body housing the Paramatma. Every individual deserves respect and should not be neglected.  Moreover, numerous impersonalists criticize temple worship, arguing that since God is omnipresent, there is no need for confined temple worship. However, if God is omnipresent, is He not present in the temple or the Deity? Despite perpetual disputes between personalists and impersonalists, a devoted follower in Krishna consciousness understands that although Krishna is the Supreme Personality, He pervades all, as affirmed in the Brahma-samhita. While His primary abode is Goloka Vrindavana, and He eternally resides there, through His diverse energy manifestations and expansions, He is omnipresent throughout the material and spiritual realms.

Chapter 9, Verse 12:

राक्षसीमासुरीं चैव प्रकृतिं मोहिनीं श्रिताः ॥ १२ ॥

People mock Krishna out of envy, leading them to be reborn in atheistic and demoniac life forms repeatedly. Their true knowledge remains obscured by delusion, and they descend into the darkest realms of existence.

Chapter 9, Verse 13:
महात्मानस् तु मां पार्थ दैवीं प्रकृतिम् आश्रिताः ।
भजन्त्य् अनन्यमनसो ज्ञात्वा भूतादिम् अव्ययम् ॥ १३ ॥
Translation: O son of Pritha, those who are not deluded, the great souls, are under the protection of the divine nature. They are fully engaged in devotional service because they know Me as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, original and inexhaustible.
Purport: Chapter 9, Text 13 This verse clearly describes the mahātmā, the great soul. The first characteristic of a mahātmā is that they are already established in the divine nature and are not influenced by material nature. This is achieved through surrendering to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Sri Krishna, as explained in the Seventh Chapter. By surrendering to the Supreme Lord, one is liberated from the control of material nature. This surrender is the key qualification. As soon as the living entity surrenders to the Supreme Lord, who is the cause of all causes, they are freed from material nature's influence and guided by the spiritual nature, known as daivī prakṛti.  The mahātmā does not waver in their focus on anything other than Krishna, recognizing Him as the original Supreme Person. Such a great soul develops by associating with other mahātmās, pure devotees, who are solely attracted to the two-armed form of Krishna and engage unwaveringly in His service in Krishna consciousness, not being distracted by other forms of the Lord or any other beings.

Chapter 9, Verse 14:
सततं कीर्तयन्तो मां यतन्तश् च दृढव्रताः ।
नमस्यन्तश् च मां भक्त्या नित्ययुक्ता उपासते ॥ १४ ॥
Translation: Those steadfastly extolling Me, striving with unwavering determination, bowing down in devotion, perpetually worship Me with love and dedication.
Purport: Chapter 9, Text 14 A mahätmä, a great soul, cannot be artificially created; his characteristics are outlined here: a mahätmä is continuously engrossed in glorifying the Supreme Lord Krishna, the Personality of Godhead. This is his primary occupation. He dedicates himself to exalting the Lord, focusing on His holy name, eternal form, divine qualities, and extraordinary pastimes. A mahätmä is not an impersonalist. When it comes to glorification, one must extol the Supreme Lord. Such a great soul is deeply connected to the Supreme Personality of Godhead.  In the Bhagavad-gita, one who is fixated on the impersonal aspect of the Supreme Lord, the brahmajyoti, is not labeled as a mahätmä. The next verse describes this individual differently. A mahätmä is consistently engaged in various devotional activities, as elaborated in the Srimad-Bhagavatam, such as hearing and chanting about Vishnu, not about demigods or humans. True devotion involves hearing, chanting, and remembering Him. A mahätmä possesses unwavering resolve to ultimately attain the association of the Supreme Lord in any of the five transcendental moods. To achieve this goal, he dedicates all his mental, physical, and vocal activities in the service of the Supreme Lord, Sri Krishna. This is known as complete Krishna consciousness.  Devotional service includes certain prescribed practices, like fasting on specific days such as Ekadasi, the eleventh day of the lunar month, and on the appearance day of the Lord. These regulations are provided by the great spiritual teachers for those sincerely seeking entry into the company of the Supreme Personality of Godhead in the spiritual realm. The mahätmäs, the exalted souls, diligently adhere to these guidelines, ensuring the fulfillment of their aspirations.  As mentioned in the second verse of this chapter, not only is devotional service simple, but it can also be performed joyfully. There is no need for severe penances or austerities. By leading a life dedicated to devotional service under the guidance of a qualified spiritual master, one can practice this path in any life circumstance—be it as a householder, renunciant, or student—anywhere in the world. By engaging in devotional service to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, one can truly become a mahätmä, a great soul.

Chapter 9, Verse 15:
ज्ञानयज्ञेन चाप्य् अन्ये यजन्तो माम् उपासते ।
एकत्वेन पृथक्त्वेन बहुधा विश्वतोमुखम् ॥ १५ ॥
Translation: Others, who engage in sacrifice through the pursuit of knowledge, worship Me in various ways – seeing Me as the singular, as distinct, and as the all-encompassing universal form.
Purport: Chapter 9, Text 15 This verse encapsulates the essence of preceding verses. Lord Krishna explains to Arjuna that those completely absorbed in Krishna consciousness, recognizing nothing but Krishna, are known as mahatmas. Additionally, there are others who, though not mahatmas, also worship Krishna in diverse manners. Some have already been categorized as the distressed, the financially deprived, the curious, and those dedicated to acquiring knowledge. Furthermore, there are those at a lower level, divided into three groups: (1) those who perceive themselves as one with the Supreme Lord and worship accordingly, (2) those who create an imagined form of the Supreme Lord for worship, and (3) those who revere the universal form, the visvarupa of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Among these three, the most prevalent are those who regard themselves as the Supreme Lord, believing in monism. They worship themselves in this self-deifying manner, acknowledging their spiritual essence beyond the material body. This self-worship, though flawed, is a form of acknowledging divinity, especially as it recognizes the soul's spiritual nature. Typically, impersonalists adopt this mode of worship. The second group comprises devotees of demigods, who attribute any form as that of the Supreme Lord. The third group cannot conceive anything beyond the material universe's manifestation, viewing the universe itself as the supreme entity and offering worship to it. The universe, as a manifestation of the Lord, is also revered in this manner.

Chapter 9, Verse 16:
अहं क्रतुर् अहं यज्ञः स्वधाहम् अहम् औषधम् । मन्त्रोऽहम् अहम् एवाज्यम् अहम् अग्निः अहम् हुतम् ॥
Translation: I am the ritual, the sacrifice, the offering to the ancestors, the healing herb, the transcendental chant. I am the butter, the fire, and the offering.
Purport: The Vedic sacrifice known as jyotiṣṭoma is also Krishna, as is the mahä-yajña mentioned in the smṛti. The oblations offered to the Pitṛloka or the sacrifice performed to please the Pitṛloka, considered a form of clarified butter, are also Krishna. The mantras chanted in this connection are also Krishna. Additionally, the milk products used in sacrifices are also Krishna. Fire, being one of the five material elements, is also Krishna, as it is considered a separated energy of Krishna. In essence, the Vedic sacrifices recommended in the karmakāṇḍa division of the Vedas are all manifestations of Krishna. Those who engage in devotional service to Krishna are deemed to have performed all Vedic sacrifices.``` Chapter 9, Text 16 ```

Chapter 9, Verse 17:
पिताहम् अस्य जगतो माता धाता पितामहः ।
वेद्यं पवित्रं ओङ्कार ऋक् साम यजुर् एव च ॥ १७ ॥
Translation: I am the father of this universe, the mother, the support, and the grandsire. I am the object of knowledge, the purifier, and the syllable om. I am also the Rig, the Sama, and the Yajur Vedas.
Purport: Chapter 9, Text 17 The entire cosmic manifestations, both moving and nonmoving, are brought forth by various activities of Krishna's energy. In the material realm, we form diverse relationships with various living beings who are essentially Krishna's marginal energy. Within the realm of prakṛti's creation, some may appear as our father, mother, grandfather, or creator, but in truth, they are all integral parts of Krishna. Hence, those entities who seem to be our father, mother, etc., are essentially Krishna Himself. Here, the term "dhātā" refers to the "creator." Our father, mother, and other creators are not only parts of Krishna but also Krishna Himself. Every living being, as a fragment of Krishna, is indeed Krishna. Therefore, all the Vedas ultimately point towards Krishna. The knowledge we seek through the Vedas is a step towards understanding Krishna. The subject matter that helps us cleanse our inherent nature is specifically related to Krishna. Likewise, a curious soul striving to comprehend the essence of Vedic principles is also a fragment of Krishna and thus, Krishna Himself. The sacred sound vibration "om," known as praṇava, is transcendental and is Krishna Himself. As the praṇava or oṁkāra is prominently featured in the hymns of the four Vedas - Sāma, Yajur, Rig, and Atharva, it is recognized as Krishna.

Chapter 9, Verse 18:
गतिर् भर्ता प्रभुः साक्षी निवासः शरणं सुहृत् ।
प्रभवः प्रलयः स्थानं निधानं बीजम् अव्ययम् ॥ १८ ॥
Translation: I am the ultimate goal, the sustainer, the master, the witness, the abode, the refuge, and the dearest friend. I am the source of creation and dissolution, the foundation of all existence, the resting place, and the eternal seed.
Purport: Chapter 9, Text 18 The term "gati" refers to the destination we aspire to reach. The true goal is Krishna, though many are unaware of it. Those who are ignorant of Krishna are led astray, and their so-called progress is either partial or illusory. Many worship various demigods as their ultimate destination, following strict rituals to reach different celestial realms like Candraloka, Suryaloka, Indraloka, Maharloka, etc. However, all these realms, being creations of Krishna, are both Krishna and not Krishna simultaneously. These realms, as manifestations of Krishna's energy, are indeed Krishna, yet they only serve as stepping stones towards realizing Krishna. Approaching Krishna's different energies indirectly is akin to approaching Krishna indirectly. It is more efficient to directly approach Krishna, saving time and energy. Just as taking an elevator to reach the top of a building is quicker than climbing stairs step by step, everything relies on Krishna's energy; hence, nothing can exist without Krishna's shelter. Krishna is the supreme ruler as everything belongs to Him and exists through His energy. Being situated in every heart, Krishna is the ultimate witness. The abodes, countries, or planets we inhabit are also manifestations of Krishna. Krishna is the ultimate refuge, so one should seek shelter in Krishna for protection or relief from distress. When seeking protection, it must be from a living source, and Krishna is the supreme living entity. As the source of our existence and the ultimate father, no one is a better friend or well-wisher than Krishna. Krishna is the original creator and the final resting place after destruction. Thus, Krishna is the eternal cause of all causes.

Chapter 9, Verse 19:
तपाभ्य् अहम् अहम् वर्षं निगृह्णाम्य् उत्सृजामि च । अमृतं चैव मृत्युश् च सद् असच् चाहम् अर्जुन ॥
Translation: O Arjuna, I am the heat; I withhold and send forth the rain. I am immortality and death, the eternal and the non-eternal, O Arjuna.
Purport: Krishna, through His diverse energies, radiates heat and light using electricity and the sun. In summer, He prevents rain, and in the rainy season, He bestows continuous downpours. The energy sustaining our life and prolonging it is Krishna, who also appears as death in the end. By understanding these various energies of Krishna, one can realize that He transcends distinctions between matter and spirit; in essence, He encompasses both. In the elevated state of Krishna consciousness, one sees only Krishna in all aspects.  As Krishna embodies both matter and spirit, the vast universal form encompassing all material manifestations is also Krishna. His pastimes in Vrindavana as the two-handed Syamasundara, playing the flute, depict the Supreme Personality of Godhead.``` Chapter 9, Text 19 ```

Chapter 9, Verse 20:
त्रैविद्या मां सोमपाः पूतपापा यज्ञैर् इष्ट्वा स्वर्गतिं प्रार्थयन्ते । ते पुण्यम् आसाद्य सुरेन्द्र लोकम् अश्नन्ति दिव्यान् दिवि देवभोगान् ॥
Translation: Those who study the Vedas and partake in the soma ritual, aspiring for heavenly realms, worship Me indirectly. Cleansed of sinful reactions, they attain the celestial abode of Indra, where they enjoy divine pleasures.
Purport: The term "trai-vidyā" refers to the three Vedas—Sama, Yajur, and Rig. A brahmana well-versed in these Vedas is known as a "tri-vedī." Those deeply immersed in the knowledge contained in these texts are esteemed in society. However, many erudite scholars of the Vedas fail to grasp the ultimate purpose of their studies. Herein, Krishna reveals Himself as the ultimate destination for the tri-vedīs. True tri-vedīs take refuge at Krishna's lotus feet and engage in pure devotional service to please the Lord. This devotional journey commences with the chanting of the Hare Krishna mantra and a sincere quest to comprehend Krishna's true nature. Regrettably, those who merely study the Vedas for academic purposes tend to focus on performing rituals for various demigods such as Indra and Chandra. Through such endeavors, the worshippers of these demigods are indeed purified of the lower material qualities and are elevated to higher celestial realms or heavenly planets like Maharloka, Janoloka, Tapoloka, and others. Once established in these elevated realms, one can gratify their senses far beyond what is possible on Earth.``` Chapter 9, Text 20 ```

Chapter 9, Verse 21:
ते तं भुक्त्वा स्वर्ग लोकं विशालं
क्षीणे पुण्ये मर्त्य लोकं विशन्ति ।
एवं त्रयीधर्मम् अनुपपन्ना
गतागतं कामकामा लभन्ते ॥ २१ ॥
Translation: After enjoying the vast heavenly pleasures, when their accumulated merits are exhausted, they return to the mortal world. Those who seek pleasure through adherence to the rituals prescribed in the Vedas find themselves trapped in the cycle of birth and death.
Purport: Chapter 9, Text 21 Even though one may experience an extended lifespan and enhanced sensory delights in higher celestial realms, such pleasures are impermanent. Upon the depletion of their virtuous merits, individuals are inevitably sent back to this earthly realm. Those who have not attained true wisdom, as elucidated in the Vedanta-sutra, or those who fail to comprehend Krishna as the ultimate cause, remain entangled in the pursuit of transient goals. Consequently, they continue to oscillate between higher and lower planetary systems, akin to a Ferris wheel's cyclical motion. Rather than being elevated to the spiritual realm, where the cycle of birth and death ceases, they remain ensnared in the perpetual transmigration between different realms. It is advisable to strive for the spiritual realm, where eternal joy and knowledge prevail, thereby transcending the cycle of material existence.

Chapter 9, Verse 22:
अनन्याश्चिन्तयन्तो मां ये जनाः पर्युपासते तेषां नित्याभियुक्तानां योगक्षेमं वहाम्य् अहम् ॥
Translation: But those who constantly worship Me with unwavering devotion, meditating on My divine form—I bear the responsibility of their necessities and protect what they possess.
Purport: A person who cannot exist for a moment without being absorbed in Krishna consciousness naturally thinks of Krishna round the clock, engaging in devotional activities such as hearing, chanting, remembering, offering prayers, worshiping, serving the Lord's lotus feet, rendering various services, fostering friendships, and completely surrendering to the Lord. These activities are all supremely beneficial and imbued with spiritual potency, leading the devotee to perfect self-realization, where their sole aspiration is to attain the companionship of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Such a devotee effortlessly approaches the Lord; this is known as yoga. Through the Lord's grace, such a devotee transcends the cycle of material existence. The term "yogakshemam" signifies the Lord's compassionate safeguarding. The Lord guides the devotee towards Krishna consciousness through yoga, and once the devotee attains complete Krishna consciousness, the Lord shields them from descending back into a distressing material life.``` Chapter 9, Text 22 ```

Chapter 9, Verse 23:
येऽप्य् अन्यदेवताभक्ता यजन्ते श्रद्धयान्विताः । तेऽपि माम् एव कौन्तेय यजन्त्य् अविधिपूर्वकम् ॥
Translation: Even those who worship other deities with faith, O Arjuna, worship Me alone, albeit in an improper manner.
Purport: Krishna explains that those who worship demigods lack true understanding, despite their indirect worship of Him. For instance, when one waters a tree's leaves and branches but neglects the roots, this demonstrates ignorance or a failure to adhere to proper guidelines. Similarly, providing nourishment to different parts of the body serves the stomach. The demigods act as various officials in the administration of the Supreme Lord. It is essential to abide by the laws established by the government, not by its officials. Likewise, all worship should be directed solely to the Supreme Lord, thereby naturally gratifying the various divine functionaries. Attempting to offer bribes to these officials, who function as representatives of the government, is illicit. This is referred to as "avidhi-pūrvakam," worship without adherence to regulations. In essence, Krishna does not endorse the unnecessary worship of demigods.""" ``` Chapter 9, Text 23 ```

Chapter 9, Verse 24:
अहं हि सर्वयज्ञानां भोक्ता च प्रभुर् एव च ।
न तु माम् अभि जानन्ति तत्त्वेनातश् च्यवन्ति ते ॥ २४ ॥
Translation: I am indeed the sole enjoyer and the supreme master of all sacrifices. Those who fail to recognize my true transcendental nature, they are doomed.
Purport: Chapter 9, Text 24 This verse emphasizes that the various sacrificial rites prescribed in the Vedic scriptures are ultimately meant to please the Supreme Lord. The term "yajna" specifically refers to Lord Vishnu. As stated in the Third Chapter of the Bhagavad-gita, one should engage in activities solely to please Yajna, who is Vishnu Himself. The Varnasrama-dharma system, which is the ideal social order, is designed to satisfy Lord Vishnu. Therefore, Krishna declares in this verse, "I am the enjoyer of all sacrifices as I am the supreme controller." Unfortunately, those lacking in spiritual understanding worship demigods seeking temporary material gains. Consequently, they remain entangled in the cycle of birth and death, failing to attain the ultimate goal of life. Even if one harbors material desires, it is advisable to pray to the Supreme Lord for their fulfillment (though this falls short of pure devotion), as doing so will lead to the desired outcome.

Chapter 9, Verse 25:
यान्ति देवव्रता देवान् पितृन् यान्ति पितृव्रताः । भूतानि यान्ति भूतेज्या यान्ति मद् याजिनोऽपि माम् ॥
Translation: Those who worship the demigods will be born among the demigods; those who worship the ancestors will go to the ancestors; those who worship spirits will be born among such beings; and those who worship Me will reside with Me.
Purport: To reach specific celestial destinations like the moon or the sun, one can follow Vedic principles like darśa-paurṇamāsī. The Vedas detail rituals to worship demigods on various heavenly planets. Similarly, performing specific yajnas can lead one to the Pitā planets. Some may go to ghostly realms and become Yakṣas, Rakṣas, or Piśācas through certain practices like black magic. Such practices are materialistic, unlike pure devotion to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, which grants access to Vaikuntha and Krishnaloka. Just as worship of demigods leads to heavenly realms, and Pitā worship to the Pitā planets, and black magic to ghostly realms, worship of the Supreme Lord guarantees entry to the abodes of Krishna or Vishnu. Unfortunately, many are unaware of these transcendental realms where Krishna and Vishnu reside, leading them to spiritual downfall. Even impersonalists fall from the brahmajyoti. The Krishna consciousness movement disseminates this sublime knowledge, teaching that by chanting the Hare Krishna mantra, one can attain perfection in this life and return to the spiritual abode.``` Chapter 9, Text 25 ```

Chapter 9, Verse 26:
पत्रं पुष्पं फलं तोयं यो मे भक्त्या प्रयच्छति।
तदहं भक्त्युपहृतमश्नामि प्रयतात्मनः॥२६॥
Translation: If one offers Me with love and devotion a leaf, a flower, fruit, or water, I will accept it.
Purport: Chapter 9, Text 26 For the wise, being in Krishna consciousness, engaging in transcendental loving service of the Lord, is crucial to attain an eternal abode filled with blissful happiness. The process to achieve this wondrous state is simple and open to all, even the most impoverished, without any prerequisites. The sole requirement is to be a sincere devotee of the Lord. It matters not one's background or circumstances. The process is so accessible that even a leaf, a little water, or fruit offered with genuine love to the Supreme Lord will be pleasing to Him. No one is excluded from Krishna consciousness, as it is universal and straightforward. Who would be so foolish as to not embrace Krishna consciousness through this uncomplicated method and thereby attain the ultimate perfection of eternal life filled with joy and wisdom? Krishna desires only loving service and nothing more. He gladly accepts even a small flower from His pure devotee, not requiring anything from a non-devotee. Being self-sufficient, He accepts offerings from His devotees out of love and affection. Developing Krishna consciousness is the pinnacle of existence. This verse emphasizes the significance of bhakti, or devotional service, as the sole means to approach Krishna. No other qualities, whether being a learned scholar, wealthy individual, or esteemed philosopher, can compel Krishna to accept offerings. Without the foundation of bhakti, the Lord cannot be induced to accept anything. Bhakti is not conditional; it is eternal and a direct service to the absolute whole.  Here, Lord Krishna, having established Himself as the supreme enjoyer, the original Lord, and the ultimate recipient of all sacrifices, reveals the types of offerings He desires. To engage in devotional service to purify oneself and attain the ultimate goal of life—transcendental loving service to God—one must understand what the Lord desires. A true lover of Krishna will offer Him what He desires and refrain from presenting anything undesirable or unasked for. Therefore, meat, fish, and eggs should not be offered to Krishna, as He explicitly requests a leaf, fruit, flowers, and water, stating, "I will accept it." Hence, it is clear that He does not accept meat, fish, or eggs. Vegetables, grains, fruits, milk, and water are the recommended foods for humans, as prescribed by Lord Krishna Himself. Other foods cannot be offered to Him, as He will not accept them. Thus, offering such foods is not an act of loving devotion.  In Chapter Three, verse thirteen, Sri Krishna explains that only the remnants of sacrifices are sanctified and suitable for consumption by those seeking spiritual advancement and liberation from material entanglement. In the same verse, He asserts that those who do not offer their food are consuming sin, further entangling themselves in material complexities. However, preparing simple and pure vegetarian dishes, offering them to the image or deity of Lord Krishna, and humbly praying for Him to accept the offering enables one to progress steadily, purify the body, and develop clear thinking. The key element in preparation, service, and offering is to act with love for Krishna.  The impersonalist philosophers, who assert that the Absolute Truth is devoid of senses, struggle to grasp this verse of the Bhagavad Gita. To them, it may seem metaphorical or indicative of Krishna's mundane nature as the speaker of the Gita. Yet, in reality, Krishna, the Supreme Godhead, possesses senses, and His senses are interchangeable, meaning one sense can perform the function of another. This illustrates Krishna's absolute nature; devoid of senses, He could not be considered complete in all opulences. In the Seventh Chapter, Krishna explains how He impregnates living entities into material nature by simply gazing upon it. Similarly, when Krishna hears a devotee's loving words while offering food, it is as if He is truly eating and relishing it. It is crucial to emphasize that due to His absolute position, Krishna's act of hearing is synonymous with His act of eating and savoring. Only a devotee who accepts Krishna as He describes Himself, without interpretation, can comprehend that the Supreme Absolute Truth can indeed consume and enjoy food.

Chapter 9, Verse 27:
यत् करोषि यद् अश्नासि यज् जुहोषि ददासि यत् । यत् तपस्यसि कौन्तेय तत् कुरुष्व मद् अर्पणम् ॥
Translation: Whatever actions you perform, whatever food you consume, whatever you offer or give away, and whatever austerities you undertake, O son of Kunti, do them as an offering unto Me.
Purport: It is the responsibility of every individual to shape their life in a manner that they do not forget Krishna in any circumstance. Each person must work to sustain both body and soul, and Krishna advises here that one should work for Him. Eating is essential for survival; hence one should partake in food offered to Krishna. Engaging in religious rituals is customary for civilized society; therefore Krishna advises, "Perform them for Me," which is known as arcana. Giving in charity is a natural inclination for many; Krishna instructs, "Give unto Me," implying that any surplus wealth should be used to advance the Krishna consciousness movement. In today's age, many are drawn to meditational practices, though not always practical. However, one who continuously meditates on Krishna by chanting the Hare Krishna mantra throughout the day using prayer beads becomes the supreme meditator and yogi, as confirmed in the Sixth Chapter of the Bhagavad Gita.``` Chapter 9, Text 27 ```

Chapter 9, Verse 28:
शुभाशुभ फलैर् एवं मोक्ष्यसे कर्मबन्धनैः । संन्यासयोगयुक्तात्मा विमुक्तो माम् उपैष्यसि ॥
Translation: In this way, you will be freed from the bondage of karma and its results, both auspicious and inauspicious. With your mind fixed on Me in the path of renunciation, you will attain liberation and come to Me.
Purport: One who acts in Krishna consciousness under superior guidance is known as yukta. This state is termed yukta-vairagya. Rupa Gosvami elaborates on this concept in the following verse from Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu:  anäsaktasya viṣayān yathärham upayujataḥ nirbandhaḥ kṛṣṇasambandhe yuktam vairägyam ucyate (Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu 2.255)  Rupa Gosvami explains that as long as we are in the material world, we must engage in actions; we cannot remain inactive. Therefore, when actions are performed and their results are offered to Krishna, it is termed yukta-vairagya. Such renunciation in action purifies the mind and gradually leads the practitioner to complete surrender to the Supreme Lord. Ultimately, the practitioner attains liberation, not merging into the impersonal Brahman, but entering the abode of the Supreme Lord. The verse clearly states, mām upaiṣyasi, "he comes to Me," returning home, back to Godhead. There are five stages of liberation, and in this context, it is specified that the devotee who has lived his life under the direction of the Supreme Lord reaches a stage where, upon leaving the body, he returns to Godhead to engage directly in the divine service of the Supreme Lord.  A true sannyasi is one who dedicates his life solely to serving the Lord. Such an individual identifies as an eternal servant, completely dependent on the divine will of the Lord. Every action he performs is for the Lord's benefit, viewing all his activities as service to the Lord. He does not prioritize the fruitive actions or prescribed duties outlined in the Vedas. While ordinary individuals must adhere to Vedic duties, a pure devotee fully engrossed in the service of the Lord may at times seem to deviate from these duties, though in reality, he does not.  Vaishnava authorities assert that even the most intelligent person cannot fully comprehend the intentions and actions of a pure devotee. It is said, tāṅra väkya, kriyä, mudrä vijñeha nä bujhaya (Caitanya-caritamrita, Madhya 23.39). A person consistently engaged in the service of the Lord, constantly contemplating and planning ways to serve the Lord, is considered liberated in the present moment, with a guaranteed return home, back to Godhead, in the future. Such a devotee transcends all materialistic criticisms, just as Krishna is beyond all criticisms. ``` Chapter 9, Text 28 ```

Chapter 9, Verse 29:

Chapter 9, Verse 30:

Translation: Even if one engages in the most abominable actions, if they are devoted to Me without deviation, they should be considered saintly, as they are firmly resolved in their spiritual path.
Purport: Chapter 9, Text 30 The term "suduräcāraḥ" in this verse is profound and merits careful consideration. A conditioned being performs two types of activities: conditional and constitutional. Conditional activities pertain to bodily maintenance and societal norms, even for devotees, whereas constitutional activities arise from full awareness of one's spiritual essence and engagement in Krishna consciousness, known as devotional service. While in a conditioned state, a devotee may sometimes blend devotional and conditional activities harmoniously, but at times they may conflict. A sincere devotee is vigilant to avoid disruptions to their spiritual progress, understanding that perfection hinges on deepening Krishna consciousness. Occasionally, a devotee in Krishna consciousness may seemingly commit socially or politically abominable acts. However, such lapses do not disqualify them. The Srimad-Bhagavatam affirms that wholehearted engagement in transcendental service purifies and absolves a fallen devotee. Material contamination can ensnare even a dedicated yogi, yet Krishna consciousness swiftly corrects such lapses, ensuring the success of devotional service. Deriding a devotee for a temporary falldown contradicts the spiritual order, as such lapses will naturally cease once one is firmly established in Krishna consciousness.  Thus, a person steadfast in Krishna consciousness and resolute in chanting the Hare Krishna mantra should be regarded as transcendentally situated, even if they have temporarily faltered. The term "sädhur eva" emphatically underscores that a devotee, despite accidental lapses, should not be disparaged but esteemed as saintly. The word "mantavyaḥ" further emphasizes this point. Disobeying this directive and mocking a devotee for a momentary lapse amounts to defying the Supreme Lord's command. A devotee's sole qualification is unwavering dedication to devotional service.  The Nṛsiṁha Purāṇa states: bhagavati ca harāv ananyacetä bhṛśamalino ’pi viräjate manuṣyaḥ na hi śaśakaluṣacchaviḥ kadäcit timiraparäbhavatām upaiti candraḥ  This verse illustrates that even if a devoted soul occasionally engages in reprehensible actions, these actions are akin to blemishes on the moon that do not obstruct its radiance. Likewise, a devotee's accidental deviation from saintly conduct does not render them abominable.  It is crucial not to misinterpret this to justify abominable behavior in the guise of transcendental devotion. This verse pertains to incidental lapses due to the potent influence of material connections. Devotional service signifies a battle against illusion. Until one gains sufficient strength to combat illusion, occasional falldowns may occur. However, once one is steadfast, such lapses cease, as previously explained. Exploiting this verse to engage in misconduct while claiming devotion signifies a lack of spiritual advancement. If one's character does not improve through devotional service, it indicates a deficiency in true devotion.

Translation: Neither the hosts of demigods nor the great sages know My origin or opulences, for in every respect, I am the source of the demigods and sages.
Purport: Chapter 10, Text 2 As stated in the Brahma-samhita, Lord Krishna is the Supreme Lord. No one is greater than Him; He is the cause of all causes. The Lord personally declares here that He is the cause of all demigods and sages. Even the demigods and great sages cannot comprehend Krishna; they are unable to grasp His name or His divine nature. So, what can be said of the scholars on this insignificant planet? No one can fathom why this Supreme God descends to Earth in the form of an ordinary human and performs extraordinary, incomprehensible deeds. It is essential to understand that mere scholarship is insufficient to comprehend Krishna. Even the demigods and great sages have attempted to understand Krishna through intellectual speculation but have failed. The Srimad-Bhagavatam also clearly states that even the great demigods are incapable of fully understanding the Supreme Personality of Godhead. They may speculate within the limits of their imperfect senses, arriving at the impersonal conclusion or concocting theories through mental gymnastics, but they cannot grasp Krishna through such futile speculations.  The Lord indirectly conveys here that anyone seeking the Absolute Truth should recognize, "I am present as the Supreme Personality of Godhead. I am the Supreme." Though the inconceivable Lord is beyond direct comprehension, He undeniably exists. By studying His teachings in the Bhagavad-gita and Srimad-Bhagavatam, we can truly comprehend Krishna, who is eternal, blissful, and full of knowledge. While the conception of God as a ruling power or as the impersonal Brahman may be accessible to those in the inferior energy of the Lord, understanding the Personality of Godhead requires a transcendental position.  Due to the inability of most individuals to grasp Krishna in His true essence, out of His causeless mercy, He descends to assist such seekers. Despite the extraordinary activities of the Supreme Lord, these speculators, influenced by material energy, persist in viewing the impersonal Brahman as supreme. Only those devotees who completely surrender to the Supreme Lord can, by His grace, recognize Krishna. Devotees do not concern themselves with the impersonal Brahman concept; their unwavering faith and devotion lead them to immediate surrender to the Supreme Lord, and by Krishna's causeless mercy, they can comprehend Him. No one else can truly understand Him. Therefore, even great sages concur: The true object of worship is the Supreme, whom we must adore.

Chapter 10, Verse 3:

Translation: He who knows Me as the unborn, as the beginningless, as the Supreme Lord of all the worlds—such a person, unclouded among humanity, is liberated from all sins.
Purport: Chapter 10, Text 3 As mentioned in the Seventh Chapter (7.3), manuṣyäṇāṁ sahasreṣu kaścid yatati siddhaye: those striving for spiritual realization are not ordinary individuals; they surpass millions of those who lack such understanding. Among those earnestly seeking spiritual enlightenment, the one who comprehends that Krishna is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the ultimate proprietor, and the unborn, is the most spiritually accomplished. Only when one fully grasps Krishna's supreme position can one be completely free from all sinful reactions.  Here, the Lord is described as aja, meaning “unborn,” distinct from the living entities described in Chapter Two as aja. The Lord is different from the living beings who undergo birth and death due to material attachments. While conditioned souls change bodies, His body remains unchanging. Even when He manifests in the material world, He appears as the eternal unborn. Thus, in the Fourth Chapter, it is stated that by His internal potency, the Lord transcends the inferior material energy and remains in the superior energy.  The phrase vetti loka-maheśvaram indicates that one should recognize Lord Krishna as the supreme owner of the planetary systems in the universe. He existed before creation and is distinct from His creation. All demigods were created within this material realm, but Krishna is said to be uncreated. Therefore, Krishna is superior even to great demigods like Brahmā and Shiva. As the creator of Brahmā, Shiva, and all other demigods, Krishna is the Supreme Being of all realms.  Sri Krishna is beyond all that is created; knowing Him as such leads to liberation from all sinful reactions. To understand the Supreme Lord, one must be free from all sinful activities. Only through devotional service can the Supreme Lord be known, as stated in the Bhagavad-gita.  One should not perceive Krishna as a mere human being. As mentioned earlier, only a foolish person regards Him as such. This is reiterated here in a different manner. A wise individual who comprehends the divine nature of the Supreme Being is always free from sinful reactions.  If Krishna is known as the son of Devaki, how can He be unborn? This is explained in the Srimad-Bhagavatam: When Krishna appeared before Devaki and Vasudeva, He did not take birth as an ordinary child; He manifested in His original form and then transformed into an ordinary child. Any action performed under Krishna's guidance is transcendental and untouched by material reactions, whether auspicious or inauspicious. The notion of auspicious and inauspicious in the material world is largely a mental construct, as there is inherently nothing auspicious in the material realm. True auspiciousness stems from engaging in activities in full devotion and service to Krishna. Therefore, for our actions to be truly auspicious, we must follow the directives of the Supreme Lord, as outlined in authoritative scriptures like Srimad-Bhagavatam and Bhagavad-gita, or from a genuine spiritual master. Since the spiritual master represents the Supreme Lord, his guidance is directly from the Lord. The spiritual master, saintly individuals, and scriptures provide consistent guidance. Actions performed under such guidance are free from the reactions of pious or impious deeds in this material world. The transcendental mindset of a devotee in performing actions is essentially that of renunciation, known as sannyasa. As stated in the first verse of the Sixth Chapter of Bhagavad-gita, one who acts dutifully as instructed by the Supreme Lord, without desiring the fruits of their actions (anäsritaḥ karmaphalam), is a true renunciant. Anyone acting under the direction of the Supreme Lord is a true renunciant and yogi, not merely someone who outwardly assumes the appearance of a renunciant or a superficial yogi.

Chapter 10, Verse 8:

इति मत्वा भजन्ते मां बुधा भावसमन्विताः ॥ ८ ॥

Purport: Chapter 10, Text 8 A learned scholar, well-versed in the Vedas and teachings of spiritual authorities like Lord Caitanya, can comprehend that Krishna is the ultimate source of all creation, both material and spiritual. This profound understanding leads such a person to wholeheartedly engage in devotional service to the Supreme Lord. Such a devotee remains steadfast in his devotion and is unaffected by misleading interpretations or ignorant criticisms. The Vedic scriptures unanimously affirm that Krishna is the source of Brahma, Shiva, and all other demigods. The Gopala-tapani Upanishad (1.24) states that it was Krishna who imparted Vedic knowledge to Brahma at the beginning of creation. Similarly, the Narayana Upanishad describes how Näräyaṇa desired to create living beings, and from Him Brahma, Shiva, and other celestial beings manifested. Lord Shiva himself is an expansion of Näräyaṇa, who is in turn an expansion of Krishna.  The Vedas declare, "The son of Devaki, Krishna, is the Supreme Personality." (Narayana Upanishad 4) They further affirm that in the primordial state, only Näräyaṇa existed, without Brahma, Shiva, or any other celestial entities. Lord Shiva, the creator of Brahma and Shiva, is thus to be worshipped as the Supreme Lord. In the Mokṣa-dharma, Krishna reveals that even patriarchs and deities like Shiva are created by Him, although they remain ignorant of this truth due to His illusory energy. The Varaha Purana also confirms that Näräyaṇa is the Supreme Godhead, from whom Brahma and Shiva originate.  Lord Krishna asserts Himself as the ultimate cause of all creation, stating, "Because everything emanates from Me, I am the primal source of all existence. All beings are subordinate to Me; there is none superior." Krishna, as the supreme controller, is unrivaled. A genuine spiritual aspirant who comprehends Krishna's supreme position through the guidance of a bona fide spiritual teacher and scriptural references immerses himself in Krishna consciousness, attaining true wisdom. In contrast, those who lack proper understanding of Krishna are considered ignorant. Only a fool would underestimate Krishna's divine nature. A devotee of Krishna should not be swayed by ignorant individuals, but should instead shun unauthorized interpretations and steadfastly progress in Krishna consciousness with unwavering determination.

Chapter 10, Verse 9:
मच्चित्ता मद्गतप्राणा बोधयन्तः परस्परम् । कथयन्तश् च मां नित्यं तुष्यन्ति च रमन्ति च ॥
Translation: The thoughts of My pure devotees dwell in Me, their lives are fully devoted to My service, and they derive great satisfaction and bliss from always enlightening one another and conversing about Me.
Purport: Pure devotees, whose characteristics are mentioned here, engage themselves fully in the transcendental loving service of the Lord. Their minds cannot be diverted from the lotus feet of Krishna. Their talks are solely on the transcendental subjects. The symptoms of the pure devotees are described in this verse specifically. Devotees of the Supreme Lord are twenty-four hours daily engaged in glorifying the qualities and pastimes of the Supreme Lord. Their hearts and souls are constantly submerged in Krishna, and they take pleasure in discussing Him with other devotees.  In the preliminary stage of devotional service, they relish the transcendental pleasure from the service itself, and in the mature stage, they are actually situated in love of God. Once situated in that transcendental position, they can relish the highest perfection exhibited by the Lord in His abode. Lord Caitanya likens transcendental devotional service to the sowing of a seed in the heart of the living entity. There are innumerable living entities traveling throughout the different planets of the universe, and out of them, there are a few who are fortunate enough to meet a pure devotee and get the chance to understand devotional service. This devotional service is just like a seed, and if it is sown in the heart of a living entity, and if he goes on hearing and chanting Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare/ Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare, that seed fructifies, just as the seed of a tree fructifies with regular watering. The spiritual plant of devotional service gradually grows and grows until it penetrates the covering of the material universe and enters into the brahmajyoti effulgence in the spiritual sky. In the spiritual sky, that plant also grows more and more until it reaches the highest planet, Goloka Vrindavana, the supreme planet of Krishna. Ultimately, the plant takes shelter under the lotus feet of Krishna and rests there. Gradually, as a plant grows fruits and flowers, the plant of devotional service also produces fruits, and the watering process in the form of chanting and hearing goes on. This plant of devotional service is fully described in the Caitanya-caritamrita (Madhya-lila, Chapter Nineteen). It is explained there that when the complete plant takes shelter under the lotus feet of the Supreme Lord, one becomes fully absorbed in love of God; then he cannot live even for a moment without being in contact with the Supreme Lord, just as a fish cannot live without water. In such a state, the devotee actually attains the transcendental qualities in contact with the Supreme Lord.  The Srimad-Bhagavatam is also full of such narrations about the relationship between the Supreme Lord and His devotees; therefore, the Srimad-Bhagavatam is very dear to the devotees, as stated in the Bhagavatam itself (12.13.18). Śrīmadbhāgavataṁ purāṇam amalaṁ yad vaiṣṇavänäṁ priyam. In this narration, there is nothing about material activities, economic development, sense gratification, or liberation. Srimad-Bhagavatam is the only narration in which the transcendental nature of the Supreme Lord and His devotees is fully described. Thus, the realized souls in Krishna consciousness take continual pleasure in hearing such transcendental literatures, just as a young boy and girl take pleasure in association. ``` Chapter 10, Text 9 ```

Chapter 10, Verse 10:
तेषां सततयुक्तानां भजतां प्रीतिपूर्वकम् ।
ददामि बुद्धियोगं तं येन माम् उपयान्ति ते ॥ १० ॥
Translation: For those who are constantly devoted to serving Me with love, I bestow the insight by which they can reach Me.
Purport: Chapter 10, Text 10 In this verse, the term "buddhi-yoga" holds great significance. Recall that in the Second Chapter, the Lord, while instructing Arjuna, mentioned speaking on many topics and promising guidance in the path of buddhi-yoga. Now, buddhi-yoga is elucidated. Buddhi-yoga signifies action in Krishna consciousness; it embodies the highest wisdom. Buddhi denotes intelligence, and yoga conveys mystical practices or spiritual elevation. When one endeavors to return to Godhead and wholeheartedly embraces Krishna consciousness through devotional service, his actions are termed buddhi-yoga. In essence, buddhi-yoga is the means to liberate oneself from the entanglements of the material world. The ultimate objective is Krishna. This realization eludes many; hence, the company of devotees and an authentic spiritual guide are crucial. Recognizing Krishna as the goal, one steadily advances on the path towards Him, ultimately attaining the supreme goal.  If a person comprehends the purpose of life but remains attached to the outcomes of his actions, he practices karma-yoga. When one understands Krishna as the goal but finds pleasure in mental speculations to grasp Krishna, he engages in jnana-yoga. However, when one recognizes the goal and wholeheartedly seeks Krishna in Krishna consciousness and devotional service, he practices bhakti-yoga, or buddhi-yoga, which embodies complete yoga. This comprehensive yoga represents the pinnacle of spiritual perfection.  Even if an individual has a genuine spiritual mentor and is affiliated with a spiritual institution, lacking the intelligence to progress, Krishna imparts guidance from within, facilitating the journey towards Him without obstacles. The prerequisite is unwavering engagement in Krishna consciousness and the wholehearted rendering of all forms of service with love and devotion. The devotee should undertake activities for Krishna with love. Should a devotee lack the acumen to advance on the path of self-realization but remains sincere and dedicated to devotional activities, the Lord grants him the opportunity to progress and ultimately unite with Him.

Chapter 10, Verse 11:
तेषाम् एवानुकम्पार्थम् अहम् अज्ञानजं तमः । नाशयाम्य् आत्मभावस्थो ज्ञानदीपेन भास्वता ॥
Translation: Out of compassion for them, I, residing in their hearts, dispel the darkness of ignorance with the luminous lamp of knowledge.
Purport: When Lord Caitanya was in Benares spreading the chanting of the holy names—Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare/ Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare—thousands of people followed Him. At that time, Prakasananda Sarasvati, a prominent and erudite scholar in Benares, criticized Lord Caitanya as sentimental. Sometimes philosophers criticize devotees, assuming them to be ignorant and sentimental. However, this is not accurate. There are highly learned scholars who have presented the philosophy of devotion. Yet, even if a devotee does not delve into such literature or teachings of spiritual masters, if they sincerely engage in devotional service, Krishna Himself in their heart assists them. Thus, a sincere devotee in Krishna consciousness is never devoid of knowledge. The essential qualification is to wholeheartedly render devotional service in complete Krishna consciousness.  Modern philosophers assert that without discernment, one cannot attain true knowledge. To them, the Supreme Lord gives this response: those immersed in pure devotional service, even lacking formal education or deep Vedic knowledge, are still supported by the Supreme God, as stated in this verse. The Lord informs Arjuna that essentially, it is impossible to comprehend the Supreme Truth, the Absolute Truth, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, solely through speculation. The Supreme Truth is so vast that understanding or realizing Him through mental efforts alone is unattainable. One may speculate endlessly, yet without devotion and love for the Supreme Truth, they will never fathom Krishna or the Supreme Truth. Only through devotional service does the Supreme Truth, Krishna, become pleased, and through His inconceivable potency, He reveals Himself to the heart of the pure devotee. The pure devotee always carries Krishna within their heart, akin to the sun, dispelling the darkness of ignorance instantaneously. This is the unique mercy bestowed upon the pure devotee by Krishna.  Due to the contamination of material association over countless lifetimes, one's heart remains veiled by the dust of materialism. However, through engaging in devotional service and constant chanting of the holy names like Hare Krishna, the dust dissipates swiftly, elevating one to the realm of pure knowledge. The ultimate goal, Vishnu, can only be achieved through this chanting and devotional service, not by mental speculation or debate. The pure devotee need not concern themselves with material needs; they need not worry, for when they cleanse their heart of darkness, the Supreme Lord automatically provides everything, pleased by the devotee's loving service. This encapsulates the essence of the teachings of Bhagavad-gita. Through studying Bhagavad-gita, one can completely surrender their soul to the Supreme Lord and engage in pure devotional service. As the Lord takes charge, one becomes entirely liberated from all material pursuits. ``` Chapter 10, Text 11 ```

Chapter 10, Verse 14:
सर्वम् एतद् ऋतम् मन्ये यन् मां वदसि केशव । न हि ते भगवन् व्यक्तिं विदुर् देवा न दानवाः ॥
Translation: O Krishna, I wholeheartedly believe in all that You have told me. Neither the demigods nor the demons, O Lord, can comprehend Your divine nature.
Purport: Arjuna affirms here that those lacking faith and with demonic tendencies cannot fathom the true nature of Krishna. Even the demigods are unable to fully understand Him, let alone the so-called scholars of this modern world. Through the grace of the Supreme Lord, Arjuna has realized that Krishna is the ultimate Truth and the perfect being. Therefore, one should follow in the footsteps of Arjuna, who received the divine knowledge of Bhagavad-gita. As explained in the Fourth Chapter, the ancient paramparä system of spiritual lineage for understanding Bhagavad-gita had been lost, and Krishna reinstated it with Arjuna due to their close friendship and Arjuna's profound devotion. Hence, as mentioned in our Introduction to Gitopanisad, the teachings of Bhagavad-gita should be understood within the paramparä system. Arjuna was chosen to revive this lineage when it was lost. Emulating Arjuna's complete acceptance of Krishna's words allows us to grasp the essence of Bhagavad-gita and recognize Krishna as the Supreme Personality of Godhead.""" Chapter 10, Text 14 """

Chapter 10, Verse 15:
स्वयम् एव आत्मनात्मानं वेत्थ त्वम् पुरुषोत्तम ।
भूतभावन भूतेश देवदेव जगत्पते ॥ १५ ॥
Translation: You alone know Yourself by Your own internal potency, O Supreme Person, origin of all, Lord of all beings, God of gods, Lord of the universe!
Purport: Chapter 10, Text 15 The Supreme Lord, Krishna, can be known by those engaged in devotional service, like Arjuna and his followers. Those with a demonic or atheistic mentality cannot understand Krishna. Speculation that leads one away from the Supreme Lord is a grave sin. Those unfamiliar with Krishna should not attempt to interpret the Bhagavad Gita. This sacred text is the revelation of Krishna and should be understood as Arjuna comprehended it, not through atheistic perspectives.  As stated in Srimad-Bhagavatam (1.2.11):  "vadanti tat tattva-vidas tattvaṁ yaj jñänam advayam brahmeti paramätmeti bhagavän iti śabdyate"  The Supreme Truth is realized in three aspects: as impersonal Brahman, localized Paramatma, and ultimately as the Supreme Personality of Godhead. The highest realization of the Absolute Truth leads one to the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Ordinary or even liberated individuals who have experienced the impersonal Brahman or localized Paramatma may struggle to comprehend God’s personality. They can seek to understand the Supreme Person through the verses of Bhagavad Gita, spoken by Krishna. Some impersonalists may acknowledge Krishna as Bhagavän or accept His authority. However, many liberated souls may not fully grasp Krishna as Purusottama, the Supreme Person. Hence, Arjuna addresses Him as Purusottama. Even if one recognizes Krishna as the father of all living beings, they may not realize His role as the supreme controller, hence He is called Bhūtesa, the ultimate controller of all. Furthermore, knowing Krishna as the supreme controller, one may still miss His position as the origin of all demigods, hence He is referred to as Devadeva, the revered God of all demigods. Even acknowledging Him as the worshipful God of all demigods, one may overlook His status as the supreme proprietor of everything, hence He is known as Jagatpati. Arjuna's realization in this verse establishes the truth about Krishna, and we should follow his example to understand Krishna in His entirety.

Chapter 10, Verse 16:
वक्तुम् अर्हस्य् अशेषेण दिव्या ह्य् आत्म विभूतयः । याभिर् विभूतिभिर् लोकान् इमांस् त्वं व्याप्य तिष्ठसि ॥
Translation: Please elaborate on Your divine manifestations through which You pervade all these worlds.
Purport: In this verse, it is evident that Arjuna is already content with his comprehension of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krishna. By Krishna’s grace, Arjuna possesses personal experience, intelligence, and knowledge, and has recognized Krishna as the Supreme Personality of Godhead. He harbors no doubts, yet he seeks an explanation from Krishna on His omnipresent nature. Common people and impersonalists are primarily intrigued by the all-pervading aspect of the Supreme. Arjuna is inquiring how Krishna exists in His all-pervasive form through His various energies. It is important to note that Arjuna is posing this question on behalf of the general populace.``` Chapter 10, Text 16 ```

Chapter 10, Verse 17:
कथम् विद्याम् अहम् योगिन् त्वाम् सदा परिचिन्तयन् ।
केषु केषु च भावेषु चिन्त्योऽसि भगवन् मया ॥ १७ ॥
Translation: O Krishna, O supreme mystic, how can I constantly contemplate upon You, and how can I understand You? In what various forms should I meditate upon You, O Supreme Personality of Godhead?
Purport: Chapter 10, Text 17 As mentioned in the previous chapter, the Supreme Personality of Godhead is veiled by His divine energy. Only surrendered souls and devotees can perceive Him. Arjuna now acknowledges that his friend, Krishna, is the Supreme Godhead, yet he seeks to understand how the all-pervading Lord can be comprehended by ordinary individuals. Common men, including demons and atheists, are unable to fathom Krishna as He is shielded by His divine energy. Arjuna poses these questions for the benefit of all. A true devotee is not only concerned with their own realization but also with the enlightenment of all beings. Thus, out of compassion as a Vaishnava devotee, Arjuna elucidates the omnipresence of the Supreme Lord for the common man. He specifically addresses Krishna as a yogin because Sri Krishna is the master of the divine energy that conceals and reveals Him to ordinary individuals. Those lacking love for Krishna cannot consistently meditate upon Him, hence they engage in material contemplation. Arjuna contemplates the mindset of materialistic individuals in this world. The phrase "keṣu keṣu ca bhäveṣu" pertains to the material realm (where "bhäva" signifies physical entities). Since materialists struggle to comprehend Krishna spiritually, they are advised to focus their minds on physical objects and attempt to perceive Krishna through physical manifestations.

Chapter 10, Verse 18:
विस्तरेणात्मनो योगं विभूतिं च जनार्दन । भूयः कथय तृप्तिर् हि शृण्वतो नास्ति मेऽमृतम् ॥
Translation: O Janardana, please elaborate on the mystic power of Your opulences. I am never satisfied in hearing about You, for the more I listen, the more I yearn to taste the nectar of Your words.
Purport: A similar sentiment was expressed to Suta Gosvami by the sages of Naimisaranya, led by Shaunaka. They said:  vayaṁ tu na vitṛpyāma uttama-śloka-vikrame yac chṛṇvatāṁ rasajñānāṁ svādu svādu pade pade  “One can never be satiated even when continually hearing the transcendental pastimes of Krishna, who is glorified by sublime prayers. Those who have developed a transcendental bond with Krishna relish, at every step, the descriptions of the Lord's activities.” (Srimad-Bhagavatam 1.1.19) Thus, Arjuna is eager to hear about Krishna, particularly how He remains the all-pervading Supreme Lord.  Regarding the nectar referred to as amritam, any narration or discussion related to Krishna is akin to nectar. This nectar can be experienced firsthand. Unlike mundane stories, fiction, and histories that eventually lose their appeal, the transcendental pastimes of Krishna are ever-fresh and captivating. This is why throughout history, the narratives of the incarnations of the Supreme Lord have been a central theme in the universe's annals. The Puranas chronicle the pastimes of the various incarnations of the Lord in ancient times. Thus, the subject matter of these texts remains perpetually engaging, even upon repeated readings.``` Chapter 10, Text 18 ```

Chapter 10, Verse 19:
श्रीभगवानुवाच हन्त ते कथयिष्यामि दिव्या ह्य् आत्म विभूतयः । प्राधान्यतः कुरुश्रेष्ठ नास्त्य् अन्तो विस्तरस्य मे ॥
Translation: The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: "O Arjuna, I shall now describe to you some of My divine manifestations, for My opulence is limitless, and I shall speak only of those that are most prominent.
Purport: The greatness of Krishna and His opulences is beyond human comprehension. The limited senses of individual souls do not allow them to fully grasp the vastness of Krishna's divine affairs. Nevertheless, devotees endeavor to understand Krishna, not with the expectation of completely comprehending Him at any specific time or stage of life, but because the topics related to Krishna are so delightful that they are like nectar to the devotees. Thus, they relish discussing and contemplating His opulences and diverse energies. Krishna, knowing that living beings cannot fathom the extent of His opulences, chooses to reveal only the primary manifestations of His various energies. The term 'pradhanyatah' ('principal') is crucial because we can only grasp a few key aspects of the Supreme Lord, as His features are limitless and cannot be fully understood. In this context, 'vibhuti' denotes the exceptional opulences through which He governs the entire creation. The Amara-kosa dictionary defines 'vibhuti' as an extraordinary opulence.  Impersonalists or pantheists are unable to comprehend the exceptional opulences of the Supreme Lord or the manifestations of His divine energies. Both in the material and spiritual realms, His energies manifest in countless forms. In this discourse, Krishna is elucidating what can be perceived directly by ordinary individuals, thereby revealing a fraction of His diverse energy."``` Chapter 10, Text 19 ```

Chapter 10, Verse 20:
अहम् आत्मा गुडाकेश सर्वभूताशयस्थितः । अहम् आदिश् च मध्यं च भूतानाम् अन्त एव च ॥
Translation: I am the Supersoul, O Arjuna, seated in the hearts of all living entities. I am the beginning, the middle, and the end of all beings.
Purport: In this verse, Arjuna is addressed as Guḍākeśa, which means “one who has conquered the darkness of sleep.” For those who are sleeping in the darkness of ignorance, it is not possible to understand how the Supreme Personality of Godhead manifests Himself in various ways in the material and spiritual worlds. Thus, this address by Krishna to Arjuna is significant. Because Arjuna is above such darkness, the Personality of Godhead agrees to describe His various opulences.  Krishna first informs Arjuna that He is the soul of the entire cosmic manifestation by dint of His primary expansion. Before the material creation, the Supreme Lord, by His plenary expansion, accepts the puruṣa incarnations, and from Him everything begins. Therefore, He is ātma, the soul of the mahat-tattva, the universal elements. The total material energy is not the cause of creation; actually, the Mahä-Vishnu enters into the mahat-tattva, the total material energy. He is the soul. When Mahä-Vishnu enters into the manifested universes, He again manifests Himself as the Supersoul in each and every entity. We have the experience that the personal body of the living entity exists due to the presence of the spiritual spark. Without the existence of the spiritual spark, the body cannot develop. Similarly, the material manifestation cannot develop unless the Supreme Soul, Krishna, enters. As stated in the Subala Upanishad, prakṛtyädi-sarva-bhūtāntaryāmī sarvaśeṣī ca närāyaṇah: “The Supreme Personality of Godhead exists as the Supersoul in all manifested universes.”  The three puruṣa-avatāras are described in Srimad-Bhagavatam. They are also described in the Sätvata-tantra. Viṣṇos tu trīṇi rūpāṇi puruṣākhyāny atho viduḥ: the Supreme Personality of Godhead manifests three features—as Käraṇodakaśāyī Vishnu, Garbhodakaśāyī Vishnu, and Kṣīrodakaśāyī Vishnu—in this material manifestation. The Mahä-Vishnu, or Käraṇodakaśāyī Vishnu, is described in the Brahma-saṁhitā (5.47). Yaḥ käraṇārṇavajale bhajati sma yoganidrām: the Supreme Lord, Krishna, the cause of all causes, lies down in the cosmic ocean as Mahä-Vishnu. Therefore, the Supreme Personality of Godhead is the beginning of this universe, the maintainer of the universal manifestations, and the end of all energy.""" Chapter 10, Text 20 """

Chapter 10, Verse 21:
आदित्यानाम् अहं विष्णुर् ज्योतिषाम् रविर् अंशुमान् । मरीचिर् मरुताम् अस्मि नक्षत्राणाम् अहं शशी ॥
Translation: Among the Adityas, I am Vishnu; among luminous bodies, I am the radiant sun; of the Maruts, I am Marici; and among the stars, I am the moon.
Purport: The Adityas are twelve celestial deities, with Vishnu being the foremost. The sun, as the principal luminary in the sky, is considered the eye of the Supreme Lord in the Brahma-samhita. The Maruts are fifty types of celestial winds, with Marici as their presiding deity, symbolizing Krishna.  The moon shines prominently among the stars at night, representing Krishna. This verse implies that the moon is a star, with its light reflecting the sun's brilliance. Vedic scriptures reject the idea of multiple suns in the universe; there is only one sun, whose light is reflected by the moon and stars. By highlighting the moon as one of the stars, the Gita clarifies that the twinkling stars are not suns but akin to the moon in their illumination.``` Chapter 10, Text 21 ```

Chapter 10, Verse 22:
वेदानां सामवेदोऽस्मि देवानाम् अस्मि वासवः । इन्द्रियाणां मनश् चास्मि भूतानाम् अस्मि चेतना ॥
Translation: Among the Vedas, I am the Sama Veda; among the celestial beings, I am Indra, the ruler of the heavens; within the senses, I am the mind; and within all living beings, I am the consciousness.
Purport: The distinction between matter and spirit lies in the fact that matter lacks consciousness, unlike sentient beings. Therefore, consciousness is supreme and eternal, transcending the material realm. Consciousness cannot be generated through the combination of material elements.""" Chapter 10, Text 22 """

Chapter 10, Verse 23:
रुद्राणां शङ्करश् चास्मि वित्तेशो यक्षरक्षसाम् । वसूनां पावकश् चास्मि मेरुः शिखरिणाम् अहम् ॥

Chapter 10, Verse 24:
पुरोधसां च मुख्यं मां विद्धि पार्थ बृहस्पतिम् । सेनानीनाम् अहं स्कन्दः सरसाम् अस्मि सागरः ॥

Chapter 10, Verse 25:
महर्षणां भृगुर् अहं गिराम् अस्मि एकम् अक्षरम् । यज्ञानां जपयोगोऽस्मि स्थावराणां हिमालयः ॥
Translation: Among the great sages, I am Bhrigu; among sounds, I am the eternal sound of om. Of all sacrifices, I am the practice of chanting the holy names [japa], and among immovable objects, I am the Himalayas.
Purport: Brahmä, the first created being in the universe, fathered various sons to populate different species. Among these sons, Bhrigu stands out as the most potent sage. The sacred sound of om (omkara) symbolizes Lord Krishna. Among all forms of worship, the chanting of the Hare Krishna mantra - Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare/ Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare - is the most sublime representation of Krishna. While animal sacrifices are sometimes prescribed in Vedic rituals, the chanting of the Hare Krishna mantra is devoid of violence, making it the simplest and purest form of devotion. Anything that exudes greatness in this world is a manifestation of Krishna. Therefore, the grandeur of the Himalayas, the tallest mountain range on Earth, also reflects His glory. Although Mount Meru was mentioned earlier, it is worth noting that Meru is occasionally movable, unlike the steadfast Himalayas, which remain immovable. Hence, the Himalayas hold greater significance than Meru.``` Chapter 10, Text 25 ```

Chapter 10, Verse 26:
अश्वत्थः सर्ववृक्षाणां देवर्षीणां च नारदः । गन्धर्वाणां चित्ररथः सिद्धानां कपिलो मुनिः ॥

Chapter 10, Verse 27:

In Vedic tradition, kings were revered as the earthly manifestations of the divine. Chapter 10, Verse 28:
आयुधानाम् अहं वज्रं धेनूनाम् अस्मि कामधुक् । प्रजनश् चास्मि कन्दर्पः सर्पाणाम् अस्मि वासुकिः ॥

Chapter 11, Verse 18:
त्वम् अक्षरम् परमम् वेदितव्यं

Translation: You are the supreme eternal truth to be known. You are the ultimate shelter of this universe. You are imperishable, the guardian of eternal dharma. In my view, You are the ancient Person.
Purport: Chapter 11, Text 18 The Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krishna, is to be revered like a father is revered by his child. He is the spiritual guide who imparted Vedic teachings to Brahmä in the past and is currently instructing Arjuna in the Bhagavad-gita. Therefore, Krishna is the original spiritual master, and any genuine spiritual teacher today must descend from the disciplic lineage originating from Krishna. Without being a representative of Krishna, one cannot authentically teach transcendental knowledge.  The Lord is offered obeisances in every way. His greatness is immeasurable. No one can surpass the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krishna, as there is no one equal to or higher than Him in any spiritual or material manifestation. Everyone is subordinate to Him; none can surpass Him. This is affirmed in the Svetasvatara Upanishad (6.8):  na tasya käryaṁ karaṇaṁ ca vidyate na tat-samaś cäbhyadhikaś ca dṛśyate  Krishna, the Supreme Lord, possesses senses and a body similar to an ordinary person, yet for Him, there is no distinction between His senses, body, mind, and self. Ignorant individuals who lack true knowledge claim that Krishna is separate from His soul, mind, heart, and other aspects. Krishna is absolute; thus, His actions and powers are supreme. Although He doesn't possess senses like ours, He can perform all sensory functions, indicating that His senses are neither deficient nor limited. No one can surpass Him, no one can be His equal, and everyone is subordinate to Him.  The knowledge, strength, and deeds of the Supreme Personality are all transcendental. As stated in the Bhagavad-gita (4.9):  janma karma ca me divyam evaṁ yo vetti tattvataḥ tyaktvä dehaṁ punar janma naiti mäm eti so ’rjuna  One who understands the divine nature of Krishna's birth and activities, upon leaving the body, returns to Him and does not reincarnate into this sorrowful world. Hence, it is crucial to recognize that Krishna's actions are distinct from others. The most effective approach is to adhere to Krishna's principles, which lead to perfection. It is also acknowledged that no one can claim mastery over Krishna; everyone is His servant. The Caitanya-caritamrita (Adi 5.142) confirms, ekale isvara krsna, ära saba bhrtya: only Krishna is God, and all others are His servants. All beings abide by His command, unable to defy it. Every action is carried out under His supervision, as stated in the Brahma-samhita, where He is recognized as the ultimate cause of all causes.

Purport: By offering these obeisances, Arjuna acknowledges that Krishna is worthy of worship by all beings. He pervades everything and is the essence of every soul. Addressing Krishna as mahätmä, Arjuna recognizes His boundless magnanimity. Ananta signifies that nothing exists beyond the reach of the Supreme Lord's influence and energy, while deveśa denotes His supremacy over all demigods. Krishna is the ultimate shelter for the entire universe. Arjuna believes it is only fitting for all perfected beings and mighty demigods to pay homage to Him, as no one surpasses Him in greatness. Arjuna specifically highlights Krishna's superiority over Brahmā because Brahmā is a creation of Krishna. Purport: Chapter 11, Text 48 The concept of divine vision must be clearly understood. Who possesses divine vision? Divine vision is godly in nature. One can only attain divine vision by becoming godly, like a demigod. According to Vedic scriptures, those devoted to Lord Vishnu are considered demigods (viṣṇubhakṭäḥ smṛtā deväḥ). Those who reject Vishnu or only acknowledge the impersonal aspect of Krishna as the Supreme cannot attain divine vision. It is impossible to denounce Krishna and expect to have divine vision. Divine vision is only accessible to those who embody divinity. In essence, individuals with divine vision can perceive reality as Arjuna did.  The Bhagavad-gita reveals the universal form. Although Bhagavad-gita serves as an introductory text on the science of God, it is so profound that it enables one to discern truth from falsehood. Followers of false incarnations may assert seeing the transcendental form of God, but without being a devotee of Krishna, this claim is invalid. One must first become a pure devotee of Krishna to genuinely witness the universal form and share their experience. A devotee of Krishna does not endorse false incarnations or their followers.

Chapter 11, Verse 52:
श्रीभगवान् उवाच
सुदुर्दर्शम् इदं रूपं दृष्टवान् असि यन् मम ।
