मनःषष्ठानीन्द्रियाणि प्रकृतिस्थानि कर्षति ॥ ७ ॥
Translation: The living entities in this world are eternal fragmental parts of Me, struggling with the six senses situated in the material energy.
Purport: Chapter 15, Text 7 This verse clarifies the identity of the living beings. The living entity is eternally a fragmental part of the Supreme Lord. It is not that in the conditioned state, the living being assumes individuality, only to merge with the Supreme Lord upon liberation. The living entity remains eternally fragmented. According to the Vedas, the Supreme Lord manifests and expands Himself in countless forms. The primary expansions are known as vishnu-tattva, and the secondary expansions are the living entities. The personal expansions of the Supreme Lord appear in various forms such as Lord Rama, Nrisimhadeva, and Vishnumurti, while the living entities are eternal servitors. Both the personal expansions of the Lord and the separated expansions of living entities have their unique identities. As fragmental parts of the Supreme Lord, living entities possess qualities of the Lord, including independence. Each living entity has individuality and a minute form of independence. Misuse of this independence leads to conditioned existence, while proper use leads to liberation. In both cases, the living entity is eternally spiritual, like the Supreme Lord. In the liberated state, the entity is free from material bondage and engaged in transcendental service to the Lord, while in the conditioned state, one is dominated by material modes and forgets the loving service of the Lord, leading to struggles in the material world.  All living entities, from humans to animals and even the great controllers like Brahma, Lord Shiva, and Vishnu, are parts of the Supreme Lord and are eternal, not temporary manifestations. The term "karṣati" (struggling) is significant, indicating the conditioned soul's bondage, driven by the mind in this material existence. When the mind is in goodness, actions are virtuous; in passion, troublesome; and in ignorance, one descends to lower species. The conditioned soul is covered by the material body, mind, and senses. Upon liberation, this material covering dissolves, revealing the spiritual body. Scriptures explain that in the spiritual world, the liberated entity regains a spiritual body to directly see, hear, and understand the Supreme Lord. In the spiritual planets, all beings have bodies resembling the Supreme Lord's. At liberation, the living entity receives a spiritual body by the grace of the Supreme Lord.  The term "mamaivāṁśaḥ" (fragmental parts of the Supreme Lord) is profound. The fragmental portion is not a material fragment but an eternal spiritual entity. As stated earlier, the spirit cannot be divided like matter. The fragmental portion of the Supreme Lord present in every individual body regains its spiritual form upon liberation and enjoys association with the Supreme Lord. The living entity, being qualitatively one with the Lord, is like gold pieces being gold itself.

Chapter 15, Verse 14:

This fire symbolizes the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Vedic scriptures, such as the Brhad-aranyaka Upanishad (5.9.1), affirm that the Supreme Lord or Brahman resides in the form of fire within the stomach, facilitating the digestion of various types of food. As such, since He aids in the digestion process, the individual is not autonomous in consuming food. Without the assistance of the Supreme Lord in digestion, eating would be impossible. He generates and processes food, and through His benevolence, we derive pleasure in life. This is also corroborated in the Vedanta-sutra (1.2.27), which states that the Lord is present within sound, the body, the air, and even the stomach as the digestive power. Chapter 15, Verse 15:
सर्वस्य चाहं हृदि संनिविष्टो मत्तः स्मृतिर् ज्ञानम् अपोहनं च ।
वेदैश् च सर्वैर् अहम् एव वेद्यो वेदान्तकृद् वेदिव् एव च अहम् ॥ १५ ॥
Translation: I am seated in everyone’s heart, and from Me come remembrance, knowledge, and forgetfulness. By all the Vedas, I am to be known. Indeed, I am the compiler of Vedanta, and I am the knower of the Vedas.
Purport: Chapter 15, Text 15 The Supreme Lord, as Paramatma, resides in the heart of every being, initiating all activities. Although the living entity forgets the past, they must act as directed by the Supreme Lord, who observes all deeds. Thus, individuals act based on their past actions, guided by knowledge, remembrance, and forgetfulness bestowed by the Lord. He is omnipresent and resides within every heart, overseeing the distribution of karmic results. The Lord is worshiped in various forms, including as the impersonal Brahman, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and the localized Paramatma. He is also revered as the embodiment of the Vedas, guiding individuals towards spiritual realization and the journey back to the Supreme abode.  The Vedas provide insights into the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Lord Krishna, with Vyasadeva compiling the Vedanta-sutra. Vyasadeva's commentary in the Srimad-Bhagavatam elucidates the essence of Vedanta-sutra. The Supreme Lord, in His infinite compassion, sustains and nourishes all beings, witnesses their actions, imparts Vedic knowledge, and manifests as Sri Krishna, the teacher of the Bhagavad-gita. He is the benevolent guide for conditioned souls, offering them opportunities for spiritual growth.  Upon leaving the current body, the living entity forgets past experiences but resumes activities under the Lord's guidance. Despite forgetfulness, the Lord bestows the intelligence to continue unfinished tasks from previous lives. Every being's actions and understanding are influenced by the Supreme Lord residing within their hearts. Those earnestly seeking Vedic knowledge receive divine intelligence from Krishna, as He desires all souls to comprehend Him individually.  The purpose of Vedic literature is to lead individuals towards understanding Krishna and realizing their relationship with Him. Through Vedic rituals, philosophical discussions, and devotional service, the Supreme Lord is attained. The Vedas serve as a roadmap for comprehending Krishna and achieving the ultimate goal of uniting with the Supreme Personality of Godhead. The Vedanta-sutra emphasizes the alignment of these stages, culminating in the realization of the Supreme Lord as the ultimate objective.

Chapter 15, Verse 16:
द्वाव् इमौ पुरुषौ लोके क्षरश् चा अक्षर एव च ।
क्षरः सर्वाणि भूतानि कूटस्थोऽक्षर उच्यते ॥ १६ ॥
Translation: In this world, there are two types of beings – the perishable and the imperishable. All living entities in the material realm are perishable, while in the spiritual realm, they are termed imperishable.
Purport: Chapter 15, Text 16 As previously elucidated, Lord Vyasadeva, in his incarnation, compiled the Vedanta-sutra. Here, the Lord succinctly presents the essence of the Vedanta-sutra. He delineates that the countless living entities can be categorized into two groups – the fallible and the infallible. These living entities are eternal fragments of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. When they are entwined with the material world, they are referred to as jīvabhūta, and the term "kṣaraḥ sarvabhūtāni" denotes their perishable nature. On the other hand, those united with the Supreme Personality of Godhead are considered infallible. This unity does not negate their individuality but signifies a harmonious alignment with the divine purpose of creation. Although in the spiritual realm there is no concept of creation, the source of all emanations is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, as expounded in the Vedanta-sutra.  According to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Lord Krishna, there exist two categories of living entities, a fact substantiated by the Vedas. Living entities entangled in this world, grappling with the mind and senses, possess material bodies that are subject to change. As long as a living entity is bound by conditions, their body undergoes alterations due to interaction with material elements, which themselves are mutable. Consequently, the living entity seems to undergo change. Conversely, in the spiritual domain, the body is devoid of material substance, thus remaining immutable. In the material realm, the living entity experiences six transformations – birth, growth, duration, reproduction, decline, and disappearance – all pertaining to the material body. In the spiritual realm, however, the body remains constant; devoid of aging, birth, or death. There, unity prevails. "Kṣaraḥ sarvabhūtāni": every living entity in contact with matter, starting from the first created being, Brahmä, down to the tiniest ant, undergoes bodily changes, rendering them fallible. In contrast, in the spiritual realm, they eternally exist in unity.

Chapter 15, Verse 18:
यस्मात् क्षरम् अतीतोऽहम् अक्षराद् अपि चोत्तमः ।
अतोऽस्मि लोके वेदे च प्रथितः पुरुषोत्तमः ॥ १८ ॥
Translation: Because I transcend the perishable and the imperishable, and because I am the greatest, I am renowned in both the world and the Vedas as the Supreme Person.
Purport: Chapter 15, Text 18 No one can surpass the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krishna—neither the conditioned soul nor the liberated soul. He is therefore the greatest of all beings. This verse clarifies that both living entities and the Supreme Personality of Godhead are distinct individuals. The difference lies in the fact that the living entities, whether in bondage or liberated, cannot exceed the inconceivable potencies of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. It is incorrect to equate the Supreme Lord and the living entities as equals in all aspects. There is always a distinction of superiority and inferiority between their personalities. The term "uttama" holds great significance, indicating that no one can surpass the Supreme Personality of Godhead.  The word "loke" refers to the "pauruṣa āgama" (the smṛti scriptures). As stated in the Nirukti dictionary, "lokyate vedärtho ’nena": "The meaning of the Vedas is explained by the smṛti scriptures."  The Supreme Lord, in His localized form as Paramatma, is also described within the Vedas themselves. A verse from the Vedas (Chandogya Upanishad 8.12.3) states: "tävad eṣa samprasādo ’smäc charīrät samutthäya paraṁ jyotirūpaṁ sampadya svena rūpeṇäbhiniṣpadyate sa uttamaḥ puruṣaḥ." This means that the Supreme Personality of Godhead manifests His spiritual effulgence, the ultimate illumination, upon leaving the body and entering the impersonal brahmajyoti. This Supreme Personality also assumes a localized form as Paramatma. By appearing as the son of Satyavati and Parasara, He imparts Vedic knowledge as Vyasadeva.

This essential teaching is reiterated throughout the entire Bhagavad Gita. Yet, there are commentators who stubbornly equate the Supreme Absolute Truth with the living entities.  Vedic knowledge, known as śruti, is acquired through aural reception from authorities like Krishna and His representatives. Here, Krishna clearly distinguishes between various aspects, and it is crucial to heed His words. Mere hearing, without understanding from authoritative sources, is insufficient. Speculative academic pursuits are not enough. One must humbly receive the teachings of Bhagavad Gita, which reveal that all living entities are eternally subordinate to the Supreme Personality of Godhead. According to Lord Krishna, only those who grasp this truth truly comprehend the purpose of the Vedas.  The term "bhajati" holds great significance, often associated with serving the Supreme Lord. When one is fully absorbed in Krishna consciousness, engaging in devotional service, it indicates a profound understanding of Vedic knowledge. Ideally, women should receive protection at every stage of life: from their fathers in youth, husbands in adulthood, and grown sons in old age. Unfortunately, modern education has propagated an inflated perception of women's roles, resulting in a distorted view of marriage in society. The moral standing of women has also declined. Purport: Chapter 17, Text 3 Each individual possesses a unique type of faith, influenced by their inherent nature. This faith can be classified as either virtuous, passionate, or ignorant based on the individual's predominant qualities. Every living being is originally a spiritual fragment of the Supreme Lord, as explained in the Fifteenth Chapter. Therefore, at the core, every being transcends the material modes of nature. However, when one forgets their divine connection and becomes entangled in material existence, they construct their identity based on their interactions with the material world. The resulting faith and identity are artificial and material in nature. Despite being influenced by various impressions and conceptions, one's true essence is transcendental and beyond material qualities. To re-establish one's relationship with the Supreme Lord, it is essential to cleanse oneself of material contamination. The path to achieving this purification without fear is through Krishna consciousness. By immersing oneself in Krishna consciousness, one is guaranteed progress towards spiritual perfection. Conversely, if one neglects this path of self-realization, they will be inevitably swayed by the influence of material modes.  The term "śraddhā" or faith holds great significance in this verse. Faith originates from the mode of goodness. One's faith may be directed towards a demigod, a fabricated deity, or a mental construct. However, in the conditioned state of material existence, actions are never completely pure; they are always tainted by a mixture of qualities. Pure goodness is transcendental, allowing one to comprehend the true nature of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. As long as faith remains unperfected, it remains susceptible to contamination by the material modes. The modes of material nature infiltrate the heart, determining the quality of one's faith. Translation: Men in the mode of goodness worship the demigods; those in the mode of passion worship the demons; and those in the mode of ignorance worship ghosts and spirits.
Purport: Chapter 17, Text 4 In this verse, the Supreme Personality of Godhead describes different types of worshipers based on their external activities. According to scriptural injunctions, only the Supreme Personality of Godhead is worthy of worship. However, those who are not well-versed in or faithful to the scriptural injunctions worship various objects based on their specific situations influenced by the modes of material nature. Those situated in goodness generally worship the demigods, such as Brahmā, Shiva, Indra, Candra, and the sun-god, for specific purposes. On the other hand, those in the mode of passion may worship demons or powerful individuals as their gods. And those in the mode of ignorance worship ghosts, spirits, or even deceased persons. These various forms of worship do not constitute true worship of God. True God worship is reserved for those who are situated in pure goodness, transcending the material modes of nature.  The Srimad-Bhagavatam (4.3.23) states, sattvaṁ viśuddhaṁ väsudevaśabditam: “When a person is completely purified and situated in pure goodness, they worship Vāsudeva, the Supreme Personality of Godhead.” This indicates that individuals who are free from the influence of material modes and are transcendentally situated can truly worship the Supreme Lord.  Impersonalists, who are considered to be in the mode of goodness, worship five types of demigods. They worship the impersonal form of Vishnu in the material world, known as philosophized Vishnu. While Vishnu is the expansion of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, impersonalists, due to their lack of belief in the personal aspect of God, view the Vishnu form as merely another aspect of the impersonal Brahman. Similarly, they consider Lord Brahmā as the impersonal form in the mode of passion. Although they may describe five worshipable gods, they ultimately reject all objects of worship as they believe the ultimate truth to be the impersonal Brahman.  In conclusion, the different qualities influenced by the material modes of nature can be purified through association with individuals who are of a transcendental nature.

ॐ तत् सद् इति निर्देशो ब्रह्मणस् त्रिविधः स्मृतः । ब्राह्मणास् तेन वेदाश् च यज्ञाश् च विहिताः पुरा ॥
Translation: From the beginning of creation, the three words om tat sat were used to indicate the Supreme Absolute Truth. Brahmanas chanted these three symbolic representations while reciting the Vedas and performing sacrifices to please the Supreme Lord.
Purport: Penance, sacrifice, charity, and dietary habits are classified into three categories based on the modes of goodness, passion, and ignorance. Regardless of their classification, all these activities are conditioned and influenced by the material modes of nature. However, when performed with the aim of pleasing the Supreme—om tat sat, the Supreme Personality of Godhead—they become a means for spiritual progress. The scriptures guide us towards this ultimate purpose. The three words om tat sat specifically represent the Absolute Truth, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, as emphasized in Vedic hymns where the word om is consistently present.  One who acts without adhering to scriptural regulations will not attain the Absolute Truth. Such actions may yield temporary results, but they will not lead to the ultimate goal of life. It is essential that acts of charity, sacrifice, and penance be performed in the mode of goodness. When executed in the modes of passion or ignorance, these activities are of inferior quality. The utterance of the three words om tat sat is coupled with the holy name of the Supreme Lord, such as oṁ tad viṣṇoḥ. Whenever a Vedic hymn or the holy name of the Supreme Lord is recited, om is included, as per Vedic tradition. These three words are derived from Vedic hymns. Om ity etad brahmaṇo nediṣṭhaṁ näma (Rig Veda) signifies the first goal, followed by tat tvam asi (Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7) representing the second goal, and sad eva saumya (Chandogya Upanishad 6.2.1) indicating the third goal. Together, they form om tat sat. When Brahmā, the first created being, performed sacrifices in ancient times, he used these three words to denote the Supreme Personality of Godhead. This tradition has been faithfully followed through the disciplic succession. Therefore, this hymn holds profound significance. The Bhagavad-gita advises us to engage in actions dedicated to om tat sat, or the Supreme Personality of Godhead. By performing penance, charity, and sacrifice with these three words, one acts in Krishna consciousness. Krishna consciousness is a systematic practice of spiritual activities that facilitate one's journey back to the spiritual realm. Acting in this transcendental manner incurs no loss of spiritual energy.``` Chapter 17, Text 23 ```

Purport: Chapter 17, Text 28 Engaging in sacrifices, charity, or penance devoid of a transcendental purpose is fruitless. This verse emphasizes the abominable nature of such endeavors. Therefore, the optimal approach is to wholeheartedly embrace Krishna consciousness from the outset, under the tutelage of an authentic spiritual master. Translation: Arjuna said: O mighty-armed one, I wish to understand the essence of renunciation and the renounced order of life, O Hrishikesha, the conqueror of the Kesi demon.
Purport: The Bhagavad-gita concludes in seventeen chapters, with the Eighteenth Chapter serving as a supplementary summary of the preceding topics. Throughout the Gita, Lord Krishna emphasizes that devotion to the Supreme Personality of Godhead is life's ultimate goal. This confidential knowledge is reiterated in the Eighteenth Chapter as the most sublime path. The initial six chapters focus on the importance of devotional service, highlighting that those who constantly remember the Lord are the foremost yogis. Subsequent chapters delve into the nature and activities of pure devotional service. The final six chapters discuss knowledge, renunciation, material and transcendental activities, and the necessity of performing all actions in conjunction with the Supreme Lord, represented by the words om tat sat, signifying Vishnu. This section reaffirms that devotional service is life's ultimate purpose, supported by the teachings of previous acharyas and the Vedanta-sutra. Despite claims by some impersonalists, the Vedanta-sutra is meant for understanding devotional service, as the Lord Himself authored it. This is clarified in the Fifteenth Chapter. Devotional service is the essence of every scripture and Veda, as elucidated in the Bhagavad-gita.  Similar to the Second Chapter's overview, the Eighteenth Chapter provides a concise summary of the entire discourse. It underscores renunciation and transcending the three material modes of nature as life's objectives. Arjuna seeks clarification on two key themes of the Bhagavad-gita: renunciation (tyaga) and the renounced order of life (sannyasa), reflecting his desire to comprehend their significance.  The choice of two names to address the Supreme Lord in this verse—Hrishikesha and Kesi-nisudana—is noteworthy. Hrishikesha, as Krishna, the master of all senses, guides us towards mental peace. Arjuna implores Him to present a comprehensive summary that will help him maintain equanimity. Despite his faith, doubts linger, likened here to demons. Thus, Arjuna invokes Krishna as Kesi-nisudana, the vanquisher of the formidable demon Kesi, symbolizing his plea for Krishna to dispel the demon of doubt.``` Chapter 18, Text 1 ```

Chapter 18, Verse 46:

Translation: By worshipping the Lord, from whom the activity of all living beings originates and by whom all this is pervaded, a person attains perfection through performing their own duties.
Purport: Chapter 18, Text 46 As mentioned in the Fifteenth Chapter, all living beings are fragments of the Supreme Lord. Therefore, the Supreme Lord is the origin of all living entities, as confirmed in the Vedanta-sutra—janmādy asya yataḥ [SB 1.1.1]. The Supreme Lord is the source of life for every living entity. Additionally, as explained in the Seventh Chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, the Supreme Lord pervades everything through His two energies: the external and internal energies. Hence, one should worship the Supreme Lord along with His energies. Vaishnava devotees generally worship the Supreme Lord through His internal energy, as the external energy is a distorted reflection of the internal energy. Although the external energy serves as a background, the Supreme Lord, through His expansion as Paramatma, is omnipresent. He is the Supersoul of all demigods, humans, and animals, existing everywhere. Therefore, recognizing oneself as a part and parcel of the Supreme Lord, one is duty-bound to offer service to the Supreme. Everyone should engage in devotional service to the Lord with full Krishna consciousness, as recommended in this verse.  One should perceive their occupation as a service to Hrisikesa, the master of the senses. By the results of one's work, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Sri Krishna, should be worshipped. If one consistently maintains this mindset, immersed in Krishna consciousness, they will gain complete awareness by the grace of the Lord. This is the perfection of life. The Lord declares in the Bhagavad Gita (12.7), teṣām ahaṁ samuddhartā, signifying that the Supreme Lord Himself personally uplifts such a devoted soul. This is the pinnacle of spiritual attainment. Regardless of one's profession, by dedicating oneself in the service of the Supreme Lord, one can attain the ultimate perfection.

Chapter 18, Verse 47:
श्रेयान् स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात् स्व् अनुष्ठितात् ।
स्वभाव नियतं कर्म कुर्वन् नाप्नोति किल्बिषम् ॥ ४७ ॥
Translation: It is better to engage in one’s own occupation, even if imperfectly performed, than to adopt another’s occupation and execute it perfectly. Actions performed in accordance with one’s innate nature are not tainted by sin.
Purport: Chapter 18, Text 47 In Bhagavad-gita, one's occupational duty is prescribed based on one's inherent nature. As discussed in previous verses, the duties of a brahmana, kshatriya, vaisya, and sudra are determined by their respective qualities. It is important not to imitate the duties of others. A person naturally inclined towards tasks typical of sudras should not falsely claim to be a brahmana, even if born into a brahmana family. Each individual should work according to their inherent nature; no task is degrading when performed in devotion to the Supreme Lord. While the duties of a brahmana are rooted in goodness, one not naturally inclined towards goodness should not imitate these duties. A kshatriya may have to resort to violence and deceit in his duties, but he should not abandon his prescribed duties to take up those of a brahmana.  One should act to please the Supreme Lord. For instance, Arjuna, a kshatriya, hesitated to engage in battle. However, if such fighting is carried out for the sake of Krishna, there is no risk of degradation. In the realm of commerce, a merchant may need to resort to falsehoods to turn a profit. Without profit, a merchant cannot survive. Thus, when a merchant claims, "I am not profiting from you," it should be understood as a necessary falsehood. Yet, the merchant should not feel compelled to switch professions to that of a brahmana due to the inherent deceit in his trade. Regardless of one's varna—be it kshatriya, vaisya, or sudra—if one serves the Supreme Personality of Godhead through their work, it is spiritually beneficial. Even brahmanas, who conduct sacrificial rituals, may at times have to sacrifice animals. Similarly, if a kshatriya kills an enemy in the line of duty, it is not sinful. The Third Chapter elaborates on these concepts, emphasizing that all actions should be dedicated to Yajna or Vishnu, the Supreme Lord. Actions driven by personal desires lead to bondage. Therefore, one should engage in work in alignment with their inherent nature and dedicate it solely to serving the supreme cause of the Supreme Lord.

Chapter 18, Verse 48:
सहजं कर्म कौन्तेय स दोषम् अपि न त्यजेत् ।
सर्वारम्भा हि दोषेण धूमेनाग्निर् इवावृताः ॥ ४८ ॥
Translation: Every endeavor is covered by some fault, just as fire is covered by smoke. Therefore, O son of Kunti, one should not abandon work that aligns with their nature, even if it is flawed.
Purport: Chapter 18, Text 48 In the conditioned material world, all actions are influenced by the modes of nature. For example, even a brahmana must perform sacrificial rituals that involve animal sacrifice. Similarly, a kshatriya, no matter how virtuous, must engage in battle when necessary. A merchant, despite his piety, may need to resort to unethical practices to sustain his business. Likewise, a sudra must obey his master's orders, even if they are unjust. These imperfections are inherent in worldly duties and cannot be avoided. Despite these shortcomings, one should faithfully carry out their prescribed duties, as they are an expression of their inherent nature.  An apt analogy is presented here: although fire is inherently pure, it is often accompanied by smoke. Yet, the presence of smoke does not tarnish the purity of fire. Similarly, if one were to switch from a kshatriya's duties to those of a brahmana, they would find that even the occupation of a brahmana entails unpleasant responsibilities. This illustrates that in the material realm, no one is entirely free from the influence of material nature. The analogy of fire and smoke effectively conveys this concept. Just as one may endure discomfort from smoke while benefiting from the warmth of a fire in winter, one should not abandon their natural occupation due to its challenges. Instead, one should steadfastly engage in their occupational duties with a consciousness of serving the Supreme Lord. This dedication to Krishna consciousness is the path to perfection. By performing one's occupational duties for the satisfaction of the Supreme Lord, all imperfections associated with that occupation are purified. When work is performed in connection with devotional service, one attains self-realization and perceives the true self within.

With this mindset, one finds contentment in dedicating all activities to the Supreme, devoid of attachment to material pleasures. Such an individual derives ultimate joy from serving the Lord and transcends mundane pleasures. A practitioner of Krishna consciousness naturally achieves the state of being free from the karmic reactions of past deeds, without needing to formally embrace the renounced order of life. Chapter 18, Verse 54:
ब्रह्मभूतः प्रसन्नात्मा न शोचति न काङ्क्षति ।
समः सर्वेषु भूतेषु मद् भक्तिं लभते पराम् ॥ ५४ ॥
Translation: One who is established in the state of transcendental realization becomes blissful, free from sorrow and desire. Such a person sees all living beings equally and attains the highest devotion unto Me.
Purport: Chapter 18, Text 54 For the impersonalist, reaching the stage of oneness with the Absolute, known as brahma-bhūta, is the ultimate goal. However, for the personalist or pure devotee, there is a further step to be taken, which is engaging in pure devotional service. A pure devotee who serves the Supreme Lord is already liberated, being in a state of brahma-bhūta, united with the Absolute. Without being united with the Supreme, one cannot truly serve Him. Although in the absolute sense there is no distinction between the served and the servitor, in a higher spiritual sense, the distinction is still present.  In the materialistic way of life, pursuing sense gratification leads to suffering. In contrast, in the realm of the absolute, engaging in pure devotional service brings about joy and contentment. A devotee in Krishna consciousness has no reason to lament or crave anything, as they are fulfilled in their service to God. Just as a river is purified of impurities, the pure devotee, whose thoughts are solely focused on Krishna, remains in a perpetual state of joy. Such a devotee does not grieve over material losses or aspire for material gains, for they are content in serving the Lord. Understanding that all living beings are eternal servants of the Supreme Lord, a devotee does not seek material pleasures or distinctions of high and low in the material world, as such designations are temporary. To a devotee, both stone and gold hold equal value. This state of brahma-bhūta is easily attained by a pure devotee.  In this elevated state, the desire to merge with the Supreme Brahman and lose one's individuality becomes abhorrent, heavenly pleasures seem illusory, and the senses lose their power to agitate. Just as a serpent with broken teeth poses no threat, the senses, when under control, no longer cause fear. While the materialistic person finds the world miserable, for a devotee, the entire world is as blissful as Vaikuntha, the spiritual abode. The most exalted personalities in the material universe are insignificant to a devotee, akin to ants. This sublime stage is attainable through the grace of Lord Caitanya, who propagated pure devotional service in this age.

Chapter 18, Verse 55:
भक्त्या माम् अभि जानाति यावान् यश् चास्मि तत्त्वतः ।
ततो मां तत्त्वतो ज्ञात्वा विशते तद् अनन्तरम् ॥ ५५ ॥
Translation: By devotion one can truly understand Me as I am, the Supreme Lord. When one comprehends Me in truth through such devotion, they enter into My abode thereafter.
Purport: Chapter 18, Text 55 The Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krishna, and His expansions cannot be grasped through intellectual speculation or by non-devotees. To truly understand the Supreme Lord, one must engage in pure devotional service under the guidance of a pure devotee. Otherwise, the essence of the Supreme Lord will remain concealed. As mentioned in the Bhagavad-gita (7.25), nähaṁ prakāśaḥ sarvasya: He does not reveal Himself to everyone. God cannot be comprehended merely through scholarly knowledge or mental analysis. Only those sincerely devoted to Krishna consciousness and engaged in devotional service can truly understand the nature of the Supreme Lord. Academic achievements are not beneficial in this pursuit.  One who is well-versed in the science of Krishna becomes qualified to enter the spiritual realm, the abode of Krishna. Attaining the state of Brahman does not entail losing one's individual identity. Devotional service persists, and as long as there is devotion, there exists God, the devotee, and the process of devotional service. This knowledge remains eternally, even after liberation. Liberation involves transcending material existence; in spiritual life, individuality and distinction persist, but in a state of pure Krishna consciousness. It is important not to misinterpret the term viśate, "enters into Me," to support the monistic idea of merging into the impersonal Brahman. Viśate signifies entering the abode of the Supreme Lord in one's individual form to engage in His association and render service unto Him. Just as a green bird enters a green tree not to merge with the tree but to enjoy its fruits. Impersonalists often cite the example of a river merging into the ocean. While this may bring joy to an impersonalist, a personalist maintains their individuality within the ocean, like aquatic beings residing in its depths. Superficial acquaintance with the ocean is insufficient; one must have a comprehensive understanding of the aquatic life within its depths.  Due to their pure devotional service, a devotee can genuinely comprehend the transcendental qualities and opulence of the Supreme Lord. As elucidated in the Eleventh Chapter, true understanding is attainable only through devotional service. This principle is reaffirmed here; through devotion, one can grasp the Supreme Personality of Godhead and enter His divine realm. Once the stage of brahma-bhūta, free from material conceptions, is reached, devotional service commences by hearing about the Lord. Hearing about the Supreme Lord leads to the development of the brahma-bhūta stage, resulting in the disappearance of material contamination such as greed and lust for sense enjoyment. As desires and attachments diminish from the heart of a devotee, their inclination towards serving the Lord intensifies, leading to freedom from material contamination. In this state, one can comprehend the Supreme Lord, as also stated in the Srimad-Bhagavatam. Even after liberation, the process of bhakti, or transcendental service, continues. The Vedanta-sutra (4.1.12) confirms this: äpräyaṇät taträpi hi dṛṣṭam. Post-liberation, the journey of devotional service endures. In the Srimad-Bhagavatam, true liberation through devotion is defined as reinstating the living entity in their original identity, their inherent position. This position is already explained: every living being is an integral fragment of the Supreme Lord and is meant to serve Him. Following liberation, this service never ceases. Real liberation involves dispelling misconceptions about life.

तत्प्रसादात् परां शान्तिं स्थानं प्राप्स्यसि शाश्वतम् ॥ ६२ ॥
Translation: O scion of Bharata, surrender unto Him completely. Through His grace, you will attain supreme peace and the eternal abode.
Purport: Chapter 18, Text 62 A living being should surrender to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who resides in everyone's heart. Translation: Wherever there is Lord Krishna, the master of all mystics, and wherever there is Arjuna, the supreme archer, there will also certainly be opulence, victory, extraordinary power, and morality. That is my opinion.
Purport: Chapter 18, Text 78 The Bhagavad-gita began with an inquiry from Dhritarashtra, who hoped for his sons' victory, supported by great warriors like Bhishma, Drona, and Karna. He anticipated success on his side. However, after describing the battlefield scene, Sanjaya informed the King, “You anticipate victory, but in my view, where Krishna and Arjuna are present, all good fortune will prevail.” He clearly indicated that victory was not to be expected on Dhritarashtra's side. Victory was assured for Arjuna's side because of Krishna's presence. Krishna's role as Arjuna's charioteer showcased another aspect of His opulence. Krishna possesses all opulences, including renunciation. There are numerous instances of His renunciation, as Krishna is the master of renunciation.  The actual battle was between Duryodhana and Yudhisthira, with Arjuna fighting on behalf of his elder brother, Yudhisthira. With Krishna and Arjuna on Yudhisthira's side, victory for him was certain. The battle determined the ruler of the world, and Sanjaya predicted the transfer of power to Yudhisthira. It was also foretold that Yudhisthira, after gaining victory, would flourish even more due to his righteousness, piety, and strict adherence to moral principles. He never spoke a falsehood throughout his life.  Some less intelligent individuals perceive the Bhagavad-gita as a conversation between friends on a battlefield, but such a book cannot be considered scripture. Some may object that Krishna incited Arjuna to fight, deeming it immoral, but the reality is clarified: the Bhagavad-gita imparts supreme moral instruction. The ultimate moral instruction is revealed in the Ninth Chapter, in the thirty-fourth verse: "Always think of Me and become My devotee." One must become a devotee of Krishna, and the essence of all religion is to surrender unto Him. The teachings of the Bhagavad-gita embody the supreme path of religion and morality. While other paths may purify and lead to this ultimate path, the Gita's final instruction is the pinnacle of morality and religion: surrender to Krishna. This is the conclusion of the Eighteenth Chapter.  From the Bhagavad-gita, we learn that realizing oneself through philosophical contemplation and meditation is one approach, but complete surrender to Krishna is the highest perfection. This is the essence of the Gita's teachings. The path of following regulatory principles based on societal orders and various religious practices may be a confidential path of knowledge. Yet, even though the rituals of religion are confidential, meditation and pursuit of knowledge are even more confidential. Surrendering to Krishna in devotional service with full Krishna consciousness is the most confidential instruction. This is the essence of the Eighteenth Chapter.  Another aspect of the Bhagavad-gita is that the ultimate truth is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krishna. The Absolute Truth is realized in three aspects—impersonal Brahman, localized Paramatma, and ultimately the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krishna. Perfect knowledge of the Absolute Truth means perfect knowledge of Krishna. Understanding Krishna encompasses all realms of knowledge. Krishna is transcendental, eternally situated in His internal potency. Living entities are manifestations of His energy, divided into eternally conditioned and eternally liberated beings. They are innumerable and are considered fundamental parts of Krishna. Material energy is divided into twenty-four categories. Creation is governed by eternal time and is manifested and dissolved by external energy. The cosmic creation repeatedly becomes visible and invisible.  The Bhagavad-gita discusses five principal topics: the Supreme Personality of Godhead, material nature, living entities, eternal time, and various activities. All are dependent on the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krishna. All conceptions of the Absolute Truth—impersonal Brahman, localized Paramatma, and other transcendental notions—fall within the realm of understanding the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Though on the surface, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, living entities, material nature, and time may seem distinct, nothing is separate from the Supreme. Yet, the Supreme always remains distinct from everything else. Lord Caitanya's philosophy embodies the concept of inconceivable oneness and difference, representing perfect knowledge of the Absolute Truth.  The living entity in their original state is pure spirit, akin to an atomic particle of the Supreme Spirit. In this analogy, Lord Krishna is likened to the sun, and living entities to sunshine. As marginal energy of Krishna, living entities have the tendency to connect with either material or spiritual energy. Positioned between the two energies of the Lord, they possess a particle of independence due to their belonging to the superior energy of the Lord. By wisely exercising this independence, they come under Krishna's direct guidance and attain their natural state within the pleasure-giving potency.  Thus concludes the Bhaktivedanta Purports to the Eighteenth Chapter of the Srimad Bhagavad-gita, focusing on its Conclusion—the Perfection of Renunciation.
